title: Printer and incremental-eval fixes surfaced by the modules stack
body:
Three fixes to code that is on `dev` today, surfaced while building the modules stack (#2496). They were originally committed inside parts 2 and 4 of that stack; they are lifted out here so they can land on their own and the stack can sit on top. Each commit carries a test that fails without its fix on `dev`.

## Incremental eval: a binding's ascription is part of its provenance

Editing a binding's ascription in place left its dependents reusing values computed under the old type: the reuse provenance recorded only *that* the binding went through an ascription, not which type. An ascription changes the bound value (a cast; further up the stack, sealing a module), so the type now travels in the provenance as `Ascribed(Typ.t)`, compared with `Typ.fast_equal`.

Pinned by retyping `let x : Int = 1 in x` as `let x : Bool = 1 in x` in place: fresh evaluation reports the inconsistency, the stale reuse handed back the old `1`. (Retyping `Int` as `?`, or relabeling a tuple ascription, is *not* observable on `dev` — casts are stripped by the comparison and a projection's index comes from the new static type — which is why the test uses the inconsistent form.)

## Keep a printed `:` apart from a following operator

`:` is one of `Token.ascii_operator_chars`, and `Token.is_potential_operator` matches any run of them, so a `:` printed flush against a leading-plus sum lexed as the single operator token `:+`, which is no form at all; Menhir has its own lexer and split them, so the two parsers disagreed. `should_add_space` already kept `:` apart from `$` and `!`, as a list of two characters; it now asks `Token.begins_with_potential_operator` for the property they share (`$` stays listed: it is a name character). Pinned at the `should_add_space` level; reaching a `:` with an unparenthesized sum in a real program takes a signature member, so that form stays in the stack.

## Stop re-parenthesizing the content of a Parens type

Printing a parenthesized min-precedence type was not idempotent: `type T = + Adid` came out as `type T = (+ Adid)` and each further trip added a layer. `parenthesize_typ`'s `Parens` case ran its content through `paren_typ_at(Precedence.min)`, which wraps exactly the types whose precedence *is* min — a bare sum, a multihole, and up the stack a Sig — on every pass. The wrapper being emitted is already the protection, so the content needs none; `already_paren` is still passed down. Pinned by printing `type T = + Adid in ?` twice.

The last two were found by the Slow `Menhir and maketerm are equivalent` fuzz property on the stack's CI; the non-idempotence is why its counterexamples could not be pinned with the round-trip helpers.

title: Hypothetical integration: Modules II parts 1-2 + hazel-html + livelits, with the HTML substrate as opt-in modules
body:
**Draft, for inspection only. Not meant to merge:** this branch is a hypothetical integration built to answer one question, and it contains merges of four other open PRs.

## What this is

dev + Modules II parts 1 and 2 (#2493 signature types and module values, #2494 width subtyping) + the HTML substrate (#2115) + the livelit stack (#2411 user-defined livelits, #2488 expansion typing, #2489 error dedup), with two follow-ups on top:

1. **The livelit code ported to real modules.** A livelit definition's `Model`, `Action` and `Expansion` are read as manifest type members of the signature `ModuleHelpers.module_sig_type` synthesizes; the livelit branch's own `collect_type_exports` and its labeled-tuple type-export injection in the `Let` case are gone. At runtime `LivelitProj.record_field` reads `ModVal` bindings by name from the evaluated `Module`. Two small changes; they are what user-livelits will need once Modules II lands.

2. **Prototype: the HTML substrate as opt-in modules.** hazel-html's ~120 global constructor names and seven global type aliases (`HTML`, `Attr`, `Cmd`, `Sub`, `App`, `KeyEvent`, `MouseEvent`) become four builtin module values `Html`, `Attr`, `Cmd`, `Sub` (`BuiltinsADT.HtmlModules`). Members are the constructors as snake_case functions, types are `Html.T`, `Attr.T`, `Cmd.T`, `Sub.T`, `Html.App`, `Attr.KeyEvent`, `Attr.MouseEvent`:

   ```
   Html.div([Attr.style([("color", "red")])], [Html.text("hi")])
   let view = fun m : Model -> ... : Html.T
   ```

   Constructor names are unchanged, so the renderer and MVU runtime are untouched. Motivation: a user module named `App` lost its type members to the builtin alias `App`, because `Typ.path_sig` tries type aliases before variables. With the modules it works.

## Performance

The naive module version was 3-4x slower than the global one. Four fixes, each at its source, bring it within ~15%:

- `sig_project_value` / `sig_project_type` substitute into the requested member only, instead of closing the whole signature to read one member.
- For a builtin module, a member's type keeps `T` as the path `Html.T` (`Typ.sig_project_value_along`), and `meet` accepts two equal paths without normalizing either.
- `normalize_ctr_type` keeps a builtin-module path compact, as it kept `Var("HTML")`.
- A builtin module's member elaborates directly to the constructor it denotes; otherwise the evaluator substitutes the whole module value into every closure that names `Html` (80 copies in one program's output).

| nutrient-rotation.hz | baseline (global names) | naive modules | final |
|---|---|---|---|
| `cli analyze` | 2.3 s | 8.1 s | 2.8 s |
| `cli run` | 2.75 s | 11 s | 3.1 s |
| printed output | 181 KB | 1.3 MB | 181 KB |

## Verified

- All 14 MVU and livelit example programs type-check in the qualified form (ported, along with the docs, `Test_MVU` and `Test_UserLivelits`).
- 1370 tests across MVU, UserLivelits, Modules, Statics, Evaluator, Equality, Elaboration, Menhir, FastParse, Unicode pass. The three tests pinning the compact `Var("HTML")` annotation are removed: that fast path applied only to global aliases.
- In the browser: the MVU counter renders and counts on clicks, the slider livelit renders and updates with its expansion type check passing, and the Modules slide's item 9 (module named `App`) no longer errors.

## Known gaps

- The projectors doc slide reports type errors around the builtin `^^sliderf` and `^^text` livelits; those lines were not touched here and the errors predate the prototype (they belong to the merge, not the modules design).
- Bare `Int(x)` still type-checks because JSON's constructor `Int` is still global, so a missed port is silent. Same collision in miniature.
- Path-preserving projection and constructor elaboration apply only to builtin modules (variables with `Id.invalid`); user modules keep Modules II's manifest substitution.

title: Blackboard MVP (M0+M1): core-logic kernel, a Bb editor sort, and documentation slides
body:
## Blackboard MVP: a proof assistant's core logic inside Hazel

An experiment: an MVP of **Blackboard**, a proposed "clean slate" proof assistant whose core logic has a type of all types, an internal typing relation, and no lambda. Two milestones are here.

**Try it:** Documentation → Blackboard → 0. Overview, at https://hazel.org/build/blackboard-mvp/

### M0 — the kernel

`src/language/blackboard/` — `BbTerm` (terms `x`, `t : T`, `type`, `(x : T₁) → T₂`, `t₁ t₂`; signatures, blocks, documents; substitution, α-equivalence, printing), `BbCheck` (the decidable fragment the paper calls `tychk`, without conversion), `BbError` (errors as data, located by signature entry), `BbParse` (the paper's concrete syntax, for fixtures). No dependency on tiles or the web layer.

Tests use the paper's own signatures as fixtures. The checker finds the paper's two slips in `cong-ap` (a name bound twice; a family used as a type) and the two in `int-elim` (missing arguments), and records where the paper's examples lean on equations the fragment cannot use.

### M1 — the editor sort

`Bb(BbSort.Term)` is a nested sort, following the ALFA derivation sub-language in `src/language/derivation/`: forms in `Form.re`, molding, `MakeTerm`, a pretty printer, and `blackboard ... end` to embed a document in an expression. `BbGrammar` / `BbTermBase` / `Bb` carry editor terms and read them back as kernel terms, entries, blocks and documents. Statics and the cursor inspector are M2, so an embedded document is inert for now.

Two decisions worth review:

- **The colon binds tighter than the arrow**, so `(x : A) -> x : B` reads as the paper writes it. In a signature entry the colon is a declaration instead, and is loosest; `Bb.rotate_entry` rotates the spine back, so `f : A -> B` declares `f` of type `A -> B`.
- **`Insert.effective_sort` no longer falls back to the enclosing sort inside Blackboard.** It is a closed sub-language, so a token with no Blackboard expansion stays a monotile. Without this, typing `type` inside a block expands into Hazel's `type _ = _ in`. This is the one change outside Blackboard-specific code that affects existing behaviour; it is guarded by `Sort.is_bb`.

### Documentation slides

Five slides under **Documentation → Blackboard**: Overview, Terms, Signatures, Checking, Metatheory. They load through the typing parser, since menhir has no Blackboard productions (as with the derivation sub-language). Both corpus ratchets ledger them with a reason, and `DocSlides.ReparseBackuptext` pins their text fidelity.

The `Bb` sort also needed a colour: with no entry in the token palette, Blackboard code rendered in the fallback colour and was effectively unreadable. Measured against the code background, it is now 6.49:1, where `Exp` is 5.33, `Typ` 4.19, `Drv` 3.73 and `Pat` 3.32.

`Test_BlackboardSlides` requires every shipped slide to read back as a document. It earns its place: three separate content bugs made part of a slide silently become a hole while the text still round-tripped. Hazel names cannot contain a hyphen, so `falsity-eq` was three tokens; `false` is a boolean literal, not a name; and `witness : a : A` associates as `(witness : a) : A`. Slides therefore use underscores where the paper uses hyphens, noted on the Terms slide. Behind two of them was a reader bug: a signature of three or more entries nests to the right, and only the top level was being read.

### `mech/`

The Rocq mechanization of the core logic (`Blackboard.v`, Rocq 9.2, no axioms) and its compile log, as the reference semantics: consistency of the bare logic, conservativity of construction blocks, and a five-point model. It covers both the rules as first printed and the author's corrected `arrow+`. Not part of the build.

### Testing

```
dune build test/idb_stub.js test/haz3ltest.bc.js --profile dev
bash test/run_node.sh test Blackboard
```

23 Blackboard tests pass. The full suite was run: the only failure was `Evaluator and stepper are consistent`, which is the known QCheck flake — it passed on three consecutive re-runs.

### Not in this PR

Implicit arguments, user-defined syntax, tactics, equational rewriting, Blackboard statics in the editor, and menhir support.

title: test: turn the stats-only statics surveys into disabled property tests
body:
The three `Slow` cases in Test_Statics_Properties.re counted how often a property held and printed a distribution. None of them asserted, so a regression in any of the three was invisible.

Each is now a real QCheck property wrapped in the `Alcotest.skip()` shape already used for `Preservation of types (disabled)` in Test_Evaluator_Properties.re, so the code stays compiled and re-enabling is a one-line edit.

All three properties are false. `Elaboration preserves type` was the surprise: its survey reported 1000/1000, but the survey seeded `Random.State.make([|0xC0FFEE|])`, and QCHECK_SEED=1 fails. The other two shrink to `(()) +. - []` (parent Float, fresh Int) and `{}`.

Dropped with the survey loops: two hand-rolled shrinkers that duplicated each other and QCheck's own shrinking, the outcome variants the loops tallied, and `show_exp`, which was a verbatim copy of QCheck_Util.show_core_exp.

`show_core_typ` moves out of `arb_typ` to a top-level let beside `show_core_exp`. Typ.show prints the whole IdTagged record, which rendered a type disagreement as two ten-line blobs rather than Float vs Int.

title: Delete Util.Either: result where it means success-or-failure, Core.Either where it means a partition
body:
Follows up [a review comment on #2439](https://github.com/hazelgrove/hazel/pull/2439#discussion_r3830911397) asking whether `Either` isn't already built into OCaml. It is — twice — and ours was redundant, but the call sites turned out to want two different things.

## Why ours had to go

`src/util/Either.re` was four lines: `type t('l, 'r) = L('l) | R('r)` with `show`/`sexp`/`yojson`. Those derivations were dead — no `[@deriving]` type in the tree embeds an `Either.t`, which was the one plausible reason to keep our own over Core's.

It also **shadowed Core's**. Every library that uses it has `-open Core` in its dune, and every file that uses it also does `open Util`, which lands second, so `Core.Either` was unreachable without qualifying it.

## What the call sites actually wanted

Of 24 references, 20 were success-or-failure wearing the wrong constructors:

| Site | Was | Now |
|---|---|---|
| `Operators.re` (13) | `Either.t(Atom.t, bad_literal)` | `result(Atom.t, bad_literal)` |
| `Atom.re` (3) | `Either.t('b, InvalidOperationError.t)` | `result('b, InvalidOperationError.t)` |
| `Transition.re` (4) | `Either.L(return_value)` / `Either.R(error)` | `Ok` / `Error` |
| `MatchedTyp.args` | `Either.t('a, int)` | `result(list(Typ.t), int)` |

`result` puts the error direction in the type instead of leaving it to a convention about which side `R` is, and `MatchedTyp.args` gets a concrete ok type rather than the `'a` it was carrying.

Only **`Aba.split`** and its single caller **`Segment.split_by_matching`** genuinely partition — each element goes to the A-stream or the B-stream, and neither side is an error. Those take `Core.Either`'s `First`/`Second`.

`src/util/Either.{re,rei}` and `Util`'s re-export of it are deleted. Removing the module made `open Util` dead in `MatchedTyp.re`, so that went too.

`BuiltinsADT`'s `Either` is the Hazel-language type alias — a different thing entirely — and is untouched.

## Verification

- `dune build @check --profile release` clean (no warnings)
- `make dev` clean
- `make test-quick`: 3556 tests pass

No behavior change is intended: this is a type-and-constructor rename, plus one type made less general.

title: CI: weekly Extended Tests, and test reports on the test job
body:
Two changes to how CI reports, and how far it searches.

**Weekly Extended Tests.** New `.github/workflows/extended-tests.yml` runs Sundays against `dev` (plus `workflow_dispatch` with `factor`/`seed`), calling a new `make ci-extended`: the whole suite with `QCHECK_LONG=1`, so every QCheck `~count` is multiplied by `QCHECK_LONG_FACTOR`. Per-push CI runs each property once, so a property that fails on one seed in a few hundred never surfaces. The job pins its seed and writes the reproducing `QCHECK_*` command to its summary. It gates nothing — a red run is a bug report.

The default factor is 100 because `Slow` turns out not to mean `QCheck`: 237 tests carry the tag, only 12 are properties, so the factor scales a minority of the run and the rest is a fixed floor. That puts it at roughly 3.7 h on CI against GitHub's 6 h cap. Correct it from the first real run.

**Test reports move off the Deploy job.** `checks.yml` passed `use-actions-summary: false` to `dorny/test-reporter@v1`, but that input doesn't exist until v2 — it was ignored and a check run was always created. GitHub picks which of a commit's check suites a check run joins, and it picked Deploy's, so test results rendered under `Deploy branch preview` and a red suite made the deploy look broken. On `@v3` the default writes the report to the running job's summary and creates no check run, which is the only placement we control.

The table now appears on the `Fast checks` / `Full tests` summaries; the `Test Report` and `Quick Test Report` rows and their inline annotations go away. Nothing is lost as a gate — those jobs already fail on a red suite, and the report checks could never have been required, since fork PRs skip them. Consequently `checks: write` is gone, and `publish-reports` (which now only gated Codecov) is renamed `upload-coverage`, with fork PRs getting their reports too.

Comments in these files lost their measured numbers in favour of the reasoning and how to re-measure — the `~32-min suite` note was already wrong at 18, and the `~92%` beside it is what made factor 8 look like four hours.

**Verifying.** This PR's CI run should show the results table under Fast checks and Full tests, with no report rows under Deploy. `extended-tests.yml` can't run until it's on `dev`; after merge, `gh workflow run "Extended Tests" --ref dev -f factor=1` smoke-tests it in a couple of minutes.

title: Folder-style tutorial lessons
body:
Stacked on #2485. **All three PRs in this stack are meant to be merged together** — they are split for review only.

## Summary

Documentation mode already renders `/`-separated slide names as nested breadcrumb dropdowns (`"B2T2 / Table API / Constructors / vcat"`). Tutorial mode has 25 lessons in one flat list. This PR names that hierarchy and then gives tutorial mode folders on top of it.

### `SlidePath`

The hierarchy was an ad-hoc convention spread across three unrelated places: a local `split_filepath` plus inline `take`/`nth`/`dedup_f` in `EditorModeView.indicator_select`, ~60 hardcoded `" / "` literals in `src/b2t2/Slides.re` and `src/docslides/Slides.re`, and `"Derivations / " ++ spec.title` in `Init.re`.

`src/web/util/SlidePath.re` makes it a type:

```reason
type t = {
  folders: list(string),
  leaf: string,
};
```

and owns the operations both modes need: `of_string`/`to_string`, `folder`/`same_folder`, the folder-scoped index arithmetic the navigation arrows use (`folder_indices`, `folder_position`, and `step_in_folder`, which clamps), and `breadcrumb` — the sibling-dropdown decomposition lifted out of the view.

`indicator_select` is now a thin render over `breadcrumb` and takes `list(SlidePath.t)`, which dropped 69 lines from it along with two latent crashes it had been carrying:

- `List.nth(parts', prefix_depth)` raised `Failure("nth")` whenever one slide name was an exact proper prefix of another — a slide named `Tables` alongside `Tables / Tables` would have taken down the whole top bar. Such a path is now skipped, making it merely unreachable from the deeper dropdown.
- `Option.get` on the changed option's index lookup.

Slide names stay plain strings at the persistence boundary — they are IndexedDB keys (`"doc:" ++ name`) and `.hzt` `@title` text — so nothing about the stored format changes; callers convert at the view/navigation boundary.

### Tutorial folders

A lesson's `@title` is now a `SlidePath`, and both arrow surfaces — the in-slide prev/next pair and the top-bar arrows — **step within the current lesson's folder**, clamping at its edges, so the last lesson of a folder shows `Done! 🎉` instead of a next arrow. Crossing folders goes through the folder dropdown. The slide heading shows just the leaf, since the breadcrumb above it already names the folder.

| Folder | Lessons |
|---|---|
| `Basics` | 19 — Holes through Labeled Tuple Projection |
| `Tuple Structural Operations` | 3 — Extension, Omission, List Conversions |
| `Tables` | 6 — Tables, Table Column Projection, Rich Probes, and the three Gradebook tasks below |

Rich Probes sits under Tables because it is a rich probe *for* tables.

### Three tasks recovered from `tables-study`

`Tables` also picks up Gradebook Midterm Mean, Gradebook Overall Grade, and Gradebook Tidy Term — study tasks that had never been ported off the `tables-study` branch, where they were `Ta_*.ml` zipper dumps of 0.5–0.9 MB each. They keep their original ids, so they are the same lessons the study ran.

They were converted by adapting the dumps to the current types (the drift was two things per file: `selection` gained `anchor_caret`/`smart_rounded`, and `refractors` dropped `autos`/`sample_cursor` with `manuals` unchanged), compiling them in alongside `TaskRefDocs`, and running `./hazel tutorial-decode` — which also expanded each task's composed `TaskRefDocs` sections into a literal `@reference`. None of that scaffolding is in the tree.

Two content fixes on top of the decode: Midterm Mean's table held 20 literals like `85.000000`, and past six significant digits a slide falls onto the quadratic parser (slowness being the only symptom), so those are normalized to `85.0`; and its hidden tests did not round-trip, because an implicit `¿` hole collapses to nothing before a `,` inside a labeled tuple, so those twelve are now the explicit `?` token.

Not ported, deliberately: the two Bug Identification tasks, which depend on live typing; the 27 pre-placed probe refractors these three carried (`Triggers.refractor_seg_to_seg` only emits `^^probe(...)` for a refractor whose id is a term root in the current parse, and these ids came from the older grammar, so 26 of 27 dropped); and the study's `setting_overrides` condition flags and `?treatment` A/B ordering, none of which has a `.hzt` marker. The commit records what each task's flags were.

All three start as real tasks — a hole in Midterm Mean, an identity-stub `tidy_term` — so their hidden tests fail until solved.

Recategorizing is safe: lesson identity is the `id=<uuid>` flag introduced in #2485, not the title, so moving a lesson between folders does not reset anyone's saved progress.

`hazel-programs/tutorial/README.md` documents the authoring rules — one folder segment per lesson, no title a proper prefix of another, a folder's lessons contiguous in `src/tutorialslides/Slides.re`, and `Basics / Holes` first because it is the lesson a fresh profile opens on.

## Deliberately not done

A ✔ on a folder's dropdown option when the whole folder is complete. It cannot be built from current data: `TutorialsMode.Update.calculate` evaluates only the current lesson and `TutorialMode.Model.persist` saves only zippers, so `all_tests_passed` is `false` for every non-current lesson — which is also why today's per-lesson ✔ from `return_title` can only ever show for the lesson you are standing on. A real folder ✔ needs persisted per-lesson completion, which is its own change.

## Test plan

- [x] `make dev` builds clean, no new warnings
- [x] `make test-quick` — 3501/3501
- [x] `./hazel tutorial-verify` — 28/28 slides round-trip cleanly
- [x] `Test_SlidePath` (23 cases) — parsing, accessors, folder navigation, and breadcrumb, including the proper-prefix path that used to raise and an out-of-range index
- [x] `Test_Tutorial` (7 cases) — ratchets the authored lessons: folder set and sizes (`Basics x19`, `Tuple Structural Operations x3`, `Tables x6`), contiguity, `Basics / Holes` first as the default lesson, no title a proper prefix of another, and that repeated next/prev traverses exactly one folder and then stops
- [x] Documentation mode — `B2T2 / …` breadcrumbs and `Derivations / …` still render and switch slides
- [x] Tutorial mode — opens on `Basics / Holes`; arrows walk one folder and stop at its ends; the dropdown crosses folders
- [x] `./hazel analyze --warnings` reports nothing on all three ported tasks' starting programs

title: Modules II, part 9: the standard library as modules (proof of concept)
body:
> [!WARNING]
> **Proof of concept, like #2508, and not close to done.** It exists to show
> what the standard library looks like once modules are real values, and to
> find out what that costs. Read "Known gaps" before reviewing anything else.

Ninth of the stack, on top of #2508. The standard library becomes modules,
and ships the vocabulary the implicits feature needs.

```
List.map([1, 2, 3], fun x -> x * 2)          -- [2, 4, 6]
String.of_int(42) ++ String.uppercase("ok")  -- "42OK"
Float.sqrt(9.0) >. Float.pi                  -- false
Option.map((Some(2), fun x -> x + 1))        -- Some(3)

let implicit A = ShowInt in
let show = fun (implicit S : SHOW, x : S.T) -> S.show(x) in
show(3)                                      -- "3"
```

## What it does

- **Six modules**: `List` (all 65 list functions), `String`, `Int`, `Float`,
  `Option`, `Pair`. The list family is the one that crowds the namespace
  worst: `map`, `filter`, `length`, `find` and `head` are all top-level
  names today.
- **Every flat name stays.** `String.length` and `string_length` are the
  same function, so no program, slide or exercise changes meaning. The
  modules are the front door from here on; nothing is deprecated in this PR.
- **Both halves are derived from the same records.** A module builtin is an
  ordinary constant whose type is a signature and whose value is a module,
  and the signature's member types and the module's member values come from
  the same builtin, so a member cannot drift from the function it names. A
  member is the implementation, not a copy: it is the term the flat name is
  bound to.
- **`SHOW` and `ORD` ship as signature types**, with an instance per base
  type: `ShowInt`, `ShowFloat`, `ShowBool`, `ShowString`, `OrdInt`,
  `OrdFloat`, `OrdString`. Each carries a manifest type member, since
  resolution selects on it.

## Two decisions worth arguing with

**The instances are not ambient.** A program marks what it wants, one line
per instance. Making them ambient is a language decision rather than a
library one, and it needs a priority or coherence rule first: with none, a
program that defines its own instance for a base type under any other name
makes every call ambiguous against the shipped one. Twelve of the implicits
tests change meaning when they are ambient, which is the same warning from
the other side. The cost is a `let implicit A = ShowInt in` line, which is
what the Module Implicits slide already writes.

**No `EQ`.** Polymorphic `==` already compares two values of a type, so an
equality signature earns its keep only once a type can choose its own
equality, which wants the sharing constraint #2495 lacks.

## Two prerequisites this found, fixed where they belong

Both are in #2493, with tests, because plain source hits them:

- A module member's name is its label, but substitution renamed it away from
  capture like any binder, so `M.x` stopped finding it. The stepper
  substitutes the whole builtin environment, so any module with a member
  named after a builtin lost that member.
- A capitalized module name parses as a constructor, and a known constructor
  won, so a module whose name matched one could not be projected at all. The
  JSON type contributes `List`, `Int`, `String`, `Float` and `Bool` to every
  program's constructor namespace, which made exactly the five most useful
  stdlib names unusable: `module List = { let f = 1 } in List.f` was an
  error. Projecting a constructor means nothing, so the module now wins in
  dot position, and `List([Int(2)])` still builds JSON.

The one change here is in the evaluator: a member holding a fixpoint has to
unroll, so a projection judges a definition the way a variable lookup does,
sharing one predicate. Only a module that came out of the environment can
hit it, which is why it is in this PR rather than #2493.

## Known gaps

1. **Cost per mention.** A module out of the environment is copied on each
   mention, so `List.map` copies a 65-member module where `map` copies one
   fixpoint. I have not measured it against a hot loop, and if it matters the
   answer is probably to bind the library once per program rather than to
   hand it out of the environment, which needs a prelude mechanism that does
   not exist.
2. **The grouping is partial.** The tuple-label operations, the ADT helpers,
   the `Ord` inversion, `print`, the SInt and Nat families and the remaining
   conversions are still only flat. `Bool` has nothing worth grouping yet.
3. **`Int`, `Float` and `String` cannot be *declared* as modules in the text
   grammar**, since those are base-type tokens: `module Int = {…}` does not
   parse, though the shipped ones are fine because nothing declares them in
   source. The editor accepts it.
4. **Nothing is deprecated.** Two names for every function is the price of
   not breaking programs, and there is no mechanism to mark the flat ones
   legacy.
5. **No `List` for other collections.** There is no `Set`, `Map` or `Seq`
   because there are no such builtins; this PR groups what exists.
6. **`Option`'s type member is `Option`'s sum type**, so `Option.T` names it,
   but the module cannot expose the constructors: constructors declared in a
   module are not members of it (#2243).

## Verification

`make dev` clean · `make ci-check` clean under the release profile ·
`make test-quick` ~~3845~~ 3982 green · new suites `Statics.BuiltinsModules` (11) and
`Evaluator.BuiltinsModules` (10), including that a member equals its flat
function and that a recursive member unrolls through a projection · CLI
probes for every module and for both signatures.

~~Expect the same two per-seed `Full tests` failures as the rest of the stack,
both unrelated and both dev's: the cyclic-alias crash in normalization and
the `:+` printer divergence explained on #2493.~~
Replacement: both are fixed at the bottom of the stack (#2493 carries the fixes with tests).

title: Load the Fumola runtime by content hash, and say which one loaded
body:
The consumer side of [Adapton/fumola#69](https://github.com/Adapton/fumola/issues/69) — the runtime is published to content-addressed URLs by [Adapton/fumola#76](https://github.com/Adapton/fumola/pull/76), and this reads the manifest that names them.

Targets `fumola-livelit-mvp` rather than `dev`, since that is where the Fumola livelit work lives.

**Order does not matter.** An origin with no `runtime.json` is exactly the fallback path. Verified against the live `fumola.org` today, which has none: the loader falls back, reports `fumola.org @ stable`, and evaluates correctly. So this can merge before, after, or independently of the Fumola side.

### The problem

The published runtime is served from stable URLs and GitHub Pages stamps `Cache-Control: max-age=600` on everything with no way to change it. So a Fumola deploy cannot invalidate the 5.6 MB binary a browser already holds, and a livelit can run against a runtime a version behind — which looks like a bug rather than a cache.

### What changed in `prebundle.js`

Reads `<origin>/runtime.json` before importing, and takes the glue and the binary from the directory it names. Both or neither — wasm-bindgen emits them as a matched set and they do not load if their versions disagree, so a half-applied manifest would be worse than ignoring one.

A published origin stays **one** source with one timeout budget rather than becoming two entries; doubling the source count would double the worst case a page waits before reporting the runtime unavailable (currently 90s across three).

### `window.fumola.source()` now says which version

```
"fumola.org @ 290846d3aad19d38"   the current build, by content hash
"fumola.org @ stable"             manifest unreachable; the root pair
"local @ stable"                  your own scripts/build-fumola-wasm.sh
```

Previously unanswerable from a browser, and it is the first question worth asking when a livelit misbehaves for someone and not for you. It also removes the need for a `fumola_version()` export compiled into the wasm — the manifest is the version stamp.

### Verification

Driven in a browser with the **real** bundle (esbuild over `prebundle.js`, same as the dune rule):

| Scenario | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Live `fumola.org` (no manifest today) | falls back, `fumola.org @ stable`, `` `x := 41; get(`x) + 1 `` → 42 |
| Locally published site with a manifest | requests `runtime.json`, then the hashed glue and binary; `source()` reports the hash; → 42 |

Plus `dune build src/web/www/bundled.js`, and `FumolaValue` 54/54, `FumolaSource` 21/21 — though see below on what those actually cover.

### `docs/fumola-runtime-changes.md`

New, and the reason this was looked at. Hazel pins no version of Fumola — no submodule, no revision, no lockfile entry — so **a change merged there reaches every Hazel user without any commit here, and nothing in Hazel's CI notices.** The doc records the dependency precisely (including that the bridge calls only 6 of the runtime's 17 exports, which is what makes "did that Fumola change break us?" a two-minute check), an event log starting with fumola#74, and a four-tier testing methodology.

Its least comfortable finding, stated plainly because green tests are easy to mistake for coverage here: **nothing in either repository tests a Fumola livelit against a live runtime.** `Evaluator.Livelit` skips all four outright; `FumolaValue` and `FumolaSource` feed hand-written JSON fixtures and would pass with the wasm deleted; `prebundle.js` has no test of any kind; there is no headless harness. Those fixtures are the only written record of the two repos' agreement and they are transcribed by hand, so a reply-shape change in Fumola leaves them passing while asserting the old shape. Generating them from the runtime is the first thing that would close it, and needs no browser.

title: Modules II, part 8: modular implicits (proof of concept, not close to done)
body:
> [!WARNING]
> **This is a proof of concept and is not close to done.** It is not intended to
> merge as it stands. Its purpose is to show that modular implicits fit Hazel's
> module system and to make one design concrete enough to argue about. The
> syntax, the resolution rule and the error reporting should all be expected to
> change. Please read "Known gaps" at the bottom before reviewing anything else,
> and treat everything above it as a sketch rather than a proposal.

Eighth of the stack, on top of #2503. A function parameter component can be
declared implicit, and a call that leaves it out has it filled in by the type
checker from the instances in scope.

```
type SHOW = { type T; let show : T -> String } in
let implicit ShowInt = { type T = Int; let show = string_of_int } in
let implicit ShowBool = { type T = Bool; let show = fun b -> if b then "true" else "false" } in
let show = fun (implicit S : SHOW, x : S.T) -> S.show(x) in
   -- show : (implicit S : SHOW, S.T) -> String
show(3) ++ show(true)     -- "3true": S resolved to ShowInt, then ShowBool
show(ShowBool, true)      -- passed by hand: the arity includes S
```

## What it does

- `implicit S : SIG` is a pattern form (`Pat.Implicit`) and, in an arrow
  domain, a type form (`Typ.Implicit`). Functions stay uncurried: the binder is
  a component of the parameter, and it scopes over the later components and the
  codomain, so `(implicit S : SHOW, S.T) -> String` is an ordinary arrow type.
- `let implicit M = ...`, and the same as a module item, declare an instance
  (`Ctx.ImplicitEntry`). Only such bindings take part in resolution. A binder is
  itself an instance inside the function body, so implicit functions compose.
- At a call, arity decides: the explicit arity resolves every implicit, the full
  arity passes them by hand, and a mix is disambiguated by signature. Resolution
  keeps the instances whose type fits the signature, then narrows by the
  explicit arguments' types and the expected type. One left is the instance;
  none or several is a mark on the application, with a hole passed in the
  instance's place so evaluation proceeds around the error.
- The instance is spliced into the elaborated argument, so the runtime sees an
  ordinary application and the stepper shows `show(ShowInt, 3)`.
- A failed resolution names what the call required, not just the signature:
  `No implicit instance of SHOW with T = String for S`.
- Since #2494's redesign, an instance fits a signature through `Typ.coercion`,
  and function types with implicit binders match exactly: a function taking a
  narrower binder is not coerced to a wider expectation (nor the reverse), so
  adapt by eta-expansion. A path through an unannotated implicit binder types
  as unknown rather than erroring, since the binder may be any module (#2493).

New module `src/language/statics/Implicits.re` holds the resolution; `docs/modules.md`
has a section on it, and the new "Module Implicits" doc slide is the worked example.

## Known gaps

Design questions left open, roughly in the order I would want them settled:

1. **Gradual typing weakens resolution.** An instance member written without an
   annotation types as `? -> String`, which fits every `{ let show : X -> String }`,
   so instances become interchangeable and calls turn ambiguous. The workaround
   in the docs (annotate members, use a manifest `type T = E.T`) is a workaround,
   not an answer. This is the part I trust least.
2. **A plain module parameter still loses the caller's type equation**, though
   it no longer loses it silently. #2498 now closes the parameter as well as
   the body, so the same program is an error rather than an unchecked call:

   ```
   let dup = fun (m : SHOW, x : m.T) -> (x, x) in
   let out : (String, String) = dup(ShowInt, 3) in out
   -- m.T escaped the scope of its module, so nothing here can have that type;
      mark the parameter implicit, or annotate it with a manifest signature

   let dup = fun (implicit S : SHOW, x : S.T) -> (x, x) in
   let out : (String, String) = dup(ShowInt, 3) in out
   -- error: Expecting type String, String but got inconsistent type
      ShowInt.T, ShowInt.T
   ```

   An implicit binder is the only type in the language that can hold what the
   caller knows, which is why the second version checks and the first only
   reports its loss. Marking the parameter implicit is a workaround; the fix
   is a dependent domain for ordinary module parameters, the way Scala's
   dependent method types work, reusing the scoping and substitution this PR
   adds, or an ML sharing constraint. Three tests in
   `Test_Statics_Implicits` pin both halves.
3. **Error attribution.** Both resolution marks sit on the application. That was
   a deliberate choice and it still reads oddly in at least one case on the doc
   slide. Narrowing also runs only when more than one candidate fits the
   signature, so a single unfitting instance reports an argument mismatch
   (`expecting ShowInt.T, got String`) instead of a missing instance. The
   candidate list in an error is every instance in scope rather than the ones
   that fit the signature, and the ambiguity message never says that nothing in
   the call constrained the binder.
4. **No implicit functors.** Instances cannot themselves take implicit
   parameters, so there is no `SHOW` for `[T]` derived from `SHOW` for `T` and no
   recursive search. That is the main thing modular implicits are for, and it is
   entirely absent.
5. **Not supported anywhere else.** `DeferredAp` with implicit components;
   resolving an implicit function that is merely mentioned rather than applied;
   any spelling of `module implicit M : S = ...`.
6. **Cost.** The argument is type-checked twice at an implicit call (a probe pass
   decides the arity), so those applications pay double.
7. **Syntax warts.** `implicit` is now a keyword. A lone
   `implicit S : SIG -> τ` needs parentheses in both the editor and the text
   grammar. The keyword needs two different tile shapes, one per sort, for
   precedence reasons.
8. **Type equality is inconsistent about binder names.** `meet`/~~`ana_meet`~~ `Typ.coercion`
   rename binders positionally, while `Equality` and `equal_up_to_aliases`
   compare them literally, so `fast_equal` distinguishes types that are
   consistent.
9. **No instance coherence check.** Nothing notices that two instances
   overlap; you find out at a call site, as an ambiguity. A canonicity or
   orphan rule would move that error to the declaration, where it belongs.

Two pre-existing bugs are fixed on the way, both in commit 1: the editor read
`A -> M.T` as `(A -> M).T` because the type-level dot bound looser than the
arrow, and the pattern-annotation printer was not idempotent (`x:(S.T)`
reprinted as `x:((S.T))`).

## Verification

Editor behavior was checked by hand; anything that turned up is tracked
outside this PR.

`make dev` clean · `make test-quick` ~~3840~~ 3961 green · `Statics.Properties`,
`MenhirFuzz` (several seeds), `MenhirCorpus` and the reparse suites green ·
`hazel analyze`/`run` on a 14-function example program and on the new doc slide.
New suites: `Statics.Implicits` (39), `Evaluator.Implicits` (15),
`Typ.Implicit` (9), `Editing.Implicit` (4), plus Menhir, MakeTerm, ExpToSegment,
Elaboration, Equality, Abbreviate and ExplainThis cases.

## Stack note

~~Parts 3 to 7 were force-pushed with this: a Coverage crash on `case m.x` with an
abstract `m.T` is fixed where it was introduced (#2495, "a stuck path type is
opaque, not non-normalized") and cascaded up the stack. No other change to those
branches.~~
Replacement: superseded. The whole stack was rebased on 2026-09-11 for #2494's
redesign; this part dropped its contravariant arrow arms on the relation and kept
its implicit-binder arms.

title: Statics: a capitalized name resolves to its most recent binding (module vs constructor)
body:
```
type T = + Text + Other in
module Text = { let f = fun n -> "x" } in
Text.f(0) == "x"
```
This reports "Expected a tuple" at `Text.f`. A capitalized name parses as a constructor and statics looked it up constructor-first, falling back to a variable binding only when no constructor of that name existed anywhere. So a module named like any constructor in scope lost to it, no matter which was bound later.

This PR makes the most recent binding of the name win, whichever kind it is (`Ctx.newest_var_or_ctr`), which is what shadowing means for every other name. Expression position only; constructor patterns are unchanged. Draft because the rule deserves a careful look: it changes what a capitalized identifier means when a module and a constructor share a name.

title: Load the Fumola runtime from a list of sources, not one
body:
Groundwork for pointing **fumola.org** at the Fumola Pages site. No behaviour change today.

### Why

`prebundle.js` hard-codes one published URL for the wasm runtime:

```js
glue: "https://adapton.github.io/fumola/fumola_wasm.js",
wasm: "https://adapton.github.io/fumola/fumola_wasm_bg.wasm",
```

Once `Adapton/fumola` takes `fumola.org` as its Pages custom domain, those URLs 301 to `https://fumola.org/...`. A GitHub Pages custom-domain redirect carries **no `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header** — verified against a live example (`pytorch.github.io/examples/`, whose org site is CNAME'd to docs.pytorch.org) — and a CORS-mode `import()` must pass the CORS check on *every* hop of a redirect chain, not just the final response. The runtime files themselves do serve `access-control-allow-origin: *`; it's the redirect in front of them that doesn't.

So the old URL works before the switch and fails after; the new one fails before and works after. Neither spans it, which would leave the deployed preview without its published-runtime fallback for as long as the two sides are out of step.

### What

`LOCAL` / `PUBLISHED` become a `SOURCES` list, tried in order — local, then `fumola.org`, then `adapton.github.io` — and the promise chain becomes a loop. Local stays first, so working on Fumola and Hazel together is unchanged. Whichever published URL is live answers; the other fails fast and costs one request.

When every source fails, `loadError` now names all of them and what each said, instead of only the last error.

### After the domain settles

The `adapton.github.io` entry will only ever redirect, and should be dropped.

### Checking it

Open the preview and look at the console: it now logs `runtime loaded from <name>`, and `window.fumola.source()` returns that name. Before the domain moves, expect `adapton.github.io`; after, `fumola.org`.

title: Modules II, part 7: a signature member declared twice is an error
body:
Seventh of the stack, on top of #2501. A signature that declares the same member twice is now an error.

- The later declaration is marked with the new `SigDuplicateMember`: `type S = { let x : Int; let x : Bool }` reports `Member x is declared more than once in this signature` on `let x : Bool`. Value and module members share a namespace (`let m` and `module m` clash); type members, manifest or abstract, have their own, so `let x : Int; type x = Int` is fine.
- The mark lives on the signature item itself. `Info.sig_` gains `marks`, which `Info.marks_of` now reads, so the cursor inspector, the problem sidebar and `hazel analyze` all report it; the CLI caret covers the whole item.
- Module bodies are unchanged: a repeated binding there is shadowing, last wins, as before.

Slide item 23a shows the error. Tests cover value, manifest type, abstract type, manifest-then-abstract, module, and value-versus-module duplicates, the shared and separate namespaces, and that the later item carries the mark.

title: Report a mismatch once: tuple components and function bodies; describe tuple shape mismatches
body:
Fixes #1958. Fixes #2507.

A term whose child already reports a mismatch against its expected type is no longer reported again itself, for tuple components and for function bodies. Tuple shape mismatches (arity, labels) say what differs.

**Before.**
- `let (a : Int, b : Int) = (1, "s") in a` produced three errors: `Expecting type Int but got inconsistent type String` on `"s"`, and `Expecting type Int, Int but got inconsistent type Int, String` on both the tuple and the parentheses around it. Arity and label mismatches were reported the same way, by printing both full types.
- `let f : Int -> Bool = fun x -> x + 1 in f(1)` produced two errors: `Expecting type Bool but got inconsistent type Int` on `x + 1`, and `Expecting type Int -> Bool but got inconsistent type Int -> Int` on the whole `fun`, whose synthesized type was built from the already-marked body. With the function shorthand (`let f(x) = x + 1` as a module member checked against a signature) the second error sat on the synthetic `fun` the desugaring introduces, which has no source span.

**Now.**
- **Tuples.** A component that already reports a mismatch contributes its expected type to the tuple's synthesized type, so the tuple, and the parentheses that forward its marks, do not repeat it. A labeled element `l=e` does the same for its value. The first example is one error, on `"s"`.
- **Functions.** A body that already reports a mismatch contributes the expected return type to the function's type, so the function is not marked again. The second example is one error, on `x + 1`. A non-function against an arrow type is still reported on itself.
- **Tuple shape.** A mismatch of the tuple's own shape is still reported on the tuple and now says what differs: `Expecting a tuple of 2 elements but got 3 elements`, or `Expecting a tuple of 2 elements with labels name, age but got 1 element with labels name; missing label age`, in the CLI and the cursor inspector alike. `LabeledTupleStaticsHelpers.shape_mismatch` computes the summary once for both. A same-shape mismatch on a non-literal (a variable of tuple type) keeps the generic message, where the two types are the useful information.

Both rules are the one line `List.exists(Mark.is_expectation_mismatch, child.marks) ? expected : child.elab_syn_ty` at the parent's type construction, in the `Tuple`/`TupLabel` and `Fun` cases of `Statics.re`.

**Tests.** The annotated-tree test for `(_=1) : (_=String)` pins the mark on the value only; tests for single reporting of a component and of a body (let-bound and as a function argument), for arity, and for a non-function against an arrow type; unit tests for `shape_mismatch`.

## Verification

`make dev` clean · `make test-quick` green (3476 tests).

title: Modules II, part 5: tuple label errors like modules, named missing members, CLI spans
body:
Fifth of the stack, on top of #2498. Improvements to error reporting that reach beyond modules, kept apart from the module fixes in parts 1 and 3.

- **Labeled tuples follow the module design for bad projections.** `t.y` with no label `y` now marks the label (`LabelNotFound`, now worded "Tuple has no label y; its labels are x") while the dot carries only a message (`Message.TupleLabelNotFound`), the same shape part 1 gave `m.y` on modules and the type-level `M.Fake` always had. Applies to tuples and lists of tuples.
- **Missing members are named for any signature-typed expression.** When an expression of signature type is analyzed against a signature that declares members it lacks, `StaticsBase.expectation_mismatch_mark` reports `ModuleMissingMembers` instead of a generic type mismatch, so a module variable, a function argument, or a function result names what is missing, as a module literal already did. The computation is shared through `Sig.missing_members`. Slide item 26a (in the Module Sealing slide) shows `greet(Carol)` with `Carol` lacking `name`.
- **CLI carets span the whole diagnosed term.** `hazel analyze` used to underline only the tile carrying the term's id, so `M.x + 1`'s error pointed at a single `.`. The caret now covers every measured id of the term (`m.x`, `a + b`, a module literal on one line), matching what the editor highlights; terms inside folded projectors keep the location-less fallback without spurious lookup warnings.

## Verification

`make test-quick` green (3855 tests) · the module slides and the tuples slide analyze with the expected errors only.

title: Modules II, part 4: module-typed functions and generative escape
body:
Fourth of the stack, on top of #2495 (parts 5 to 9 follow). Functions take and return modules with abstract types; a path cannot escape the scope of its root.

- **Avoidance.** `Typ.avoid` runs at function bodies, `let` bodies (so `module … in` too) and each `case` arm. A module path rooted at the binder going out of scope is first reduced in the body's context, so a manifest member simply expands. A path that is still abstract stays abstract as an escaped type (see below), except that a signature member defined as that path becomes abstract and later members refer to it by name. So `fun (m : S) -> m` has type `S -> S`, `fun (m : S) -> m.x` has an escaped abstract type as its result, and each call of a function returning a module with abstract members yields a fresh type (generativity). Inside the scope `m.x : m.T` is unchanged; the part-3 tests that pinned root types now read the in-scope type from the info map. `let f : S -> S = fun m -> m` checks because #2494 seals a function literal's body to the expected codomain.
- **Sibling paths.** The signature walk binds value member names as well, so a member typed by a sibling module's abstract type projects as `M.Inner.T` instead of silently becoming `?`. A written-out signature left behind by a type alias (`{ type T = Int }.T`) also projects.
- **Runtime.** A cast to an abstract path type is a no-op: elaboration normalizes manifest paths away, so a path reaching the runtime is abstract. Before, `let z : m.U = m.y` left the stuck value `1:m.U`.
- **Editor.** Deleting the `=` of a signature `type T = Int` downgrades the tile to the bare abstract form (the inverse of part 3's upgrade), leaving the old definition dangling as a stray type to remove or reattach by retyping `=`. `Editing.SigAbstract` grows to 34 cases: typing the bare form, adding `=` in every position, removing it backward, forward and by selection, round trips, and a MakeTerm-level check of the resulting item kinds.
- **Property test.** The QCheck AST generator emits signature types (with a shrinker), and a new property checks that no binder inside a random program leaks into its root type.

**Doc slide.** ~~The split into `modules.hz` and `module-signatures.hz` now lands in part 3; this part adds section G (module-typed functions) to the second slide. Background: adding that section to the combined slide overflowed the JavaScript stack in the CLI. It is not a loop: statics in jsoo overflows node's default stack at roughly 100 plain nested `let`s (about 10 to 16KB per level), and the combined slide had about 70 nesting levels plus 30 `module` bindings. The C3 build needed a stack between 950 and 984KB for it and this one between 984 and 1000KB, against a default of 984KB. The slide is now two: `modules.hz` (construction, qualified types, signatures, errors) and `module-signatures.hz` (width subtyping, abstract types, module-typed functions), both registered in `Slides.re`.~~
Replacement: the slides are split lower in the stack (#2493: Modules and Module Signatures; #2494: Module Sealing). This part moves part 3's section F out of the sealing slide into a new Module Abstract Types slide and adds section G to it, since G's examples use F's `Counter`. The measured reason for keeping slides small is the Web Worker: it evaluates programs with about half the main thread's stack, so a slide whose evaluation needs more than roughly 450KB under node overflows on the first edit. Each module slide now needs 370KB to 445KB. The stack depth itself deserves an issue.

## Avoidance keeps the type abstract

Where a path outlives its root, avoidance used to fall back to unknown, and
unknown is consistent with everything, so the loss was silent: nothing told
the author, and every later use checked against nothing. It now mints an
escaped abstract type (`Typ.Escaped`), which is consistent with `?` and with
itself and inconsistent with everything else. That is the relation an
in-scope abstract member already has, so no new rule is invented; what is new
is a representation that survives the loss of its root, generalizing the
clause avoidance already had for signature members.

```
let get = fun (m : BOX) -> m.x in get(B) + 1
-- This has the abstract type m.T, which escaped the scope of its module,
   so it cannot be used where a concrete type is required

let dup = fun (m : SHOW, x : m.T) -> (x, x) in dup(ShowInt, "s")
-- m.T escaped the scope of its module, so nothing here can have that type;
   mark the parameter implicit, or annotate it with a manifest signature,
   to keep the caller's type
```

Binding an escaped value, passing it to an unannotated function and giving it
to a hole all still work: the error appears where the author wrote something
concrete, which is the gradual half of the bargain.

- **The parameter is closed too.** The function arm avoided only its body, so
  a component annotated with an earlier component's member left the type
  mentioning a binder no caller can name, and every argument passed, since
  normalization maps a path with an unbound root to unknown. Only the copy
  that becomes the function's type is closed; the pattern's own type and the
  elaborated ascription keep the precise path, so runtime casts and
  incremental-evaluation keys do not move.
- **Generative per application.** `Typ.freshen_escaped` gives each call its
  own identity, so two calls of one function escape different types and
  joining them is an error, while a value bound once and used twice is fine.
  Identities are derived from the application's id rather than generated, so
  re-checking an elaboration still yields an equal type.
- **`Mark.EscapedType` says which side escaped**, so the advice fits the
  case, and an escaped type displays as its path plus a short tag of its
  identity, since two escapes of one path are different types. A failed
  implicit resolution keeps erasing to unknown (`Typ.escape_to`): that
  failure is already marked, and opacity there would only cascade.
- **Not fixed here:** what the caller knows, that the parameter is a
  particular module, still cannot be written in an ordinary arrow type. An
  implicit binder can hold it (#2508); an ML sharing constraint for ordinary
  module parameters is the missing feature. A tuple argument also still
  reports the component and the tuple, which is the pre-existing cascade
  fixed off-stack in #2502.

Two commits: the type form, inert, with its `meet` rules and traversals; then
minting, the closed parameter, freshening and the diagnostics. The escape
tests in the modules suite now assert the escaped type where they asserted
unknown, five new cases cover the behavior, slide item 42 keeps its abstract
type and 43 shows the error.

## Fixes the fuzz properties turned up

Three defects, each found only through a Slow-tagged QCheck property and so only on seeds that generated the shape — parts 5-8 went red while this part stayed green on the very same bugs. Each now has a deterministic test, so the seeds no longer decide.

- **A cyclic alias crashed the analysis.** `type x = x.a in ?` aborted with `weak_head_normalize exceeded 1000 recursive calls`. `TyAlias` already guards self-reference by wrapping the definition in `Rec`, and normalization leaves a `Rec` alone — but from this part `x.a` is a module member projection, so normalizing it asks `path_sig`, and `as_sig` unrolls that `Rec` looking for a signature, handing the projection straight back. Out of fuel the type now comes back unreduced, stuck, which is what the function already returns for everything else it cannot reduce; the program reports `Expected a module or tuple type, found type rec x -> x.a`. `Typ.CyclicAlias` pins it.
- **A printed `:` glued to a leading-plus sum.** `Menhir and maketerm are equivalent` failed on `(()) @< ({ let _:+ Adid }) >`: `:` is an operator character and `Token.is_potential_operator` matches any run of them, so `:+` lexes as one token that is no form at all, while Menhir's separate lexer splits it. `should_add_space` already knew this hazard, but as a list of two characters (`$`, `!`) rather than the property they share; it now asks `Token.begins_with_potential_operator`, which covers `!` along with every other operator character. `$` stays listed, being a name character. An unparenthesized sum only ever reaches a `:` as a sig member's ascription, which is why this appears here.
- **Printing was not idempotent.** `type T = { … }` printed as `({ … })`, then `(({ … }))`, a layer per trip. `parenthesize_typ`'s `Parens` case ran its own content through `paren_typ_at(Precedence.min)`; precedences count down from `max = 0`, so that test wraps exactly the types whose precedence *is* `min` — a Sig, a bare sum, a multihole — and re-wrapped them every pass. The wrapper being emitted is already the protection: nothing outside can bind into it. **Not specific to modules** — `dev` grows the same layers on a parenthesized bare sum (`type T = (+ Adid) in 7`), so this fixes that too and carries it along with the stack.

## Known gaps

- **No dependent domain for ordinary module parameters.** An explicit
  parameter cannot be named later in its own parameter list or in the result
  type, which is exactly the equation this PR reports the loss of. An
  implicit binder (#2508) is the only construct that can hold it, so marking
  the parameter implicit is the current substitute for a sharing constraint.
- **No existentials with an unpacking form.** An escaped abstract type is now
  a real type rather than unknown, but there is no way to give one a name and
  use it, so such a value stays inert. Storing modules with differing
  abstract members in a list, or returning one from a conditional, therefore
  still loses the shared type.

## Verification

`make dev` clean · `make test-quick` green (~~3658~~ ~~3809~~ 3851 tests) · `Statics.Properties` (crash and closedness properties, with signatures generated) and `MenhirFuzz` pass · ~~both slides~~ all four module slides analyze with errors only under their "Error" items · the Menhir and elaboration properties also pass at the five seeds that had been failing (803422318, 57351729, 931683130, 541095201, 92308926) · `make ci-check` clean under the release profile.

title: Modules II, part 3: abstract type members, sealing, path types
body:
Third of the stack, on top of #2494. A signature may declare `type T` with no definition; a module sealed by it must define `T`, but outside the module `T` is known only as the path `M.T`.

- **Syntax.** `type T` is a signature item (`SigTypeAbstract`) in the grammar, the tile forms (listed before the manifest form so that `type` typed in a signature expands to it), `MakeTerm`, the Menhir `sigItem` rule, the printers, equality, abbreviation and ExplainThis. In the editor, typing `=` after a bare `type T` upgrades the tile to `type T = …` (`Insert.upgrade_bare_sig_type`); there is no downgrade.
- **Sealing.** A module analyzed against `{ type T; let x : T }` must define `T` (a missing definition is a `ModuleMissingMembers`; a value named `T` does not count), and its members are checked against its own definition. `Typ.sig_sub` realizes an abstract member of the required signature by whatever the module provides; a manifest member is not satisfied by an abstract one. `Typ.meet` matches abstract members only with abstract members. Since #2494 the directional relation is `Typ.coercion` and runs only at coercion sites (an ascription, an annotated binder, an application argument, and a function literal's body under an expected arrow type); elsewhere signatures match exactly.
- **Path types.** An abstract member projected from a module path is the stuck normal form `M.T`, consistent with itself and `?` only. `Typ.path_sig` now returns the path along with the items; `weak_head_normalize`, `normalize` and `meet` stop at a stuck path. A module variable's type is strengthened (`Typ.strengthen`, at `Var`, the capitalized-constructor fallback and `Dot`), so `M.x : M.T` and `module N = M` shares `M.T`, while two modules sealed by the same signature have distinct types. Only a path can name an abstract type: projecting from any other expression, or through a signature alias, gives `?`. The cursor inspector reports `M.T` as an abstract type (`Message.PathAbstract`).
- **Dynamics.** Abstract members have no runtime content. Runtime sealing now ascribes each kept member to its closed type, so an abstract member casts to `?` (previously a bare `T` left stuck casts such as `0:T`).

Tests: eighteen `Statics.Modules` cases (sealing, path types, aliasing, distinct sealings, transparency, missing and kind mismatches, forward references), `Typ.SigPaths`, `Evaluator.Modules`, `Editing.SigAbstract` (bare form, `=` upgrade, Cmd+D), plus MakeTerm, Menhir, round-trip, TyDi and Equality cases. Slide section F (a `Counter` module) and `docs/modules.md` describe the design.

Known, planned for the next PR: `fun (m : { type T; let x : T }) -> m.x` currently types as `S -> m.T` with `m` escaping its scope; the generative `Typ.avoid` handles that.

## Known gaps

- **No sharing constraint.** There is no `with type` spelling, so a signature
  cannot be refined by fixing one member, and nothing says the equivalent of
  `SHOW with T = Int`. The workaround is a hand-written signature literal
  carrying a manifest member, which is verbose and easy to get wrong; the
  implicits part (#2508) documents it because resolution needs it often.
- **No opaque-versus-transparent ascription.** One colon seals, and a sealed
  module's type members can never be selected by an argument type, so a
  sealed implicit instance is unusable. That is documentation today rather
  than a language distinction; a second spelling that checks against a
  signature while keeping manifest types would remove the footgun.
- **Type members cannot take parameters.** The type-pattern grammar admits a
  bare name, so nothing abstracting over a type constructor is expressible:
  no collection, monad or functor signature. Value members may be
  polymorphic, so signatures in the style of show, equality and monoid are
  unaffected.

## Verification

`make dev` clean · `make test-quick` green (~~3600~~ 3777 tests) · `dune build @check --profile release` clean.

## Follow-up commits

- **Report a missing member once, and let signatures name sibling members.** The synthetic `x : T` expectation checked inside a module body no longer shares ids with the signature's type nodes, and is skipped when it mentions a name the module does not define, so a missing `type T` is reported only on the module. Signature items can now see earlier value and module members, so `{ module Inner : { type T }; let y : Inner.T }` is well-formed; in subtyping a sibling is bound to the type the module provides.
- ~~**The Modules slide is split here** rather than in part 4: sections E and F move to `module-signatures.hz`, because statics recursion depth grows with the `let` chain and the combined slide was at the JavaScript stack limit (jsoo overflows node's default stack at roughly 100 nested lets).~~
  Replacement: the split now happens in #2493 (Modules: sections A and B; Module Signatures: C and D) and #2494 (Module Sealing: E). This part appends section F to the Module Sealing slide; #2498 moves F into its own Module Abstract Types slide together with G. The commit that did the split here was dropped as superseded.
- **An abstract member cannot be named through a signature alias.** `type S = { type T; … } in let y : S.T = …` used to type `S.T` as `?`, so any value passed and the inspector called `?` an abstract type. The alias names no module, so there is no particular `T` to name: it is now an error on the label (`TypAbstractMemberOfSignature`), with the dot explaining that a module `M` of the signature names it as `M.T`; TyDi no longer suggests such members. Manifest members through an alias, and abstract members through a module path, are unchanged. A type path rooted at a base type name (`Nat.T`) now says the name is a base type, not a module. Slide item 36a.

title: Modules II, part 2: sealing at explicit coercion sites
body:
Second of the stack, on top of #2493. Where a module is ascribed a signature, bound with one, or passed to a function expecting one, it may have more members than the signature declares; the extra members are sealed away. Everywhere else signatures match exactly.

> **Revised 2026-09-11.** The first version of this PR checked width subtyping at every analysis position. After discussing it with Cyrus it now seals only at explicit coercion sites; the struck lines below are the claims that changed.
>
> ~~Where an expression is analyzed against a signature, the module may have more members than the signature declares. Only at **analysis positions**: places where the program states the type an expression must have.~~ Replacement: only at coercion sites (an ascription, an annotated binder, an application argument), found through parentheses, tuple-literal components and a function literal's body.
> ~~Annotated pattern: `fun (m : { let x : Int }) -> …` binds `m` at the narrower type.~~ Replacement: patterns are exact; the function's argument is sealed at the application instead.
> ~~Function domains, contravariantly: a `{ let x : Int } -> Int` fits where a `{ let x : Int; let y : Int } -> Int` is required.~~ Replacement: function types are not contravariant; eta-expand.
> ~~The check is `Typ.ana_meet(ctx, ~ana, ~syn)`.~~ Replacement: `Typ.coercion(ctx, ~from, ~to_)`.
> ~~Known gap: analysis-position subtyping has no list arm.~~ Replacement: a wider module as a list element is a mismatch by design, with a message that says an ascription seals it.

## Motivation

Part 1 made modules first-class values whose types are signatures, with an exact relation between them: `{ let x = 1; let y = 2 }` had type `{ let x : Int; let y : Int }` and nothing else. That rules out the things modules exist for: interfaces (`fun (m : { let name : String }) -> …` accepting any module with a `name`), information hiding (a `module Stack : S = { let default = 0; … }` keeping `default` private), and evolution (adding a member without breaking code written against the signature).

This part adds exactly the coercion ML has, at exactly the places ML has it.

### Where it applies

| Site | Example |
| --- | --- |
| Ascription | `({ let x = 1; let y = 2 } : { let x : Int })` |
| Annotated binder | `module M : { let x : Int } = { let x = 1; let y = 2 }`, `let m : S = wide`, a module item under a signature |
| Application argument | `greet({ let name = "Alice"; let age = 30 })`, `greet(Alice)`, `f(wide, 1)` |

The operand of a site is found through parentheses (and the other transparent forms: projectors, filters, closures), through the components of a tuple literal, since an n-ary application argument is a tuple, and through a function literal's body: under an expected arrow type the body is sealed to the codomain, as a functor body is to its result signature, so `let f : S -> S = fun m -> m` checks; the parameter is matched exactly. Sub-module members may themselves be wider than declared, and the coercion is structural through tuples, so a variable of tuple type is coerced componentwise at a site too.

The members the signature omits are sealed away: the binder's type is the signature as written, `m.y` on an omitted member is an error, and at runtime the module value keeps only the signature's members (`Ascriptions.re`).

### Everywhere else, signatures match exactly

A wider module as a list element, in an `if` or `case` branch, under a pattern annotation, or reached through a variable of list or function type is an `ExpectationMismatch`, and the message says so: "Expecting type S but got the wider type T; an ascription seals the extra members". Function types are not contravariant; eta-expand instead. Consistency (`Typ.meet`) is unchanged and remains the relation for joins, `==`, `is_consistent` and incremental-evaluation reuse.

### Why coercion sites rather than subsumption everywhere

The first version checked the directional relation at every analysis position, from the subsumption step. Cyrus pointed out that general width subtyping under bidirectional gradual typing belongs in one subsumption rule with a relation total over the type grammar, and the half-way point was neither: the relation had only signature and arrow arms, so `(1, m) : (Int, S)` and `[m] : [S]` were rejected while `f(m)` was accepted, and `if`/`case` joins rejected sealed branches. Rather than grow the relation and change the joins, this part takes the ML design: coercion at named sites, exact consistency elsewhere.

- **OCaml**: signature matching happens at `module M : S = …`, at functor application, at `(module M : S)`, and a functor body is sealed to its result signature; nowhere else is there subtyping between module types, and module-typed function types are not contravariant.
- **1ML** (Rossberg, ICFP 2015, Fig. 4): the subtyping judgment with a coercion appears in exactly three expression rules, EAPP (`E : T` is application sugar), ESEAL, and EIF, whose conditional is annotated in the core syntax so each branch is checked against the annotation with no join. There is no standalone subsumption rule. This part has the first two; forwarding into `if`/`case` branches is a follow-up that depends on a fix to how those joins report in analysis mode.

## What changed

- `Typ.coercion(ctx, ~from, ~to_)` (was `ana_meet`): coercive subtyping, consistency or, structurally through tuple components, a signature with more members than declared (`Typ.sig_sub`). The arrow arm is gone.
- `StaticsBase.subsume(~coercible, …)` picks `Typ.coercion` or `Typ.meet` for `fixed_typ`, `expectation_mismatch_mark` and `syn_ana_ok_common`; the flipped `_pat` variants are gone and patterns are exact.
- `Statics.uexp_to_info_map` and its `go` take `~coercible=false`. `Asc`, `Let` (all analyses of the definition), `ModuleExp` and `Ap` set it on their operand; `Parens`, `Projector`, `DynamicErrorHole`, `Closure`, `Filter`, `TupLabel`, tuple components and a `Fun`'s body pass it on; nothing else does. A sealed function body carries the sealing cast and the function's codomain is the body's checked type.
- `ErrorPrint` and the cursor inspector say "wider type … an ascription seals the extra members" when the coercion would have succeeded.
- `ModuleExtraMembers` (part 1) stays retired; hole-named signature members are not required members.
- Dynamics: the last binding step yields the module value marked final (re-traversal double-sampled probed literals). Incremental evaluation: a binding's ascription type is part of its reuse provenance (`Ascribed(Typ.t)`).
- Doc slide: section E becomes its own Module Sealing slide (evaluating the combined slide overflowed the Web Worker's stack); its contravariance item is replaced by the list example with its ascribed fix.

Tests: the sealing group in `Test_Statics_Modules.re` (sites, depth, hidden helpers, the `if` boundary with the mark on the branch, the sealed function body) plus a non-sites group (list element, module literal in a list, tuple argument, annotated tuple literal, labeled component, tuple variable, case pattern, ascribed scrutinee, parentheses, let body, `if` branches, constructor argument, sum variable, no contravariance); `Typ.Coercion` in `Test_Typ.re`; runtime sealing and probes unchanged.

## Verification

`make test-quick` green (3718 tests) · `dune build @check --profile release` clean · CLI probes for each row above.
