title: Modules II, part 1: first-class signature types and module values
body:
Bottom of stack #2496 (~~width subtyping~~ sealing at coercion sites, abstract type members, module-typed functions and the rest follow). This one replaces the labeled-tuple gloss described in `docs/modules.md` with real module statics and dynamics; the next two add ~~width subtyping~~ sealing and abstract type members on top.

## Statics

- `Sig` is a distinct, first-class type. `Typ.desugar_sig` is gone and a signature is inconsistent with a labeled tuple type in both directions. Signatures are dependent records: `free_vars`, `subst`, `normalize` and `meet` treat type members as sequential binders, and `meet` requires the same member names (exact; ~~width arrives in the next PR~~ sealing at coercion sites arrives in the next PR). `Sig.re` exposes the member view (`Val`, `TypeManifest`).
- A module synthesizes its signature in source order (`ModuleHelpers.module_sig_type`). Against an annotated signature, manifest type members are checked (~~`ModuleTypeMemberMismatch` on the `type` item~~ `ModuleTypeMemberMismatch` on the member's definition type, so the editor highlights `Bool` in `type T = Bool` rather than the whole item) and substituted into member expectations; missing members mark the module (`ModuleMissingMembers`), unless one of the items is a hole where a member could still be bound, in which case the missing members are assumed (see below).
- `M.T` resolves through the module variable's signature (`Typ.path_sig`, including `M.P.T`, module aliasing and signature aliases). The `TVarEntry` injection in the `Let` case is removed. `Dot` projects signature members. A type path rooted at a value of unknown type (`let n : ? = … in let y : n.T = …`) is accepted, since `n` may be a module; a root of a known non-signature type is still `TypWantModule`.
- `module M : S` is a signature item too (`SigModule`), so capitalized sub-modules can be declared inline. Module items report the member they declare in the cursor inspector.

## Dynamics

- Modules evaluate as modules. `Transition.re` steps `Module(items)` item by item with sequential scoping; an evaluated binding becomes the dynamics-only item `ModVal(x, v)`, and a module of `ModVal`s is a value. `Dot` reads bindings by name; ascribing a module value to a signature seals it. New `EvalCtx.ModuleItem` / `ModuleVal` contexts.
- Statics still lowers a module body to a `Let`/`TyAlias` chain for type checking (reusing the `Let` and pattern machinery); elaboration refolds the checked chain back into a `Module`.

## Also

TyDi qualified completions read signature members; the cursor inspector and `ErrorPrint` render the new marks; `docs/modules.md` and the Modules doc slide are rewritten; tests migrated (module types are signatures, module values are modules). One skipped test pins a known gap: `{ let ? : ? }` should eventually match any member once the hole is filled.

## Fixes to `dev` code, carried at the bottom of this PR

Three bugs in code that is on `dev` today, surfaced while building this stack. They were briefly a separate PR (#2528, closed) and now sit as the first three commits here, each with a test that fails without its fix on `dev`.

- **Incremental eval: a binding's ascription is part of its provenance.** Editing a binding's ascription in place left its dependents reusing values computed under the old type: the reuse provenance recorded only *that* the binding went through an ascription, not which type. An ascription changes the bound value (a cast; here, sealing a module), so the type now travels in the provenance as `Ascribed(Typ.t)`, compared with `Typ.fast_equal`. Pinned by retyping `let x : Int = 1 in x` as `x : Bool` in place — the one ascription edit whose stale value is observable on `dev` (retyping to `?` or relabeling a tuple is not: casts are stripped by the comparison and a projection's index comes from the new static type). Part 2 keeps the signature form of the test, where dropping a member from `module Stack : { ... }` must invalidate the cached `Stack.default`.
- **Keep a printed `:` apart from a following operator.** `:` is one of `Token.ascii_operator_chars` and `Token.is_potential_operator` matches any run of them, so a `:` printed flush against a leading-plus sum lexed as the single token `:+`, which is no form at all; Menhir has its own lexer and split them, so the two parsers disagreed (the Slow `Menhir and maketerm are equivalent` fuzz property found it). `should_add_space` kept `:` apart from `$` and `!` as a list of two characters; it now asks `Token.begins_with_potential_operator` for the property they share (`$` stays listed: it is a name character). Pinned at the `should_add_space` level here and on `{ let _ : + Adid }` in part 4.
- **Stop re-parenthesizing the content of a Parens type.** Printing a parenthesized min-precedence type was not idempotent: `type T = + Adid` came out as `type T = (+ Adid)` and each further trip added a layer. `parenthesize_typ`'s `Parens` case ran its content through `paren_typ_at(Precedence.min)`, which wraps exactly the types whose precedence *is* min — a bare sum, a multihole, a `Sig` — on every pass. The wrapper being emitted is already the protection, so the content needs none; `already_paren` is still passed down. Pinned by printing `type T = + Adid in ?` twice; part 4 keeps the `Sig` form.

## Known gaps

Module structure, roughly by how much each blocks real programs. None is a
regression; they are what this construct does not reach yet.

- **Constructors declared inside a module are not members of it** (#2243).
  Qualified access fails and the bare name leaks into the enclosing scope, so
  two modules declaring the same constructor make that name unusable. This
  breaks the ordinary idiom of a type and its operations in one module.
- **Signature items accept arbitrary patterns and then bind nothing** (#2242).
  A tuple-pattern member is accepted, declares no members, and member access
  on the binder then reports that the module has none.
- **No `include` and no `open`** (#2260, #2261). Reusing a signature or
  bringing members into scope is copy-paste, which makes larger signatures
  repetitive.
- **No module destructuring in patterns.** Only a name, optionally
  signature-annotated, can bind a module; there is no way to pull several
  members out at once.
- **No mutually recursive modules**, and modules are values inside one
  program rather than compilation units, so there is no import story.
- **Module equality is not rejected statically**, only incomparable at
  runtime.

## Verification

`make dev` clean · `make test-quick` green (3665 tests) · `dune build @check --profile release` clean · the editor checked by hand on the two slides.

## Follow-up commits

- **Module-aware projection errors, one error per differing type member.** `m.y` with no member `y` now marks the label (`ModuleMemberNotFound`, which also says when `y` is a type member used as a value) and gives the dot only a message, the design the type-level `M.Fake` already had. `M.T` with no type member `T`, a missing sub-module in `M.P.T`, and a value used as the root of a type path get module-aware marks and wording; the dot marks that said "tuple" say "module or tuple". A manifest type member that differs from the signature is reported once, ~~on its `type` item~~ on its definition type: members are checked against the module's own definition. Slide items 11a to 11d show the messages.
- **The function shorthand binds a member.** `let f(x) = ...` in a module body exported `x` rather than `f` (#2467, #2295): binders were read with `Pat.bound_vars`, which treats an applied pattern as a constructor application. The lowering reads a let item's binder through `FunctionSugar.binder` and annotates a shorthand at its name with the type its signature expects; the `Let` case of statics then desugars it exactly as it does a top-level shorthand.
- **A cyclic member path is a type error, not a crash.** A signature that names a same-named outer binding, `let m = { type T = Int } in let m : { type T = m.T } = ...`, has no weak head normal form: normalizing `m.T` asks `path_sig` what `m` denotes, finds the inner `m` (`path_sig` looks in the value namespace, new with module paths), whose signature defines `T` as `m.T`, and is back where it started. Running out of fuel raised `Failure("weak_head_normalize exceeded 1000 recursive calls")` and aborted the whole analysis. Out of fuel the type now comes back unreduced — stuck, which is what the function already returns for anything else it cannot reduce — so the member that fails to match it gets an ordinary `ModuleTypeMemberMismatch`; anything that reduced within the fuel budget reduces identically. Pinned at the `Typ` level and on both the `let m : S` and `module M : S` programs. (The cyclic *alias* form, `type x = x.a`, cannot reach this until part 4's `path_sig` catch-all arm; it is pinned there.)
- **Expectations reach sub-modules and destructured binders.** `modlet_pat` annotated only a bare variable binder with its expected member type. It now annotates every variable inside a destructuring pattern (`let (a, b) = …` is checked as `(a : Int, b : Int)`, so a wrong component is reported on that component) and `module Inner = …` items, which receive the sub-signature the outer signature declares for them, so a member the sub-module lacks, a differing type member or a wrong definition is reported inside the sub-module rather than as one mismatch on the outer module. A binder the user annotated keeps its annotation; the refold strips the synthetic ascriptions by walking the user's pattern and its elaboration together. Slide items 20a and 20b. The form of the kept-annotation test that needs ~~width subtyping~~ sealing lives in part 6.
- **The Modules doc slide is split: Modules (construction, qualified type access) and Module Signatures (signatures, signature errors).** Evaluating the combined slide needed about 750KB of stack and the Web Worker that evaluates programs has about half the main thread's stack, so the first edit on the slide overflowed it. Section letters and item numbers are unchanged. Later parts add Module Sealing, Module Abstract Types and Module Implicits the same way.
- **A type path may be rooted at a value of unknown type.** `let n : ? = 1 in let y : n.T = …` reported "n is a value of type ?, not a module"; a root of unknown type may be a module, so the path is accepted and its type is unknown.
- **A differing type member is marked on its definition type**, not the whole `type` item; the CLI and the cursor inspector share one message for the mark on the type side.
- **A hole among the items stands in for missing members.** A module checked against a signature reported every member it lacked even when one of its items was a hole that could still be filled with them: a hole item, or a hole in a binding position of a `let` pattern or module or type name. Such a module now assumes the missing members, so nothing is reported and the module has the signature's type. Only binding positions count (not labels, constructors, definitions or annotations), and a wildcard binder still reports. Slide item 20c.
- **Editing: an incomplete tile takes the form its shards spell in its sort.** Typing a second module item before the `;` of the first made it an expression `let` owed an `in`; adding the `;` then left it incomplete in the module body, with the `in` stuck in the backpack. When a tile's label has no form in the sort at its position and its present shards spell a complete compound form of that sort, remolding gives it that form, so the item completes as `let y = 2` (`type` and `module` items likewise). Compound forms only: a lone keyword shard must not become a variable, which the agent-tools reserved-keyword paste test guards.

Closes #2467. Closes #2295.

title: Fumola livelits: running an incremental Fumola runtime from Hazel
body:
An experimental integration between Hazel and **Fumola**, a language whose execution model uses Adapton / demanded computation graphs, so that editing and re-running a program can reuse prior computation rather than starting over.

**Try it:** `hazel.org/build/fumola-livelit-mvp`, or `make && make serve`. No setup — the Fumola runtime is fetched from its published build. Type `^fumola_thunk` or `^fumola_editor` then space.

**Depends on** [Adapton/fumola#45](https://github.com/Adapton/fumola/pull/45) and [#46](https://github.com/Adapton/fumola/pull/46), both merged. Nothing binary is tracked here.

# Purpose of the MVP

Hazel and Fumola are each exploring live, responsive evaluation, and each relates itself to spreadsheets. Hazel's livelits are one such semantics; Fumola's demanded computation graph, where editing a program repairs prior computation rather than redoing it, is another.

This branch puts the second one *inside* the first: a Fumola runtime becomes something a Hazel program can hold and name, so two live evaluation models sit in one document, side by side, where they can be compared and composed.

Two livelits are the ways of reaching across. A **thunk** livelit holds a program whose value you are editing: it is wrapped in a named thunk, so re-forcing that name on each edit is what lets Fumola repair rather than recompute. An **editor** livelit holds a program run at the top level, for setting things up and for the operations a thunk cannot host — writing cells that thunks will read, making bindings that outlive the program, and reaching Adapton's own introspection.

**Instance ids are what keep Fumolas apart.** An id names a runtime, so a document can hold several independent ones, and livelits sharing an id share a store, a set of bindings and a demanded computation graph. Isolation and communication are both just a question of which id you write.

That framing is what makes the rest of this interesting. Every livelit shipped today is self-contained: `^slider`'s model *is* its value. These are the first whose model holds a **name for state that lives outside Hazel**, so the interesting question is not the widget but what it means for a Hazel value to denote something a foreign runtime owns.

A livelit's model names an entry of an external store

```text
Σ : FumolaInstanceId -> FumolaRuntimeState
```

held by the Fumola wasm module and reached through the `window.fumola` shim. The Fumola interpreter and its demanded computation graph are deliberately *not* serialized into the model; only the name is. Three consequences, each implemented explicitly rather than inherited:

- **Editing preserves the name**, so an edit re-evaluates against the same live runtime and state written in one edit is there in the next.
- **Expansion is an observation of Σ**, never a second source of truth in the model.
- **The runtime does the work.** There is no repair API in Fumola and none was needed: a thunk livelit wraps its program as ``force(`name := thunk { ... })``, and re-assigning that name and forcing it again is what makes the edit incremental. `:=` and `thunk` do the rest.

## Two livelits and a value

| | |
| --- | --- |
| `^fumola_thunk(instance, name, program)` | wraps its program in a named thunk; incremental across edits |
| `^fumola_editor(instance, program)` | evaluates at the top level; no reuse, but bindings outlive it |
| `FumolaPeek` | not a livelit — what a returned *pointer* becomes |

`^fumola_editor` is strictly more expressive: you can write the ``force(... := thunk { ... })`` yourself. What the thunk livelit adds is generating that wrapper with a distinct name. The editor is also the only way to reach what the wrapper forbids — `Adapton.reset()` clears the store the enclosing force is still inside, and `Adapton.peekForce` asserts there.

The **thunk name** is Fumola source for a symbol, parsed by Fumola itself, so ``​`myThunk``, `7` and ``​`a(`b)`` all work and Hazel needs to know about none of them. It is written rather than derived on purpose: a name taken from a Hazel id would start a *new* thunk whenever that id changed, quietly losing the history the thunk exists to keep.

Both name an instance, so **two livelits carrying the same id share one runtime**.

# Simple programs to try

Both livelits require an annotation — they only expand in checking mode, since the result's shape depends on the program.

**State surviving an edit.** Run this, then edit the program to just `get(1)`; it still reads `2`.

```
let n : Int = ^fumola_thunk(0, "`a", "1 := 2; get(1)") in n
```

**The worked example**, also in Documentation → Livelits → builtins. Three livelits over one runtime:

```
let x  : Int = ^fumola_thunk(0, "`t", "`x := 137 + 137; 137") in
let x_ : Int = ^fumola_editor(0, "pointer(`x)") in
let y  : Int = ^fumola_editor(0, "force(pointer(`t))") in
(x, x_, y)                    ->  (137, peek(`x)! = 274, 137)
```

The thunk writes a cell and returns 137. The first editor asks for a pointer to that cell, which arrives as a peek value showing **both the reference and what it holds**, typing as `Int` so the ascription is satisfied and evaluation continues through it. The second editor forces the thunk the *first livelit* made, by its name ``​`t`` — which is why explicit thunk names matter.

**Values that cross the boundary**, each verified against the runtime:

```
1 + 2                       ->  3
`counter := 41; get(`counter) + 1
                            ->  42
(1 := 10, 2 := 20)          ->  a pair of peek values
{x = 1; y = true}           ->  a Hazel record
peek(1)                     ->  Some(10)
peek(404)                   ->  None
`hello                      ->  "hello"
Gcd.gcd(12, 18)             ->  6     (module library, no import)
```

**Things needing `^fumola_editor`**, since they cannot run inside a thunk:

```
Adapton.reset()             ->  ()
Adapton.peekEvents()        ->  a list of records carrying events, spaces and times
```

**Always in scope:** `pointer(s)`, `get(s)`, `peek(s)`. They exist because Hazel string literals admit no escapes — `Token.is_string` permits at most two quote characters in a token — so a livelit's program can never contain a `"`, and every adapton primitive needs one. Note that `:=` coerces its left side into a pointer but `@` does not, so a cell is read back with `get(s)`.

**The module library is compiled into the runtime** and bound at the top level: `Adapton`, `List`, `LazyList`, `PureList`, `LevelTree`, `HashMap`, `Counters`, `RandomInput`, `MergeSort`, `Gcd`, `DelayedPut`. Anything else is reachable by path.

# Future work to explore

**Expansions are not typed.** Statics splices a livelit's expansion in as an already-elaborated term and never traverses it ([Statics.re](src/language/statics/Statics.re)). Three things follow: a livelit nested in an expansion is never expanded, so `FumolaPeek` cannot render as a widget; constructors inside an expansion are never resolved; and no annotation anywhere in the program can reach inside one. This branch works around it with type-directed expansion, but making expansions real syntax is the change that would dissolve several problems at once.

**Sum types across the boundary.** Fumola tags are structural and live in one flat namespace: `#Bar(3)` is a value whether or not anyone declared `Bar`. Hazel constructors are declaration-bound. So the boundary is lossy in the direction that matters — Fumola hands you a tag, Hazel needs a tag *plus* a home type. Expansion now resolves tags against the expected type, but round-tripping Hazel → Fumola → Hazel can still land in a different sum type.

**`Space` and `Time` both declare a `Symbol` constructor.** With an expected type it resolves correctly; without one it falls back to a context lookup that could pick either.

**Generative copy is not implemented.** A copied livelit inherits its original's instance id and shares its execution history. Doing it properly needs a projector identity that survives a model edit, which this branch does not establish.

**Instance lifetime across sessions.** A saved program naming instance 17 in a session with no `Σ(17)` realizes a fresh runtime, which then has no history. What *should* happen on reload is unsettled.

**The peek snapshot is load-bearing.** `FumolaPeek` carries a value that is sound only because it is regenerated on every expansion. Persisting one into a saved model would silently disagree with the runtime.

**Hazel has no parameterized types.** There is no type-level application, so `Option` is monomorphic with payload `?`. That is why `Option(SomeThing)` cannot be written, and why an option's payload type is lost on the way across.

**Pre-existing livelit issues found along the way**, two fixed here and two not — see the section below.

**Smaller ones.** Instance creation costs ~250ms and the wasm is 5.5MB, both from compiling in the module library; `Dot` symbols have no Fumola parser support; and `Adapton.peekForce` still fails inside a thunk, so introspection wants the editor.

# Pre-existing issues found along the way

Four problems in the livelit machinery with nothing to do with Fumola. Two were in the way and are fixed here; two are recorded but untouched.

**Fixed — clicking any livelit crashed.** `JsUtil.get_elem_by_id` ends in `assert(false)`, and `LivelitProj.focus_pointer` calls it on every pointer click — but the projector attaches its id only where `get_model` succeeds, so the `No livelit found` fallback asserted. Confirmed against deployed `dev`: `^slider` and `^emotion` crash on click there today.

**Fixed — a livelit with a text field could not be typed into.** Clicking the field focused it, then `Focus` refocused the projector's wrapper `<div>`, which has no `tabindex`; focusing an unfocusable element drops focus to `<body>`. So the field lost focus the instant it was clicked, and the only way to edit was to unproject the livelit. **This affects `^js` too.**

**Not fixed — livelits do not render in the Documentation slides.** All of them show `No livelit found`; verified on deployed `dev`. This is also why the two above went unnoticed: the widgets are invisible in the one place the docs point you at.

**Not fixed — livelits have no keyboard handoff.** `focusable.keyboard = None`, so arrow-key navigation into and out of one does not work. `TextAreaProj` is the model to follow: it puts the projector id directly on its textarea, which would subsume the focus fix above.

# Reviewer notes

- **The livelit interface changed**: `view` now takes `~id`, and `expand` takes `~id`, `~ana` and a `type_tools` record. Closures rather than a `Ctx.t`, because `Ctx` already depends on `LivelitCtx` and naming it there would be circular. The other three livelits ignore the new arguments.
- **One new `exp_term` constructor**, `FumolaPeek`, which is the only change under `term/`. The sweep touched ~19 files; the parts worth reading are dynamics, statics, unboxing, equality and `ExpToSegment`.
- **Nothing binary is tracked.** The runtime is published to GitHub Pages from the Fumola repo, deliberately rather than as a release asset: release downloads carry no `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header, so a browser can never fetch one. An earlier revision committed the wasm into `src/web/www`, which put it in the deployed preview directory and made Pages fail to build the entire `hazelgrove/build` site.
- **A red `Full tests` run on this branch is probably #2499, not this PR.** `Evaluator.Properties` checks randomly generated programs, and a different sample is drawn each run, so a case that fails shows up as intermittent. It failed once here on `05be2f0276` -- a commit whose full suite passes locally, on a branch that does not touch the evaluator. The shrunk counterexample and seed in #2499 suggest a real disagreement between incremental and fresh evaluation rather than harness noise.

title: SPIKE: compile the Hazel evaluator with wasm_of_ocaml and benchmark it
body:
## What this is

A **spike**, not a merge candidate. It answers one question: is Hazel's
evaluator meaningfully faster compiled by `wasm_of_ocaml` than by
`js_of_ocaml`? The evaluator is compute-bound and already runs off the UI
thread in a Web Worker, which makes it the part of Hazel most likely to
benefit from Wasm GC — boundary-crossing costs, which is where Wasm usually
loses, barely apply there.

## The constraint that shaped the whole branch

`virtual_dom` v0.16 requires `js_of_ocaml < 6.0.0`. `wasm_of_ocaml` is only
released from 6.0.1 onward. **They cannot coexist in one opam switch.**

Everything else here follows from that:

- the benchmark links only `language` + `menhirParser`, never `haz3lcore`
  or `web`;
- parsing goes through `menhirParser` rather than the zipper path the CLI
  uses, since `PersistentZipper`/`MakeTerm` live in `haz3lcore`;
- `language` had to be made Bonsai-free, which is what the `util` split and
  the livelit removal are for.

## Changes

- **Split `util`** into `util` (pure + `js_of_ocaml` only) and `util_web`
  (Bonsai/Virtual_dom). `Util_web` re-exports all of `Util`, so most
  consumers only changed `open Util` to `open Util_web`. `JsUtil` and `Key`
  were each *split* rather than moved, keeping their `js_of_ocaml`-only
  majority in `util` — that alone avoided ~48 files of churn.
- **Dropped livelits from the language core.** The three builtin livelits
  construct vdom directly and were the last thing holding `Virtual_dom`.
  `LivelitCtx` keeps its types so `Ctx.LivelitEntry` still typechecks, but
  nothing populates it and `LivelitProj` renders a placeholder.
- **Added `bench/wasm/`**: the benchmark, a switch-setup script, and a
  runner that builds both backends from the same compiler version.
- Bumped `(lang dune 3.16)` to `3.17` for `(modes wasm)`.

Resulting dependency closure is
`language → util → {ptmap, bignum, uuidm, unionFind, csv}` — verifiably
Bonsai-free.

## What it gives up

The livelit deletion is the part that must not merge. The principled version
registers livelit views from the web layer rather than deleting them; the
`util` split, by contrast, is worth keeping on its own merits and is the
same prerequisite an Internet Computer port would need.

Two livelit tests were removed (`^slider(50)` elaboration, `^emotion(50)`
statics-map ids) because they assert behaviour the builtins provided. The
`^^slider` tests exercise the projector, a separate mechanism, and are
untouched.

## Verification

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| `dune build @check` (dev) | clean |
| `dune build src` (release, `-warn-error +A`) | clean |
| `@test-quick` | 3457 tests, 0 failures |
| benchmark runs end-to-end on node 22 | yes |

## Numbers

Not yet — the comparison needs the second opam switch, which is still being
built. A `js_of_ocaml` 5.9.1 smoke run gives 607 ms plain / 596 ms incr on
`bench/eval-bench.hz`, but that is *not* the baseline: `run.sh` rebuilds
both backends from the same 6.x compiler so the delta is attributable to the
backend rather than the toolchain. Results to follow in a comment.

Caveat worth stating up front: `eval-bench.hz` is a single workload. Under
`wasm_of_ocaml` the OCaml heap is managed by the browser's collector rather
than OCaml's, so allocation-heavy and allocation-light programs may not move
in the same direction — one number is a signal, not a characterization.

## Running it

```
bench/wasm/setup-switch.sh
git worktree add --detach ../hazel-wasm-bench wasm-eval-bench-spike
cd ../hazel-wasm-bench && bench/wasm/run.sh hazel-wasm 20
```

Node 22+ is required; Wasm GC postdates the node 18 this repo otherwise
builds against.

title: Report each error once, not once per wrapper
body:
Follows #2488, and parked here rather than folded into it until reviewers weigh in on which layer the fix belongs in (see https://github.com/hazelgrove/hazel/pull/2488#issuecomment-5529767668).

## The problem

A transparent wrapper restates the marks of the term it wraps — `Parens` and `Projector` in `Statics` pass `~marks` straight through — so one error occupies a chain of nested ids and the problems sidebar lists every one of them:

| program | static errors reported |
| --- | --- |
| `y` | 1 |
| `(y)` | 2 |
| `((y))` | 3 |
| `^s(1)` (mistyped `expand`) | 1 |
| `^^livelit(^s(1))` (same) | 2 |

Not livelit-specific, but guaranteed to bite for livelits: a use is always inside a projector, so a `BadLivelitExpansion` was always duplicated.

## The fix

Collapse each chain at the collection layer (`ProblemCollection.make_problem_context`). `Statics` hands a wrapper the child's mark list itself, so physical equality identifies exactly the ids that inherited a mark — never two equal-looking marks on unrelated terms — and the innermost id of a chain is the one that owns it.

Ids under a projector have no measurement of their own, so when the owner of a mark is hidden the row is reported at the innermost wrapper the user can actually see: the projector. That keeps the row clickable and lets it highlight with the caret.

`statics.error_ids` is untouched, so code decorations — including the projector's own error styling — are unchanged.

## The open question

The alternative is to stop propagating marks through wrappers in `Statics` at all. Cleaner in principle, but the projector's error decoration reads the projector node's info, so it would go with it. Happy to move the fix there instead if that's the preference.

## Testing

Four cases added to `Test_ProblemCollection`: parens don't multiply an error, a collapsed chain reports the marked term, a projected livelit use reports one error, a hidden marked term reports at its projector. `ProblemCollection` (19), `UserLivelits` (34), `AgentTools` (174) and `ErrorPrint` (5) pass.

title: Type-check the expansion of each user-defined livelit
body:
`user-livelits` does the heavy lifting. This is a small modification on top of it.

Before:

- No `Expansion` type member being looked at.
- No check against this absent member.

Now:

- The type member `Expansion` is required, and so are `Model` and `Action`.
- The check is performed for each expansion, on its output.

The tuple definition form goes with this, having nowhere to declare the types.

### Coming into alignment with livelits in PLDI 2021

**Part 1 — this PR.** The check against the statically named type, performed at the dynamic sites. That is the paper's own strategy rather than an approximation of it: §3.2.5 records that Hazel does not statically check `expand`'s definition, and that the parameterized expansion is instead "validated at each livelit invocation site, with errors reported to the client." With no splices that expansion takes no arguments, so validating it degenerates to checking the expansion at the expansion type.

**Parts 2+ — outside the scope here, and absent from `dev` too.** These introduce:

- the `SpliceRef` primitive type and its operations — `new_splice`, `set_splice` and `eval_splice`, in the paper's `UpdateCmd` and `ViewCmd` monads;
- the quoted AST — `Exp`, an encoding of Hazel's syntax, whose introduction form is quasiquotation, `` `0` `` (§3.2.1);
- `expand` extended to return a pair with that list of `SpliceRef`s, as in Fig. 3 of the [paper](https://hazel.org/papers/livelits-pldi2021.pdf): `expand : Model -> (Exp, List(SpliceRef))`.

The pair is there because "the expansion must treat splices parametrically" (§3.2.5): the first component takes one argument per listed `SpliceRef` and returns the expansion type. Note that `expand` itself stays pure — splices bring the monads, but not to `expand`.

The quotation is entailed by the splices rather than an independent choice. We can do without `Exp` here only because the splice list is empty: a closed expansion need not be code at all, so `expand` returns an ordinary value of the expansion type and application does the work quotation would have done. Splices force the issue, since a parameterized expansion embedding client-site expressions cannot be an ordinary value. (§3 flags the paper's quasiquotation and do notation as presentational sugar rather than implemented Hazel, so both are new surface syntax, not just new library types.)

The paper names one further alternative we are not pursuing: definition-site verification via "a typed quotation system as in, e.g., MetaOCaml." That is a distinct thing from the quasiquotation above — untyped quotation merely introduces `Exp`, whereas typed quotation is what would move Part 1's check from the invocation site to the definition site. The paper notes it is awkward because "the type of the quotation depends on the type of each splice in the splice list."

body:
Stacked on #2250, with #2513 on top. **All three PRs in this stack are meant to be merged together** — they are split for review only.

## Summary

Adopts the text-authored tutorial system from `probes-study-rebuilt` and converts all 25 lessons to it.

Each lesson used to be an `.ml` file holding a serialized zipper alongside its prose — ~26,000 lines of generated data that had to be regenerated by hand for any edit. Lessons are now plain-text `.hzt` files in `hazel-programs/tutorial/`, embedded with `ppx_blob` via a new `src/tutorialslides` library (a clone of `src/docslides`) and parsed into `Tutorial.spec` at startup by `TutorialText`:

```
@title      the lesson name
@flags      wrapper show_report version=N id=<uuid>
@prompt     markdown for the instructions panel
@hint       one-liner
@reference  markdown for the Task Reference sidebar
@hints      one per line
@code       editor contents (holes are ¿, or ? to survive a container)
@test       hidden tests
```

Net: **+2,855 / −26,285**.

The conversion was mechanical. `TutorialDecode` reads whatever lesson list is compiled in and emits `.hzt` via `MarkerParse.to_text`, so the CLI landed first and generated all 25 from the existing `Tu_*.ml`. `./hazel tutorial-verify` checks that each slide's impl and tests are a fixed point of `to_text ∘ of_text ∘ to_text`; all 25 are. `TaskRefDocs` is gone — decode inlines each lesson's composed `task_reference` into its own `@reference`.

One marker is ours rather than upstream's: **`@title`**. Upstream derives the title from the filename, which would renumber every lesson and mangle four of them (`Reverse Function Application (Pipelining)` losing its parens; `and`/`of` capitalising). `@title` pins the exact title and falls back to the derived one.

## Bugs the round-trip check surfaced

- **`$==` in the Case Expressions and Folding Lists hidden tests.** `$` does not lex in Hazel, so those six tests were unsatisfiable and always reported indeterminate — a live bug the serialized form hid. Now `==`, and both suites pass.
- **`[¿]` in List Literals** collapsed to `[]` on reparse, losing the fillable hole. Explicit `[?]` round-trips.
- Stray trailing grouts in five hidden-test cells.

## Tutorial-mode chrome

Also ports the styling/UX work from that branch:

- a collapsible **Tasks** section, split from the prompt at its `Task` header (all 25 lessons now have one)
- the hint as a keyed `<details>`, so its open state no longer leaks across slides
- first/last slide nav gating — **required**, since `.hzt` `version` defaults to 1 and the old `version > 1` / `version < 10` gates would break
- SAND background, focus-driven cell accent, `{{video:}}` and `{{no_editor}}` prompt markers
- per-slide scroll memory, and driving the slide `<select>` from the model so it follows keyboard navigation
- `Zipper.caret_to_start`, so `@code` loads with the caret at the start of the program

`show_report` changes meaning under the new `show_task_ui` gate — it now marks a slide as a *task* (grading face + report icon) rather than "start with the report panel expanded" — so it is set on the six converted lessons that have real hidden tests. Only Probes, whose sole test is `test true end`, leaves it off.

Four general CSS fixes come along: a broken pin-icon URL in `style.css` (which sits in `www/`, so `../img/` resolved outside it), the test sigil's `z-index` (it painted above projector overlays), `nowrap` on context-menu items, and overscroll containment so a nested horizontal scroll does not fire the browser back-gesture.

## Deliberately left behind

`TutorialProbeStrip` and `TutorialSlideInit` — both are exhaustive hardcoded tables over that branch's own slide ids and need `AutoProbe.t` plus new `ProbeProj.Settings` variants — and the probe/evaluator/Card rework they depend on.

## Test plan

- [x] `make dev` builds clean
- [x] `make test-quick` — 3465/3465
- [x] `./hazel tutorial-verify` — 25/25 slides round-trip cleanly
- [x] All 25 lessons in the dropdown, in order, with their exact original titles
- [x] Tables driven to 3/3 passing; Folding Lists to 3/3 (previously impossible)
- [x] Tasks + Hint collapsibles, grading face and panel, prev/next gating, Task Reference sidebar

title: test: disable two seed-flaky evaluator properties, pin them as expected failures
body:
Two `Evaluator.Properties` QCheck properties fail occasionally.

This disables both and pins each bug deterministically instead. **It fixes neither bug** — #2128, #2372 and #2457 stay open.

| property | issue | reddened |
|---|---|---|
| `Evaluator and stepper are consistent` (case 5) | #2128, dup #2372 | a random local seed while preparing this PR |
| `Incremental eval agrees with fresh eval after a literal edit` (case 7) | #2457 | [33513972427](https://github.com/hazelgrove/hazel/actions/runs/33513972427), [33513747011](https://github.com/hazelgrove/hazel/actions/runs/33513747011), [33412342909](https://github.com/hazelgrove/hazel/actions/runs/33412342909) — three unrelated branches, each dying on case 7 alone |

Disabled the way `Preservation of types (disabled)` already is here: a `test_case` that skips but still `ignore`s the QCheck test, so it keeps compiling and re-enabling is one line.

### The pins

Each disabled property is replaced by a unit test on its issue's counterexample:

- **#2128/#2372** — `fun (x::x) -> x`: one engine freshens the duplicate binder, the other doesn't, and `Equality.semantic.exp` doesn't equate the alpha-variants.
- **#2457** — `{ let x = (); let _ = 4; let true = A }` with the literal bumped: fresh eval substitutes `x` into the residual environment, incremental leaves it a variable.

Both assert the **current, wrong** behaviour, so they go red the day the bug is fixed and name the property to re-enable. Hence not `skip_known_bug` (`test/Test_Elaboration.re:456`, `test/statics/Test_Statics_Prelude.re:269`) — a skipped test can never fail, so it stays silent forever.

So pin and property can't drift, the shared work is extracted and called by both: `reduce_both_engines` and `eval_after_literal_edit`, each returning `None` for vacuous cases (step limit, known-benign raise).

### Notes

**#2408** fixes a different confluence cause — uncollapsed casts in indeterminate `if` branches, not binder freshening — so the #2128 pin should still be red after it lands. Both PRs edit this file; happy to rebase on it, or to drop the confluence half here and keep only the #2457 disable.

**#2397** is untouched: "Pattern equivalence" exhausts node's 4 GB heap on ~1 seed in 6, and an OOM kills the process rather than failing a test, so it can't be pinned this way. Wants a lower `~count`/step limit, separately.

### Verification

`make ci-check` (release, warnings-as-errors over `test/`) and `dune fmt` clean. `Evaluator.Properties` green, including #2457's seeds 3 and 468045375 which previously failed. Both pins confirmed to fail when the disagreement they assert goes away.

title: Colors: one semantic vocabulary, from the config slide to the stylesheets
body:
Stacked on #1591 (`configuration`).

The Colors slide's type used to *be* the CSS variable list with Hazel syntax on
it: `expected_type` was generated from lists of raw custom-property names, and
the header said so outright — "The label IS the CSS custom-property name,
verbatim." So a themer edited CSS internals: `BR2`, `T3`, `shard-caret-tpat`,
`GB1`, and a misspelling (`backback-targets`) that was load-bearing because it
was a CSS name.

This gives the theme an explicit, semantic representation and maps it onto CSS,
then collapses the three stacked CSS vocabularies into one.

## What changed

**The shape of a theme is a type.** `BuiltinsColorScheme.re` holds it as Hazel
types in the builtin context — `ColorSeeds`, `ColorPalette`, `ColorRoles`,
`ColorScheme` — and the slide writes them in its own signatures:
`let theme_of(p: ColorPalette, role: ColorOverrides): ColorScheme`.
`ColorRamp`/`ColorOverrides` are declared in the slide, being seams between its
own two functions. That puts each check on the record a mistake is in; without
it the only analysis is the whole-program one, which lands on the final `case`
as a single inconsistency between two enormous products.

**The slide names roles**, grouped by the part of the UI they dress (`menu`,
`editor`, `cursor`, `hole`, `probe`, …), with a fan-out table in
`ColorConfiguration.re` expanding each field to the CSS properties that carry
it — one field per *decision*, several targets where several properties carry
one decision. ~~`expected_type` and
`all_targets` both derive from that table, so they cannot drift apart.~~
`all_targets` derives from that table; `expected_type` is the named
`ColorScheme`, and a test pins that the slide fills it exactly.

The two layers differ by **reuse, not derivation**: a palette color is one the
theme is built out of, fanned out to several properties at once; a role is one
job a color is put to, usually carrying one. Roles that only forwarded a
stated color are palette entries now, renamed for what they are (`exp-base` →
`probe-value`, `main-base` → `statics-background`).

**~~The palette took the slide's names: `--Y1` → `--attention-2`, `--T1` →
`--surface-1`, `--SAND` → `--code-background`.~~** The rename landed, and then
the names went: nothing read `--ink`, `--frame-1` or the rest — no stylesheet,
no OCaml, no script, and the only references left in the tree were commented
out. A palette color now reaches CSS only under the semantic names the fan-out
gives it, which makes "components consume roles, not the palette" structural
rather than lint-enforced.

**`roles.css` is deleted.** It was a third vocabulary: hand-written aliases
carrying nearly half the component `var()` sites, and its names resolved to far
fewer palette colors than there were names, so `--text-faint`,
`--border-soft` and `--shadow-soft` were one color with no way to separate
them. Every entry was a bare alias, so they fold into the fan-out table and the
theme writes them itself. ~~**No component stylesheet changed** — every site
reads the same names as before.~~ None changed for *that*; elsewhere on the
branch some sites were renamed off the raw palette names.

**`variables.css` has no hand-written color left**: type, timing and the
z-index ladder. ~~Type, a generated block (`make update-css-defaults`, guarded
by a test), and the z-index ladder.~~ The generated defaults are their own
labelled file, `style/theme-generated.css`, byte-identical to what the theme
sets so nothing shifts when it lands.

**The gap is closed.** The colors the theme did not own were dead, pure
indirection, or derived by CSS itself (the `doc` hue rotations, the
`incremental-pending` fades); they are decided in the slide now.

**Two flags, and they compose.** `--hazel-color-scheme` feeds the standard
`color-scheme` property; `--hazel-contrast` is new, so a stylesheet can answer
high contrast with a style query. Four schemes from two booleans, one `case`.

**Also fixed:** `color-scheme` was set nowhere, so native scrollbars rendered
light on a dark editor; the two flags overrode each other instead of composing;
`proj-fold.css` had an inert `color: --var(BLACK)`; and table rows and headers
were near-illegible in high contrast, because a row highlight was placed on the
page's contrast axis when table rows sit on the code background.

**The slide reads better.** It opens with every scheme but the first folded;
tuple extension instead of restating records, direct function definitions, and
a smaller `ColorOverrides` — several of its fields turned out to be one
decision spelled a few ways. `style/README.md` is new, and documents the
dataflow, file ownership and both layers.

## How it is checked

- **Golden** (`test/goldens/colors.tsv`): every property × every scheme.
  Written sorted by name, so a pure restructuring leaves it and
  `theme-generated.css` byte-identical — which is how every refactor after the
  vocabulary work was verified.
- **Reverse substitution** for renames: mapping the new names back reproduces
  every touched file byte for byte.
- **Chrome**, at each stage: every variable resolves to the golden in all four
  schemes, and a stylesheet-only page with no JavaScript resolves them all to
  the light column.
- **`./hazel analyze hazel-programs/config/colors.hz`** names the offending
  term when an annotation stops holding.
- `lint_css_roles.py` rewritten for the two-layer shape: components read roles
  not the palette, only the generated file declares a theme-owned color on
  `:root`, and the dangling-reference ratchet stays.

## Known gaps

- Folding kept "one field per decision", so `--text-faint` and `--border-soft`
  still come off one `palette.frame-1` row. Splitting a case is a two-file
  change; a field per property was rejected as worse to read.
- Two further override merges would each move a color by one ramp step, so
  they want an eye rather than a green test: collapsing the `frame-*` dials,
  and merging `projector.textarea-text` into `inspector.text`.
- **TODO:** we still need some way of enforcing that newly added colors stay
  themeable. The lint catches a component declaring a theme-owned color on
  `:root`, but not a new hardcoded literal in a rule.

title: W2: worker-resident program segments (stacked on modular-editors)
body:
## Goals

Stacked on `modular-editors` (#2469) — review the diff against that base, not dev. This is the experimental next stage of the same perf program: move semantic computation (statics, elaboration, eval bookkeeping) off the UI thread entirely, so the main thread retains only what keystroke latency needs. Everything here is flag-gated and off by default — including shadow mode itself, as of the review fixes (it duplicates statics derivation and worker messaging, so it is a development diagnostic: `__w2shadowToggle(true)` enables it, `__w2flip(true)` implies it). The branch exists to de-risk the architecture with parity evidence before any flip.

## What's here

- **Segment-residency protocol**: the worker holds its own copy of the program segment and applies the same edit deltas the main thread does, so semantic requests ship deltas rather than documents. A headless loopback harness parity-gates worker-side state against the main thread's.
- **Shadow mode**: the app runs the worker pipeline alongside the main-thread one and compares summaries, counting mismatches (`SUMMARY MISMATCH` console reports). This is diagnostic scaffolding, deliberately noisy.
- **Budgeted synchronous statics**: a small time-budgeted synchronous statics pass for the caret's item only, so type-directed feedback at the caret stays immediate even when full statics moves to the worker.
- **Worker summary payload + consumer flip**: the view-side consumers can read statics summaries from the worker instead of the main thread, behind a runtime toggle (`__w2flip`).
- **Instrumentation**: `__staticsProf` per-phase statics-tick diagnostics (gated, zero-cost off); `Test_SerBench` serialization-cost harness (temporary, for the persistence sizing decisions).

## Status / caveats for review

- Codex review findings 1–6 are addressed in `d59762623c`: Resident evals are generation-gated (a rejected delta can no longer evaluate the old program under the new generation's label), recovery is immediate and restart-proof (cached authoritative Full resync on NeedResync and on worker restart, before any retried eval posts), flip toggles bust every DefStatics cache (`reset_caches`), summary grafts update the keyed cache entry and schedule a recalculate (durable + observable), and shadow mode defaults off. Gates in `Test_W2Protocol`.
- Shadow mode (when enabled) reports summary mismatches on some documents; under investigation — treat the comparison logic itself as review-worthy (false positives are as plausible as real divergence).
- The residency protocol's delta-application path remains the highest-value review target: it must reproduce main-thread edit semantics exactly (the loopback parity gate covers what it covers, no more).

title: Concave-grout marker: round-trip operator holes as ⧖
body:
Concave grout printed as `¿`, the same marker as convex grout, so persisted text was ambiguous — and a text-persisted document with an infix hole hit the slow recovering parser on every reload, because `1 ¿ 2` lexes as three operands.

Concave grout now prints as `⧖` (U+29D6) and round-trips through the fast path: lexer token, identifier-class carve-out (same pattern as `¿`), and a `BinHole` production in every sort the editor molds it for — Exp, Pat (including fun parameters), Typ (including fun-parameter ascriptions) and TPat.

Precedence follows the editor's `Precedence.concave_grout`: looser than every binary operator, tighter than `;` and the let/fun/if/case bodies, so `let x = 1 in x ⧖ 2` keeps the hole in the body and `(Int -> Bool) ⧖ String` reduces the arrow first. To express the latter with one token, the arrow-bodied binders (`fun`/`fix`/`typfun`, `poly`/`rec`) take their own `BINDER_BODY` level instead of the arrow token's; their behaviour is otherwise unchanged (the existing Menhir/fuzz/corpus suites pass as before).

Conversion flattens a parsed chain into one flat `MultiHole` and prints a uniform-sort `MultiHole` back as a chain; mixed-sort holes have no textual spelling and stay on the slow path.

Base-type keywords (`Int`, `Bool`, `String`, …) are now constructor patterns in Menhir as they already were in exp position: deleting the arrow in `let x : Int -> Bool` leaves a pattern-level hole beside `Bool`, and that document (and plain `let Bool = 1`) used to fall to the recovering parser on every load.

Gates: `TextRoundtrip.EditedGrout` — 12 programs where grout is left by simulated typing (not hand-written markers) in every sort: the persisted text must fast-parse, keep its grout through the load-time regrout, and reprint as a fixed point. `MenhirParser.ConcaveMarker` — 33 cases pinning Menhir ≡ MakeTerm through the marker load path (`MarkerParse.of_text`, where the marker becomes real grout) across all four sorts — and `TextRoundtrip.ConcaveMarker` (14 fast-parse/fixed-point cases incl. legacy `¿` canonicalization). One divergence class is deliberately not pinned: the sort tag MakeTerm gives a hole's neighbour (`let x : Int ⧖ y` sorts `y` as a type, Menhir as a pattern — same structure, same tokens).

Grammar conflicts: +1 s/r state and +1 r/r state over dev, both in the documented families (UNIT lookahead after `pat ⧖ pat`; funAscAtom sharing nonAscriptingPat), listed in the grammar's KNOWN CONFLICT FAMILIES comment.

title: Migrate src/haz3lcore to Jane Street Core
body:
Migrates `src/haz3lcore` to Jane Street Core — the last layer between `src/language` and `src/web`. Two commits: typed equality then the flip.

**Point-free re-export shims were the interesting failure mode.** `haz3lcore/lang/Token.re` aliases stdlib functions (`let concat = String.concat;`, `let sort_uniq = List.sort_uniq(compare);`). An alias silently inherits Core's argument order and labels, so every caller changes meaning without the alias itself failing to compile. Each one now has an explicit arity:

```reason
let concat = (sep, xs) => String.concat(~sep, xs);
let starts_with = (~prefix, s) => String.is_prefix(s, ~prefix);
```

**Operator sections** are the same hazard in miniature: `(==)(x)` is polymorphic equality partially applied. Six in this library, and they were not all strings — `Skel` compares a `Token.t list`, `Segment` a `Sort.t`.

Also worth noting for review: a `let compare = compare;` inside a comparator module was polymorphic under stdlib and becomes int-only under Core, which breaks the `Set.Make` it feeds. And `Core.Random.State.t` is not `Stdlib.Random.State.t` — QCheck wants the stdlib one, so seeded generators keep `Stdlib.Random`.

## Verification
`make dev` clean · `make test-quick` green (3448) · `dune build --profile release src/haz3lcore` warning-free.

title: Migrate src/web to Jane Street Core
body:
Migrates `src/web` to Jane Street Core — 168 files, the largest library in the stack. Two commits: typed equality (104 sites) then the flip.

`src/web/dune` has **four** OCaml stanzas — libraries `web` and `workerServer` plus executables `main` and `worker` — and all four need the flag. It also compiles 17 `.ml`/`.mli` example files under `exercises/` and `derivation/`, which are easy to miss when sweeping for `.re`.

**Poly usage is much higher here than in `src/language`** — 42 of 223 modules take `open Poly`, versus 4 of 112. View and model code compares whole variants and records constantly, and Poly is exactly the semantics that code already had. It was applied compiler-driven rather than pre-emptively.

**Two things reviewers should look at closely:**
- `DerivationExercise`'s key parser *relies on* `String.index` raising, and catches `Not_found`. Core's `index_exn` raises `Not_found_s`, which that handler would silently stop matching — so it uses `Stdlib.String.index` and `Stdlib.Not_found` on purpose.
- Core's `Option` has `some` but no `none`, and doesn't re-declare the `None`/`Some` constructors. Where the original wrote `Option.None` *deliberately* to disambiguate from another `None` in scope, it's now `Stdlib.Option.none` to preserve that.

title: Migrate src/language to Jane Street Core
body:
Migrates `src/language` to Jane Street Core. **Zero downstream edits** were needed.

Two commits, reviewable separately:

1. **`Make equality explicit at the type in src/language`** — 126 sites, no Core involved. Names the equality witness at each comparison (`String.equal`, `Id.equal`, `Bigint.equal`, or a `[@deriving eq]`-generated one). This lands standalone and is worth reading on its own.
2. **`Migrate src/language to Jane Street Core`** — the flip.

**Equality strategy.** `int` needs nothing (Core permits `=` there, ~92 sites). Concrete types name their witness. Whole-term structural comparison uses `Poly` — 26 explicit `Poly.equal` plus `open Poly` in the four modules whose *job* is structural comparison (`Equality`, `MatchExp`, `DrvTermBase`, `Operators`). `Typ.re` deliberately stays under Core's discipline with its sites fixed individually; it's where an accidental equality matters most.

**Traps worth knowing about for review.** Several stdlib functions have same-named *total* counterparts in Core, so the flip changes the return type rather than failing to compile — `List.hd`/`tl`/`nth`/`find` become options and only break at the use site. `IdTagged.rep_id = List.hd(ids)` silently became `Id.t option` and surfaced two modules away. All swept to `_exn`. `Float.modf` returns a record, not a tuple, and `BuiltinsBase.re` uses `Stdlib.ceil` etc. deliberately — those back Hazel's *language-level* float builtins, so they need to be exact rather than a plausible Core equivalent.

Migrates `src/util` to Jane Street Core. This is the first library in the migration and the minimum atomic step, since `-open Core` applies per dune library — every `.re` in the stanza has to compile at once.

title: Modular editors
body:
## Goals

Two thrusts, deliberately on one branch because they feed each other:

1. **Outline mode + stacked subeditors** as a UI feature: navigate a large program by its structure (modules / definitions / types / tests as a collapsible outline) and edit any definition in a small focused cell while whole-program semantics (results, tests, probes) stay live.
2. **Editor performance**, aimed at concrete editing metrics — per-keystroke latency, held-key throughput, worst-case action spikes, slide switching, reload, and autosave cost — across several modes and use cases: flat editing of large programs, stacked/outline editing, and documentation-style slide decks.

The perf work is not incidental: the stacked UI is only viable if editing a 1k–4k-line program is responsive, so most of the pipeline (statics, parse, remold/regrout, view, persistence) was made incremental along the way.

## Try it

Open Documentation → Mega 1k (a ~1,000-line, 10-module program), click `running_sum` in the outline sidebar, and just that definition opens as an editor: typing costs 40–120ms per keystroke while the whole program's result, tests, and probes stay live below the stack. The same program is unusable to edit on dev. For raw-scale editing, the Documentation → "Perf /" folder has Mega 1k/2k/4k flat slides.

## Outline view

- **Outline sidebar**: modules/definitions/types as a collapsible, resizable tree; error badges attach to the deepest visible row and roll up onto collapsed ancestors; erroring names tint red.
- **Stacked per-definition editors**: clicking ⊙ opens a definition as a header cell (`name : type`, pat-rooted) plus a body cell, stacked in program order with module-path qualifier chips. Contexts are frozen at the definition and refreshed when upstream exports change, so cross-definition renames error their dependents live.
- **Whole-program semantics while stacked**: the master keeps evaluating the spliced program — result strip and test results below the stack, and probes sample even when every call site is outside the open cell (samples appear on placement, no follow-up edit needed).
- **Navigation**: jump-to-definition works across cells (opens the target and aligns it only if it isn't already visible); arrow keys walk the caret seamlessly across header/body/cell boundaries and between stacked panes.
- **Structural ops**: right-click an outline row for new definition / new type / new module below, duplicate, move up/down, delete — segment surgery on the live program, so unchanged definitions keep their ids (open cells and probes stay pinned). Ops cost the changed item plus its downstream users, not the program (mega-2k: ~3s → ~220–260ms steady-state; the term itself is parsed per item and grafted — `MakeTerm.Incr`, exact-parity test-gated). With a cell open at mega-2k, an idle 8s window has zero long tasks.
- **Tests, statements, and trailing bodies in the outline — in every block**: `test …;` statements get rows with live ✓/✗ icons at any depth (module-member tests included), other `…;` statements get `;` rows, and trailing bodies get `⇒` rows — each opens as a headerless cell.
- **Pins and collapse persist** per slide, across slide switches and reloads (name-anchored via outline label paths); collapse is modeled state, so folding no longer bleeds between slides or resets on structural edits.
- **Structural ops at every level**: the row context menu works on module members and function-body items too — inserts mint proper member forms inside modules — and moves stay within their block.
- **Headers got real**: cell statics are projected from the whole-program per-item analysis (one statics run, cells read it) — unannotated headers show their inferred types, module headers have live statics, unused-binder warnings reach headers.
- **Statics in every cell kind**: expression bodies, type-alias bodies, and pat/tpat headers all get cursor-inspector info and sort-correct coloring.
- **Persistence**: autosave is per-item serialized (`ItemPersist`): each top-level item's segment is stored as its own sexp under an ordered roster — the edited item's write is ~3–10ms — and reload restores the segment exactly, incomplete tiles included, with no text parse. A content-changing pause additionally rewrites the whole-document text blob (schema-drift fallback), which keeps an O(document) print on the autosave path (~11ms at 1k / ~27ms at 4k in the headless SerBench harness); making that blob per-item too is an open follow-up. Caret survives reloads via a side key.

## Performance

- **Compositional statics** (`DefStatics`): whole-program statics computed per top-level item with chained contexts; a typical edit re-analyzes the dirty set — the edited item plus export-affected dependents, e.g. 16 of 891 items (56ms headless) on a surgical 4k edit vs 872ms for the cold pass. Member-granular items inside module literals analyze per member. Fixes the browser stack-overflow crash that made mega-2k unloadable. Parity with monolithic statics is test-gated (errors, grafted-elaboration eval, probe capture). Per-document LRU slots make returning to a slide a warm lookup instead of a full cold re-analysis.
- **Sparse remold/regrout** (`Segment`/`Zipper`): remold short-circuits on same-mold tiles; regrout runs only on a caret window whose extent is derived from a read-only normal-form scan, memoized by tile identity — the remold/regrout phase drops from ~1.2s per 60 keystrokes at 4k lines to ~1ms/action. Parity-gated: the test runner executes both the sparse and the global pipeline on every call and asserts equivalence across the whole suite.
- **Read-free caret reveal** (`CaretReveal`): scroll-into-view no longer forces layout on every keystroke — the caret decoration publishes its model-side row geometry; during typing bursts the reveal is pure arithmetic against mirrored scroll state, with a same-frame rAF anchor read only on cold (post-pause) reveals and a throttled heal for drift. Held-key benchmarks at 4k: enter p95/max 550/936 → 133/448, letter 367/960 → 200/360.
- **Identity-preserving splices**: stacked-mode edits re-mint only the changed item's pieces, which is what makes the per-item dirty tracking (statics, persistence, vdom) actually fire; plus cached stacked parse and outline vdom memo for the stacked-mode edit spikes.
- **Incremental view**: chunked measurement and per-chunk content-keyed vdom — 4k flat edit ~1.6s → ~100ms attributable; 2k edit 690 → ~53ms.
- **Text round-trip for operator holes**: the printer now spells concave grout ⧖ (convex stays ¿), so documents containing infix holes survive text persistence without hitting the quadratic recovering parser (previously a multi-minute reload at ~27k chars). Lexer/parser support landed separately on dev (#2479); this branch carries the integration.
- **Worker-resident incremental eval cache / streaming overhaul / memory fixes**: unchanged from the earlier description — request payloads no longer ship the previous cache; incremental stream collector (parity-gated); exponential co_ctx leak fixed; undo snapshots compacted; render-generation closure chain broken. Mega-2k slide open: ~47s main-thread busy → ~3s.

## Review notes

The design docs live in a gitignored `plans/` tree, so this description is the context. Recent, least-reviewed range: `9c24363bcc..8e0c9d7dbc` (sparse regrout, caret reveal, per-item persistence, ⧖ integration); older subsystems have had more soak time.

Codex review findings 1–3 are addressed in `29b726d3c8` (occurrence-qualified sexp-encoded outline paths, content-key-tagged pending restore state, CaretReveal single listener + caret-identity anchoring), with gates in `Test_OutlinePaths`.

Where extra scrutiny would help most:
- `src/haz3lcore/tiles/Segment.re` — the normal-form scan (`stale_in_seg`/`stale_affix_ids`) and its identity memo (global id-keyed table, pointer-validated, 200k cap): memo soundness and multi-editor sharing.
- `src/haz3lcore/zipper/Zipper.re` — `split_window`/`window_bound`: the caret-window bounds for sparse regrout (the window bound is deliberately the boundary solid's shape *complement*; threading the true shape double-decides out-of-scope runs).
- `src/haz3lcore/zipper/ItemPersist.re` + `src/web/view/ScratchPersist.re` — write ordering (items → roster → GC), load fallback on any inconsistency, and the root-repair path.
- `src/util/CaretReveal.re` — mirrored scroll geometry and the WAAPI-vs-CSS animation filtering (the caret's CSS blink must not pin reveals cold).
- `src/haz3lcore/derived/DefStatics.re` — `head_equal` uses polymorphic compare on term heads; derived stable ids for mod-item wrappers; LRU keying by whole-term rep id.

Deliberate decisions (please don't re-litigate without a failure case): the whole-text autosave blob is kept as schema-drift fallback alongside the per-item sexps; parity gates for sparse regrout stay enabled in the test runner; DOM virtualization is planned but explicitly not built (the remaining 4k spikiness is GC + per-key view floor, semantics-independent).

Known follow-ups: stepper while stacked, projector sidebar apps while stacked, worker-resident program segments (stacked PR: w2-worker-residency), hierarchical (sub-item) chunking and persistence for huge single items, episodic eval frame at 4k.

title: Fix cross-term id collisions in ExpToSegment pad_ids
body:
In a pretty-printed program with two multi-case `case` expressions, the k-th rule tile of each case ends up with the SAME id: several `pad_ids` call sites pass the `List.tl` of a term's ids without `~base`, so for freshly-parsed single-id terms the base falls back to `Id.invalid`, and the deterministic `Id.derive("pad<k>", invalid)` sequence repeats across terms. Anything grouping shards by tile id then misbehaves — observed as a `Highlight.of_tile: shard mismatch` crash (three 2-shard rule tiles under one id). Same latent collision for list-lit commas, deferred-ap commas, module semicolons, pat list-lits, and derivation rules.

Fix: pass `~base` = the term's head id at all seven sites, as pad_ids' own doc comment prescribes.

title: Make clipboard access an Effect instead of scheduling one by hand
body:
Addresses https://github.com/hazelgrove/hazel/pull/2341#discussion_r3806658226 — the `Bonsai.Effect.Expert.handle` in `CodeEditable`'s paste path. Targets `context-menu-clipboard` so the decision can be reviewed on its own.

## The problem

`Expert.handle` runs an effect outside the scheduler, and `ui_effect`'s own docs call it "only intended for internal use by this library, specifically by the attribute code." It was there because of `JsUtil.read_clipboard`'s signature:

```reason
let read_clipboard = (on_text: string => unit): unit => ...
```

A `string => unit` callback leaves the caller no way to hand the resulting `Paste` back as an effect, so the only option was to run one by hand.

## The fix

Both clipboard directions are now defined with `Ui_effect.Define1`, the mechanism Bonsai itself builds `Effect.of_deferred_fun` from (`bonsai/web/effect.ml`):

```reason
module ClipboardHandler = {
  module Action = {
    type t(_) =
      | Read_text: t(string)
      | Write_text(string): t(unit);
  };
  let handle = (type a, action: Action.t(a), ~on_response: a => unit) => ...;
};
module Clipboard = Ui_effect.Define1(ClipboardHandler);

let write_clipboard = (str: string): Effect.t(unit) => Clipboard.inject(Write_text(str));
let read_clipboard = (): Effect.t(string) =>
  has_clipboard_api() ? Clipboard.inject(Read_text) : Effect.never;
```

`Define`/`Define1` look like the intended public extension point rather than an escape hatch: they carry no `Expert`/`Private`/`For_testing` marker, and Bonsai uses them across the library boundary for `of_deferred_fun`, for the app's own `inject` in `web/start.ml`, and in `bonsai_driver`. Since `Effect.t` is an extensible variant with a private dispatch table, they're also the only way to add a case at all. Happy to switch to `Effect.Expert.of_fun` (one line, no GADT) if you'd rather — it only *constructs* an effect so it can't break scheduler discipline the way `handle` does, but it does sit in `Expert`.

Callers then just compose:

```reason
let paste_from_clipboard = () =>
  Effect.bind(JsUtil.read_clipboard(), ~f=text => inject(Perform(Paste(...))));
```

## Notes for review

- **The JS is unchanged** — same `navigator.clipboard.readText/writeText` calls, same `execCommand` fallback. Only the delivery mechanism moved.
- **Call ordering is preserved.** Copy/paste now run as items of the handler's `Effect.Many` rather than as eager calls before it, so the clipboard call happens a few stack frames later — still synchronously inside the same DOM event dispatch (`virtual_dom/attr.ml:340`), which is what the permission gate needs. They're ordered ahead of `Prevent_default` to match the previous sequence exactly.
- **`Parser.set_segment_cache` stays local**, lifted with `of_sync_fun`. It's a core mutation rather than a clipboard operation, so it didn't belong in `JsUtil`.
- **`DebugSidebar` came along** because `write_clipboard` changed type. Its five copy buttons had the same shape (`on_copy(); Effect.Ignore` inside `on_click`) and are now `unit => Effect.t(unit)`. They stay *thunks* deliberately: `copy_segment` runs `Printer.of_segment`, and an eager effect value would print every field on every render, which the comment at `DebugSidebar.re:61` explicitly guards against.
- **Still one `Expert.handle` left** at `CodeEditable.re:925`, in `EdgeScroll`'s `on_scroll`. Pre-existing, unrelated to clipboard, and a timer callback with no effect-returning seam — separate piece of work.

## Follow-up, deliberately not in this PR

`JsUtil.read_file` is the one other place in the tree with this exact shape — a callback-based one-shot async read whose result becomes an action — and `CSVProjector.re:182` pays for it with the same `Expert.handle` this PR removes:

```reason
JsUtil.read_file(file, content => Bonsai.Effect.Expert.handle(Effect.Many([...])));
```

Giving `read_file` the same treatment (`Effect.t(option(string))`) would turn that into an `Effect.bind`. I left it out because it is not a free swap: `read_file`'s three other callers (`Page.re:212`, `Logged.re:49`, `ScratchMode.re:921`) are all inside `update`, where the available seam is `~schedule_action: t => unit`. That seam is legitimate — `Main.re:79` defines it as `x => schedule_event(inject(x))`, Bonsai's own apply-action scheduler, not `Expert.handle` — so converting `read_file` means either keeping a callback variant for those three or moving the read up into the view layer. Worth doing, but it is a separate decision from this one.

For what it's worth, the other remaining `Expert.handle` sites (`BonsaiUtil`'s ResizeObserver, `MenuListener`, ninja-keys, `EdgeScroll`) are a different shape — repeating pushes *into* the framework, which `Define1` cannot express, since its `on_response` is one-shot. Those want other seams (`web_ui_element_size_hooks`, `Global_listeners`), not this one.

Manually verified in Firefox by @7h3kk1d (keyboard paste); `make dev` clean. Chrome pass still worth doing before this merges up.

title: Don't reuse a cached value that carries no environment
body:
Fixes #2462.

`IncrEval.reuse_check` could hand back a cached value that was a bare `Fun` — no `Closure`, so no environment. Applying it then lands in `Transition`'s

```reason
| FunNoEnv(dp, d3) when mode == `Substitution => …step…
| FunNoEnv(_) => Indet          // environment mode: silently final
```

and the application is final-but-stuck forever. The issue has the full mechanism and why it presents nondeterministically in a live session; the short version is that `Transition`'s `Closure` rule evaluates subterms with `~in_closure`, which correctly omits the `Closure` wrapper for a function value nested under one — but a cache entry is keyed by id alone and is replayed at top level, where that enclosing `Closure` is gone.

The fix is a `carries_env` guard: don't reuse a value that carries no environment of its own.

## Testing

The bug is a good example of a class of defect our evaluator tests structurally could not reach, so the test is worth a look.

**Why a normal evaluator test can't see it.** Reuse is keyed on ids, so the cached ids have to survive from one program into the next. That only happens when the *same document* is edited in place. Two separate parses of the same text mint disjoint ids, so nothing is reused and nothing is exercised. Any reuse bug of this shape is invisible to a test that calls `Evaluator.evaluate` on parsed terms, however the terms are built.

**The test runs the editor's real update loop**, one frame of what `ScratchMode` does:

```reason
CellEditor.Update.update(~settings, MainEditor(Perform(action)), model).model
|> CellEditor.Update.calculate(
     ~settings=settings.core, ~is_edited=true, ~queue_worker=None, ~stitch=x => x)
```

With `~queue_worker=None`, `EvalResult.Update.calculate` builds the request itself, evaluates it through `WorkerServer.evaluate_sync`, and stores `incr_eval` in the model. So request construction, the choice of `EvalInfo.of_info_map`, and the threading of `prev` across keystrokes are all **covered** rather than restated by the test, and evaluation happens after every keystroke because that is what the editor does. Settings come from `Settings.Model.init`, the app's own defaults, rather than a hand-built `CoreSettings`.

That property is the point. An earlier version of this test built the request itself, and the first version of it reached for `EvalInfo.of_targets` — which leaves `reuse_check`'s `EvalInfo.find_opt` empty, so **incremental reuse never fires and the test passes no matter what `reuse_check` does**. A harness that restates the web stack can silently stop testing the thing it was written for; one that calls into it cannot. Worth knowing for any future evaluator harness.

What's left in the test file is fixture setup (`Parser.to_zipper` into a `CellEditor.Model.t`), a two-line action wrapper, and reading the value out of `model.result`.

**Determinism.** In a live session `prev` is a function of the whole editing history, so the same final text reproduces or not depending on how it was reached. The `test` block in the fixture pins that ingredient down so the regression test doesn't depend on history — see the comment above it.

It lives in `test/Test_CellEditor.re`, since `CellEditor` is the module it drives.

## Verification

- The new test fails on `dev` and passes with the guard.
- 460 `Evaluator` tests pass, including all incremental-reuse tests.
- `make` clean, no new warnings.
- Also confirmed end-to-end in the browser on the branch where this was found.

## Follow-up, not in this PR

`| FunNoEnv(_) => Indet` fails silently — no error, no warning, just an application that stops reducing. A `DynamicErrorHole` there would have made this a much faster diagnosis. Noted on #2462.
