title: Add telemetry sections to the Debug sidebar (Evaluation, Statics, Editor & Memory, Frame Timing)
body:
Adds four Debug sidebar sections — **Evaluation**, **Statics**, **Editor &
Memory**, **Frame Timing** — showing where a keystroke's time goes and what the
editor currently holds. They share a table, a formatter and a heat map with
#2370's **Worker Messaging** panel, which moves onto the same pieces.

## Up front: refs and side effects, deliberately

The collectors are module-level refs, written by side-effecting calls at the
points being measured rather than values threaded through the component tree.
Deliberately: this is developer instrumentation — tangential to the codebase, off
a normal user's path, inert unless a panel is open — and doing it properly would
mean widening every `update` / `calculate` signature along the way to carry a
value only a debug panel reads. Worth revisiting if these panels ever become
load-bearing.

What a section touches is still closed: each collector and `PerfFormat` has a
`.rei`, each section is pinned to `DebugSection.S`, and the mutation stays inside
the collectors.

## What gets collected

**Stage timings, per keystroke.** The edit action's `perform` (update phase), then
each calculate-phase stage — statics + elaboration, the syntax-cache rebuild
(MakeTerm + Measured), cursor info, the ExplainThis color map — and the total. 30
frames kept; a stage that didn't run shows `—`, never a misleading `0`.

**The eval round trip, per request.** The latency the main thread sees
(`postMessage` → `onmessage`) beside the worker's own evaluator time, which it now
returns in a new `eval_time` on `ServerMessage.result` — so the gap between them
is queue + serialization + transfer. Plus the outcome, encoded payload sizes and a
restart count. 10 requests kept.

**Structural counts, per frame.** Info-map entries, error and warning counts, why
statics ran or didn't (recomputed / forced / deferred / cached), segment tokens,
tiles, rows, projectors, and live undo/redo/backpack depth.

Durations are `Core.Time_ns.Span`, sizes `Core.Byte_units`. Byte-exact heap sizes
are deliberately absent — walking the heap per frame is too expensive, and timings
plus counts answer the question.

## The changes, in reading order

1. **`util/Metrics.re`** (new) — the gate and bounded history every collector
   shares, as a functor; recorders run through `when_enabled`. Read first.
2. **`util/PerfMetrics.re`** — per-frame collector: the `frame` record, the
   `time_*` stage wrappers, the count recorders.
3. **`util/EvalMetrics.re`** — round-trip collector, keyed by request id so its
   rows line up with Worker Messaging's.
4. **`util/WorkerMetrics.re`** — pre-existing; moved onto the functor.
5. **`CodeEditable`, `CodeWithStatics`, `Page`, `History`** — where the timings
   are taken, and where gating syncs once per cycle.
6. **`util/WorkerServer.re`, `util/WorkerClient.re`** — evaluator time on the
   wire, and the recording around the request lifecycle.
7. **`sidebar/PerfFormat.re`** — the table vocabulary: a `column` carries header,
   tooltip and cell projection; `cell` is opaque; `view` assembles a body.
8. **`sidebar/*Section.re`** — one per panel: columns plus a `view` call.
9. **`sidebar/SidebarModel.re`, `Settings.re`** — sidebar settings store
   `debug_expanded`, so the whole Debug sidebar starts collapsed.
10. **`util/TimeUtil.re`** — `timed`, and the `span` alias that lets a deriving
    type carry a `Time_ns.Span`. The only file outside `src/web/`.

## Closed panels cost nothing

Each collector is gated on **its own** section being expanded, synced once per
cycle in `Page.Update.calculate`, and every section ships collapsed — so ordinary
editing pays nothing.

## Testing

`make dev` clean, `make test-quick` green (3311), and a manual pass over all five
sections in Chrome. `Test_WorkerServer` covers a `Time_ns.Span` surviving Marshal
+ `structuredClone` and its nanosecond json encoding.

title: Evaluator perf: skip dead reuse-map work, StringMap reuse maps, cheap Id.mk (~1.7x)
body:
Evaluating the same program repeatedly (`./hazel bench-eval -n 20 bench/eval-bench.hz`, new subcommand that parses/elaborates once and times evaluation only, dev profile under node): on current dev (evaluator streaming) plain evaluation goes 811 -> 467 ms/iter and incremental cache-seeding 797 -> 485. Profiling showed two pre-existing evaluator costs dominating every dispatch: `IncrEval.remove_pat_bindings` (~50%) and `Id.mk` (~30%).

Three changes:
- The evaluator skips all reuse-map maintenance (including the streaming-era `ReusePass` whole-program pre-pass) when there is no prior state to reuse and no statics to target (CLI `run`, MVU dispatch): the map is provably never consumed on that path, but its upkeep dominated evaluation.
- `IncrEval.reuse_map` is now a StringMap instead of an assoc list, so `remove_pat_bindings` no longer walks ~180 builtin entries with polymorphic `List.mem` at every binder.
- `Id.mk` mints from a session-tagged monotonic counter instead of drawing a v4 UUID from the OCaml 5 LXM generator (~1.5us/call under jsoo, ~264k calls per bench iteration). Ids stay v4-shaped and unique: counter in the leading bytes (so `Id.str8`/`cls` abbreviations stay distinct), 62 session-random tail bits for cross-runtime uniqueness. Environment ids are load-bearing (closure `fast_equal`, serialization sharing keys) and are still minted.

Pre-streaming this measured 1648 -> 336 / 1539 -> 432 (~4.9x/3.6x); evaluator streaming (#2339) independently captured part of the same win (it gates reuse-map upkeep inside call stacks), which is why the marginal multiplier on top of it is smaller. Streaming also adds ~40% overhead to the fully-optimized plain path (336 -> 467 on the same machine) — a separate future target.

Added 2026-08-10, two upstream-of-evaluator costs found while profiling livelit-heavy programs:
- Statics no longer deep-normalizes types: alias references flow compact and consumers resolve heads on demand and compare names first (`equal_up_to_aliases`, `canonicalize`, `normalize(~expand)` for module exports). Graph-benchmark statics 650 -> 101 ms warm (HTML-heavy synthetic 7.7s -> 155ms); worst in-editor keystroke stall 1.6–2.1s -> ~100ms; plain code unchanged. Design + site table in plans/type-normalization.md.
- Molding's hot token predicates (`is_infix_delimiter_op_prefix`, `is_ambiguous_polymorph`) were `List.mem` scans with polymorphic compare per atomic-form candidate on every molding query — now hash-set membership, ~1.3x on batch parse of a 120-line program (agent insert-text edits, CLI, load).

Full suite green (3297 tests after the dev merge); the pattern-equivalence property's FAIL-then-skip seeds are unchanged vs dev (pre-existing).

title: Improved Unicode support
body:
This extends and improves Hazel's unicode support, both the editor and the language, permitting unicode use in identifiers (user facing) and in arbitrary delimiters, as well as fixing bugs and inconsistencies around unicode use in comments and quoted tuple levels

Previously non-ASCII chars like emojis only really worked inside string literals. Comments, quoted labels and operator tokens could technically hold them but were buggy because width handling was gated on `is_string`: `#😀#` measured one column narrower than it rendered, shifting carets, selections and click-mapping for the rest of the row. Non-paste insertion of non-unicode characters was impossible anywhere, because `Insert` key handling gated on single-byte length, so any multi-byte entry silently produced no insert.

**Identifiers take Unicode**, so `café`, `日本語` and `x😀` lex as one tile. Constructors are still distinguished by capitalization, with caseless characters counting as non-uppercase: `😀foo` is a variable, `Foo😀` a constructor.

**Operators are now defined positively.** They were previously whatever was left over after excluding names, whitespace and delimiters; technically on dev now loose pasted emoji become operators without anyone having decided that. Now: the 18 ASCII characters already in use, plus the five the language actually uses in operator position (`∈ ≠ ≮ ≯ ⊆`, display-only, emitted by `ExpToSegment` for derivation operators). Identifiers are now the complement, so the two remain disjoint by construction.

**Hazel's string builtins now use grapheme indexing**. `string_search` returns an index that composes with `string_sub` and is bounded by `string_length`; these agreed before only by all being bytes. `string_length("😀")` was 4.

Also fixed: truncation in `Abbreviate`/`ProbeText` cutting mid-cluster; CLI type error message code indexing columns as bytes being wrong in the presence of unicode, `wrap_quote`/`wrap_balanced` wrapping a whole token when only part of it was selected.

`ocamllex` has no Unicode properties, so the text lexer admits well-formed UTF-8 in names minus the whitelist, which is a superset of the editor's rule. The `MakeTerm`/Menhir equivalence properties now generate non-ASCII identifiers and string literals. Note:  the Unicode operator whitelist is hand-maintained in both `Token.re` and `Lexer.mll` with no compile-time link.

**Invisible characters render as labeled cells, and pasted code is NFC-normalized.** With names the complement of operators, every invisible format character (zero-width space, bidi controls, soft hyphen, …) became a valid name character: `ba​r` with a hidden ZWSP looks identical to `bar` but is a different variable, and measured one column wider than it rendered. A cluster consisting only of such codepoints now draws as a small hex-labeled box with a tooltip, restoring measurement/render agreement (attached forms like an emoji's VS16 are untouched). `unicode-bidi: isolate` on tokens keeps RTL text or a stray direction override in one token from visually reordering its neighbors. Pasted and agent-introduced code is NFC-normalized outside string literals — macOS paste sources emit decomposed accents, so a pasted `café` otherwise never matches a typed one — while literal contents are preserved byte-for-byte (per UTS #55, which recommends exactly this editor/language split; a fuller options survey lives in local plans/unicode-due-diligence.md).

title: Coding agent: review fixes + cleanup pass
body:
Fixes the functional issues from the #2210 review plus problems surfaced by live agent sessions, and does a structural cleanup pass. Example of the headline bug: asking the agent to fill the body hole after `let x = 1 in` produced `let x = 1 inlet e = 2 in x`, token fusion that reparses as the identifier `inlet` when copied. Root cause was in hole-fill path; fixed by padding only where adjacent tokens would lex as one.

Behavioral changes, agent tools:
- Leading whitespace stripped from tool code on all paths. Vertical whitespace normalized after edits: one blank line between top-level definitions, no leading blank, no accumulating trailing blanks.
- Ambiguous paths (shadowing) return an error with `name#k` retry syntax instead of silently editing the earliest match. Function-sugar bindings can now be addressed by bare name (`f`, not `f((x, y))`).
- Pattern rename rejects capture and binder-count changes and re-checks statics. Renaming recursive sugared functions now works (use sites in the definition were previously skipped, so those renames always failed). Note: renaming a recursive `let f = fun ...` (unsugared) now rejects rather than silently leaving the old name dangling in the recursive call.
- Paste failures name reserved keywords (`eval` etc.) instead of a bare `CantPaste`. Node-map builds no longer fail with the cursor inside a sugared binding, and are no longer quadratic.

Behavioral changes, chat UX:
- Enter appends the message and clears the input immediately; the heavy context/payload work runs a tick later. Stop pressed in that gap cancels before anything is sent.
- Streaming replies render as markdown live, with dangling `**`/backticks auto-closed instead of flashing raw markers.
- API failures surface for real: 401s show the provider message instead of empty-reply retry churn, network errors report immediately, a Node-side error path no longer hangs, and per-request debug logging is removed.
- The context meter says "budget used" with a tooltip naming the model window when the 100k compaction cap is what's displayed.

Prompts: function-definition sugar (`let f(x, y) = ...`) documented as preferred; tiered reserved-word warning, empirically verified (e.g. `rec`/`val`/`valid` are not term keywords); audit fixes (nonexistent `string_of_int`, broken doc examples, missing float ops and `|>`, `table` projector kind).

Internals, briefly: `AgentUpdate.re` split 2081 to 385 lines across seven modules; single tool registry replacing four drifting name lists (which exposed four unregistered workbench tools); append-message dedup; dead code and comment trims; all inline comments from the #2210 review addressed or answered on the branch.

title: Make tiles slightly less illegal
body:
Tiles stored their label and mold even though both are determined by form. Each serialized tile carried redundant strings and precedence numbers so operator-precedence changes required migrating every serialized file, and nothing prevented label/mold mismatches.

Now a tile is `{id, form, sort, shards, children}` where `form = Compound(family) | Tok(token) | TokInfix(token)`, with 92 form families (label x shape-role) plus free-text tokens, and label/mold are derived. `TokInfix` is a technical detail that will die with virtual grout.

This isn't quite a pure refactor, but my hope is that there are no observable logic changes.

- Serialized syntax shrinks ~40%, and precedence/mold changes no longer require migrations.
- MakeTerm dispatches on constructors instead of token-string lists. This technically causes some behavior changes in edge cases, but I have never seen the relevant behaviors in the wild.
- Exercise/derivation examples now ship as serialized-zipper text literals rather than OCaml literals, so they survive representation changes; slide files were regenerated id- and refractor-preservingly.
- The stored `sort` is an explicitly isolated local cache (well-sorted <=> `mold_of(form, sort).out == sort`); experimental follow up work will hopefully make sort a derived property, eliminating this field
- The grammar's string layer now lives in the language library (src/language/grammar/), including Token, Label, and FormId (the family enums and the per-family label table), following the existing Sort re-export pattern. This deduplicates the token/string mirrors that src/language previously hand-maintained
- TyDi's suggestion-type tables are now derived from the grammar at startup instead of hand-maintained.

title: Drag-to-refactor: a pointer front-end to the gesture system
body:
Enable Settings > Drag Refactoring, then pull tokens: grab a definition by any of its tokens and pull down -- a full-size copy flies into its nearest use; pull a param sideways to swap it; pull a case's end down to grow an arm; pull where nothing can happen and the token leans in your hand and springs back.

title: Term-level refactorings
body:
13 context-menu/palette refactorings built on the round-trip (#2374): parse buffer -> transform term -> print -> splice. Ids survive, so probes, statics, and incremental caches do too.

### Gestural - Naming
- **Inline Let**: `let x = 1 + 2 in x + 3` -> `1 + 2 + 3`; offered at the let, its binder, or any occurrence of `x`. Parens only where a reparse oracle proves the bare form changes the program: `let x = 1 + 2 in 3 + x` -> `3 + (1 + 2)`.
- **Add Parameter**: `let f = fun x -> x + 1 in f(2)` -> `let f = fun (x, x1) -> x + 1 in f(2, ?)` — definition and every call site atomically, including recursive calls. Handles `let f(x) = x + 1 in f(2)` -> `let f(x, x1) = x + 1 in f(2, ?)` and annotated bindings (`Int -> Int` becomes `(Int, ?) -> Int`). Gated off when `f` is used as a bare value (`map(f, xs)`).
- **Hoist Let**: `fun n -> let x = 2 in x + n` -> `let x = 2 in fun n -> x + n` — one level per invocation (through chains, out of defs, out of lambdas). The explicit opt-in to evaluation-count changes that Extract avoids.
- **Sink Let**: `let x = 2 in case m | 1 => x | _ => 0 end` -> `case m | 1 => let x = 2 in x | _ => 0 end` — into the single arm/branch/lambda that uses the binding. Both movements are scope-gated and shadow-aware; blocked moves are simply not offered.
- **Extract to Let**: binds at the nearest enclosing line — `let a = 1 in g(f(2))` extracting `f(2)` -> `let a = 1 in let x = f(2) in g(x)`; a def-site hoists above its line (`let a = g(f(2)) in ...` -> `let x = f(2) in let a = g(x) in ...`). Never escapes a lambda or case arm, so evaluation count/conditionality never changes.

### Gestural - Choice
- **Add Missing Case Arm**: `case b | true => 1 end` -> `case b | true => 1 | false => ? end`, one arm per invocation from the Coverage witness — real constructors for finite domains (`Green`), literals wildified for infinite ones (`case n | 1 => 2 end` gains `| _ => ?`). Label names the witness: "Add Arm | false".

### Naming (non-gestural)
- **Rename (bind free occurrences)**: rename a binder by ordinary editing — `let vel = 1 in v + v` (was `v`) marks the old uses free, and the binder token offers "Rename v to vel" -> `let vel = 1 in vel + vel`. Stateless: reconstructed from scope state, no edit tracking. Works at let heads, `f(x)`-sugar names and params, fun params, and case-arm pats; per-occurrence shadow-precise.
- **Remove Unused Let**: `let x = 1 in 2 + 2` -> `2 + 2`; gated on the statics unused-binding warning. Works on annotated heads and unused `f(x)`-sugar fns.

### Equational (syntactic)
- **Convert to Case**: `if a then 1 else 2` -> `case a | true => 1 | false => 2 end`.
- **Convert to If**: the inverse, either arm order: `case a | false => 2 | true => 1 end` -> `if a then 1 else 2`.
- **Negate & Swap Branches**: `if a && b then 1 else 2` -> `if !(a && b) then 2 else 1` — arms swap with their formatting untouched; condition parens by the oracle (`if a ...` gives bare `!a`).
- **Eta-Reduce**: `fun y -> f(y)` -> `f`, gated on `y` not occurring in `f`.

### Equational (semantic)
- **Add Type Annotation**: `let x = 1 + 2 in x` -> `let x : Int = 1 + 2 in x`, type from statics; only offered when the inferred type is hole-free. Oracle-parenthesized: `let p = (1, true) in p` -> `let p : (Int,Bool) = (1, true) in p`.


Formatting is preserved by construction: whitespace runs belong to line slots and transforms move/copy them explicitly, so multiline layouts survive swaps, extractions, and conversions. Menu gating never prints, parses, or runs the oracle (invocation only). ~110 tests in Test_Refactor.re.

Stacked on #2374; retarget to dev when it merges.

title: Roundtrip: Canonical completion + Shard/Lexeme Provenance
body:
Closes #2381
Closes #1792
Closes #2296
Subsumes #2079
References #2373 (known-outstanding)

## Goal: round-tripping

This PR makes every editor-reachable state round-trip: the buffer's segment parses to a term, and printing that term (segment-to-segment, via ExpToSegment) reproduces the original (tile ids, labels, shards, secondary) up to a small quotient described below. This is supported by property-based testing. Previously many states didn't survive the trip: incomplete tiles were dumped or dropped, quotes around labels and leading + in sum types disappeared, literal spellings normalized (007 -> 7, 4.0 -> 4.), unknown infix operators created multiholes which lost the operator string, etc.

This enables transforms on terms (eg refactorings, agent edits) while perserving all previously ephemeral editor state. The stacked refactorings PR is the first consumer.

The mechanism has two halves: canonical completion turns every incomplete segment into a well-formed one deterministically, and a small amount of lexical provenance recorded on terms lets the segment printer reconstruct exactly what the user had typed.

## Canonical completion

This assigns a canonical completion to every incomplete segment. Unlike the previous dump logic, canonical completions do not depend on caret position. However, ergonomic completions can't depend simply on
term structure: when inserting a new form, e.g. a let expression above existing code, term structure alone is ambiguous as to whether the new code wraps the code below or sits purely above it. The caret-based heuristic used previously is (a) only useful for incomplete forms in the caret segment, and (b) necessitates either re-completing on caret movement (expensive and potentially confusing) or a hidden history dependence (confusing).

The new heuristic is based on partitioning, meaning which following content an incomplete form absorbs. This is decided by indentation: after a linebreak, content at same-or-lesser indentation than the incomplete tile's line ends the partition. This subsumes the old, somewhat ugly "reset after a blank line" heuristic and is the intent-based discrimination discussed next.

Where the missing delimiters go — placement follows an evidence hierarchy (details in plans/completion-heuristics.md): a leftover prefix token (`i` for a deleted `in`, `-` for `->`) or the deletion's own junction debris pins the delimiter exactly where it was; only evidence-free states fall back to the structural defaults below. The engine completes ONE tile per pass (strongest evidence first, weak ties innermost-first) and recurses on the materialized result, so the suggestion set is a replay script: applying everything shown reproduces the computed result by construction, and jointly-broken forms (delete a case's `end` AND its let's `in`) restore compatibly.
- Missing closers are appended at the end of their partition, stopping before a span-final trailing operator when that strictly reduces synthesized holes (`test 1 == 1 end;` restores with the `end` before the `;`). A single-line form's closer glues back over a trailing linebreak (`let x = 1` + blank line + `2` takes its `in` on the definition line); a multiline form keeps its closer on its own line (a broken multiline case-def restores `end in` exactly where it was).
- Missing openers are placed at the start of their closer's left-operand span in the partition skel — the maximal span the completed form can absorb without crossing enclosing structure — bounded by line-walls: a deleted mid-program `let`/`if`/`case` head stays on its own line instead of absorbing the definitions above. So let a = 1,2] completes to let a = [1,2] in ?, not by hoisting [ above the let. Same-position ties open the later closer outermost: 1) + 2) -> ((1) + 2). Opener spans are also clamped by slot sort: a restored head lands at the nearest span that fits its interior slot (the second `let` of `let a = 1 in let b = 2 in b`, deleted inline, restores at `b` — a complete let can't be a pattern), while Exp-slot wrappers like a deleted `(` keep the maximal wrap.
- Missing middle delimiters (let x in 2, if true else 2; targeted put-down can strand an interior delimiter in the backpack) can't be appended like the others, because reassembly requires shard order. The tile is instead completed in place: each original child stays in the slot opened by its original left shard, and newly created slots get a hole, so let x in 2 completes to let x = ? in 2. The synthesized grout ids derive deterministically from surrounding tile ids, so completion is stable across recomputation.

## Indentation now user-owned

A non-obvious part of this design is that the indentation heuristic requires making indentation user-owned. This isn't
essential for round-tripping itself, but it's what makes canonical completion ergonomic, as well as resolveing a problem of its own.

Indentation around incomplete code has the same wrapping-uncertainty as completion, and on dev it leads to indentation thrashing: typing on one line causes lines below to indent and unindent repeatedly. So the row-indentation system is removed in favor of 'traditional' indentation: indentation is now simply regular whitespace (secondary), owned by the user.

Like conventional editors, we don't re-indent everything on every edit. Pressing enter inserts indentation after the new linebreak only, using the same indentation logic as before, so left-to-right entry gets the indentation you expect and nothing below the caret moves. **Cmd+S formats per a 4-level setting (none / indent / spaces / breaks; default respaces + re-indents); Cmd+Shift+S always pretty-prints.**

There is a nut menu setting, on by default, for limited auto-identation: Completing a delimiter re-indents the lines it affects. Settled (roughly: not containing incomplete tiles) regions get exact re-indentation; unsettled ones a uniform shift.

The presence of user-owned indentation is what allows intent-based discrimination: the completion only absorbs following lines if they are indented relative to the incomplete form's line. The user can indent/dedent to get the behavior they want, but in practice they don't have to, because the enter-inserted indentation suffices for the completion to do what you expect during left-to-right entry, whether writing new code or code above existing code.

The general principle is to move all history sensitivity into secondary, and all system history-dependence into auto-formatting behavior. The user has full control over secondary, so none of this is fundamentally hidden or out of their control. When the code is complete, autoformat erases any trace of historical dependence; it exists purely during incomplete states.

## What round-tripping adds data-structure-wise

Two new fields on the IdTag annotation:
- incomplete: list((Id.t, list(int))): for each canonically completed tile, which shards the user actually typed. The
printer strips synthesized shards on the way back out, so incomplete tiles survive the trip; MakeTerm threads the same masks so statics sees the completed form.
- lexeme: option(string): surface spellings the term normalizes, e.g. 007, 1e3, implicit vs ? vs ?? hole flavor, quoted labels, unknown infix operators (which now elaborate as stuck applications rather than evaluating to their last operand as multi-holes do).

Copy semantics are documented on the type: id-bearing fields drop on copy, value-meaning fields persist.

All other roundtrip gaps filled exploit existing structure rather than new fields. A representative trick: whether a sum type had a leading + is encoded by collected id count, as a leading-plus parse absorbs the separator ids, yielding n ids for n variants, while a bare binary sum carries only the n-1 separators; evaluator-built sums (single id) print bare, which reparses to the same type. Similarly, middle-completion hole ids derive from the tile id instead of being stored.

## Preserved property + fuzzing

The roundtrip property is enforced by a QCheck fuzzer driving Perform.go with random insert/move/destruct sequences from the empty buffer, sampling the actual editor-reachable domain, which parser based generators would undersample (rule tiles only form inside cases; deleted openers, standalone |/=> tokens, some grout cases are edit-reachable only). Also added a corpus and shrunk-counterexample regression suites.

What's compared: canonical completion yields a deeply complete segment whose parse prints back with identical text and piece sequence (tile ids, labels, shards, secondary), modulo a canonical quotient (grout (ephemeral by design), and mold sorts). Spelling, shapes, and precedences compare strictly.

Measured on the fuzzer (5 seeds, 290 states): the grout quotient earns its keep on placement, not ids — grout lands where the parsed term doesn't reproduce it in ~23% of reachable states (dangling boundary grout, stray grout glommed through MakeTerm), while ids agree whenever placement does. (The 4 id-only exceptions traced to the printer minting fresh ids on multihole id shortfalls; padding is now derived, so printing is a pure function of the term.)

The decision to quotient grout ids & sorts is pragmatic; there are currently a number of edge cases, some of which have been addressed, but i think the move it towards making both of these dervied; this is already underway for grout on the virtual-grout branch. If we don't decided to make these derived, we could add more annotations to avoid the need to quotient. In any case you can currently roptionally un the fuzzer with the quotient disabled enumerates to exactly the disagreement states derivation or annotation must handle.

An example of an outstanding sort issue: type : then ]. The editor molds the orphan ] at Typ — the caret sits on the typ side of the :. but canonical completion places the missing [ at the start, reading the state as [? : ?] (an Exp list whose element is the ascription, not ? : [?]), so the reprint derives the ] at Exp. 

Other known generator limitations: it fuzzes single-char insertion, char-wise movement, and backspace (so no selections, backpack pick-up/put-down, or copy/paste) and excludes projectors (follow-up work).

## Later additions (building on the roundtrip)

- **Completion heuristics**: missing delimiters drop into the concave junction their deletion left when shape + sort + uniqueness agree (`let x 1 in 2` -> `let x = 1 in 2`; deleted `else`/`in`/case-bars restore in place); `fun x` over a let-body clips the arrow at the sort frontier instead of absorbing the let into the pattern; a backspaced delimiter's leftover prefix token (`i` for `in`) is completed in place, recorded as a partially-typed shard (`{present, prefixes}` mask) so the roundtrip still closes exactly; leading witnesses restore deleted form heads from their remnants (`le` -> `let`, mid-program); sort-aware symbolic witnesses complete `-` -> `->` and `=` -> `=>`; broken cases repair as one case (wrap/opener arbitration + rule walls), and rules are treated as case-content throughout — mid-entry `case foo |` keeps its `end` after the growing rule.
- **Scoreboard instruments** (Test_CompletionScoreboard, pinned): deletion-inverse restoration over a corpus — full-deletion, last-char-prefix, joint pair-deletion (restoration + delimiter-completeness), and acceptance-stability (applying one suggestion must not move the rest; 96/104 stable, shifts only on known jointly-interacting states). Every remaining miss is a documented accepted-inherent (e.g. `f(3 + f(4)` is byte-identical to a freshly typed wide paren).
- **Quiver chips**: completion suggestions render as interline signposts at their exact placements — a bubble on the line boundary with a ghost-caret pole pinning the insertion column — replacing the old end-of-line boxes. Pins follow the caret through semantically-free whitespace; typed prefixes render cut-out; colorways distinguish tab-territory (pale) from other-segment obligations (gold); at caret coincidence the real caret is authoritative and the chip's pole steps aside.
- **Discharge routes**: `ApplyCompletion(All | One(tile))` materializes the virtual completion into the buffer (caret preserved by id). Alt+M completes everything (replacing the old greedy Dump, now deleted); cmd/ctrl+click on a chip completes exactly that delimiter (pointer cursor while the modifier is held; unmodified clicks pass through to the editor); tab still puts down at the caret. Agent/composition flows materialize through the same engine.
- **TyDi delimiter suffixes**: the ghost suggestion survives on prefix states where completion consumed the token's statics entry (ci-free witness route), 1-char expectation-backed prefixes bypass the length gate (`-`/`=` get arrow completions), and suggestions come from the same witness recognition the engine uses — ghost and quiver agree by construction. Tab at `els` accepts to `else` instead of dropping a fresh delimiter after it.
- **Reassociation**: retyping a deleted keyword char mid-program re-pairs with its orphaned shards (rescan matches singletons only; the repair fallback now explodes remnants and tries the sibling scope); `deep_reassociate` is no longer a setting — reassociation is unconditional, and the harnesses run it (they previously silently didn't, hiding this bug class from every edit-derived test).
- **Formatting**: SpaceNormalize gains an opt-in canonicalize mode (mold-aware within-line respacing: `f (x)` -> `f(x)`, one space around infix ops, comments/linebreaks untouched) backing the new Spaces format level; format actions restore the caret via CaretPreserving (from #2231 — exact piece, else surviving predecessor, else ancestors). Printing is now a pure function of the term (pad_ids derives instead of minting).
- **Auto-reindent triggers**: paste re-indents the pasted lines (settled exact / unsettled uniform shift) and, like TyDi accept, destruct, and comment-toggle, runs the completion-triggered re-indent when a tile completes.
- **Indentation UX** (gated on a core setting, on by default): arrow movement skips leading whitespace (every line keeps one reachable position; clicks/selection stay char-exact); backspace at first-content inverts enter (indent + linebreak, one keystroke, one undo); Cmd+[/] indent/dedent lines from any position; Shift+Backspace dedents at the line-start boundary only.

## Removals

The backpack display is retired (the quiver is the completion display; the put-down mechanism and derived missing-shards machinery remain — internals renamed from "backpack" to missing_shards), along with `Dump`, the `deep_reassociate` setting, and the redundant NutMenu Docs toggle. Persisted settings blobs lose two fields, so browsers may see a one-time settings reset.

## Addendum

- A batch of fidelity fixes found by the fuzzer along the way, including the two closed issues above.
(cross-sort tiles in MakeTerm, crossed synthesized delimiters, adjacent-operator lexemes, typ-side incomplete forms, and more); #2373 remains outstanding.
- docs/segments.md documents the round-trip contract, the provenance fields, and the sort-quotient rationale with the example above.
- Possible future refinements, deferred: sort re-derivation as above; virtual grout (#2165) as the same derive-don't-store program applied to grout.

title: Fix eval worker postMessage stack overflow on deep results (#2368)
body:
## Problem

Evaluating certain programs threw in the eval worker on **Chrome only**:

```
Uncaught RangeError: Failed to execute 'postMessage' on 'DedicatedWorkerGlobalScope': Maximum call stack size exceeded
    at post_message (worker.ml)
    at on_request (WorkerServer.re)
```

Repro: a large list bound to a variable (e.g. ~100 rows of labeled tuples) even when the computed result is trivial, like `length(x)` or `3 + 1`. Does not reproduce in Firefox.

## Root cause

`WorkerServer.on_request` / `WorkerClient.request` posted the raw OCaml value graph across the worker boundary. `postMessage` hands it to the browser's structured-clone serializer, which in Chrome is **recursive** and overflows its (relatively small) stack on a deep — but finite, acyclic — payload. Firefox's limit is higher, so it tolerated the same payload.

## Fix

Encode the request/response with jsoo's **`Marshal`** (iterative → a flat string that structured clone copies without recursing), so a deep-but-finite payload crosses the boundary without hitting the clone serializer's recursion limit. This is the active encoding — `WorkerServer.Active`, a one-line alias `module Active = MarshalEncoding`.

The boundary stays typed `Worker.worker(request, response)` via an abstract `WorkerServer.ENCODING` module signature: only `encode`/`decode` can cross it and the two directions can't be swapped.

## Worker Messaging debug panel

To choose an encoding on real workloads, the diff keeps an **`encoding` variant** (`Direct | Marshal | Sexp`, with display strings and `all_of_encoding` ppx-derived — no hand-maintained name lists) behind the abstract `ENCODING` signature, plus a **"Worker Messaging" section in the Debug sidebar** — how the main thread talks to the eval Web Worker — that benchmarks each enabled encoding per request (encode / structuredClone / decode timing + size), correlated by request id.

- Metrics are typed: durations are `Core.Time_ns.Span`, sizes `Core.Byte_units` (each encoding reports its own size via the `ENCODING` signature). A stage that throws renders as `—` with the error on a tooltip, not a misleading `0`.
- **Defaults:** the section starts **collapsed** (so no benchmarking runs) and only **`marshal`** is enabled; the enabled set (`worker_encodings`) and per-encoding toggles persist in settings, so a slow encoding like `sexp` stays off.
- Benchmarking is gated on the panel being visible and synced once per cycle via `WorkerMetrics.sync` (the settings that gate it aren't reachable at the `WorkerClient.request` call site).
- The section lives in its own `WorkerMessagingSection.re` behind a small `DebugSection.S` interface, rendered by a generic driver in `DebugSidebar`. Swapping the active encoding is the one-line `module Active = …` alias.

## What we explored, then removed

Two additional encodings were benchmarked during the analysis and have since been **removed from the code** (preserved in git history on this branch). Documenting them here for the record:

- ~~**`columnar`** — was briefly the active protocol.~~ Packs the jsoo value graph into a handful of flat typed arrays (`flatten`/`unflatten`, custom JS via `Js.Unsafe`): a fixed set of `Float64Array`s regardless of depth, so structured clone never recurses *and* no intermediate string is built. Blocks are numbered by identity, so sharing/DAG structure is preserved. Benchmarks put it at **~2× faster than Marshal and fully depth-proof**. **Dropped** because it leaned on `Js.Unsafe`/`Obj.magic` and jsoo's block-representation internals for a payload where Marshal is already fast enough — Marshal's simplicity and safety won once the metrics settled the question. (added in `4e47e876fe`)
- **`array`** — converts only the top-level request/response list spine to an OCaml array. Everything *inside* each entry still crosses as its natural nested graph, so a payload that is deep inside an entry still overflows structured clone — i.e. it does **not** fix #2368. Kept only as a benchmark contrast to the columnar packing; removed.

## Testing

- `Test_WorkerServer` (4 tests): **Marshal is depth-proof** — a 20k-deep payload round-trips through `structuredClone`; and **every encoding is isomorphic** — one round-trip-equality test each for `direct` / `marshal` / `sexp`. (Deep failure of direct/sexp isn't asserted: raw `structuredClone` on a deep graph segfaults node uncatchably, whereas in-browser it throws a catchable `RangeError`.)
- `make dev` clean, no compiler warnings.
- **Chrome (manual):** the original `Marshal`-based fix (`a5c49701eb`) evaluated the repro correctly. Re-verification of the current active path + the Worker Messaging panel (durations/sizes render via `Span`/`Byte_units`; a failed `direct` shows `—`) is pending against the latest rebuild.

Closes #2368

  • #251 7672842 Thanks @​sapphi-red! - Add name property to the rename object form and allow rename functions to return a RenameObject. The name property replaces the file's basename (filename + extension), and can be combined with stripBase to both flatten directory structure and rename the file in one step.     // node_modules/lib/dist/index.js → vendor/lib.js

vite-plugin-static-copy@4.0.1

Patch Changes

  • #249 c6bf44c Thanks @​sapphi-red! - Fix absolute dest paths being nested under the output directory

    When dest was an absolute path and the source file had a directory component (structured output), the path was incorrectly converted to a relative path, causing files to be nested under the build output directory instead of being copied to the specified absolute path.

    { src: 'foo/foo.txt', dest: '/home/user/my-repo/bar' }

    Before: /home/user/my-repo/dist/home/user/my-repo/bar/foo/foo.txt After: /home/user/my-repo/bar/foo/foo.txt

    Previously, stripBase counted .. as directory segments, causing incorrect output paths when copying from parent directories.

title: Probes IV
body:
Probes features and fixes from the study branch. Subsumes #2321 and #2325 (now closed).

Closes #2067
Closes #2323
Closes #2276
Closes #2217

## Features

- **Drawer mode.** Expand a probe's sample into a multi-line, pretty-printed block below the code line (`Cmd/Ctrl+↓` open / `Cmd/Ctrl+↑` close, or the row's chevron; Esc exits). Per-probe state, capped at 15 rows (scrolls beyond). Built on a new `below` projector view slot reserving rows via `Tab(n)`.
- **Enhanced Auto-probe** Auto-probe now probes top-level expressions as well ad defiitions. Auto-probe now has an `All` mode. Modes are `Off | Caret | All` (was on/off). _Caret_ probes the top-level definition under the cursor; _All_ probes the whole program, one probe per source row (a single root multiprobe). `Cmd/Ctrl+P` cycles Off↔All; the sidebar's segmented control also reaches Caret.
- **"Simple" color scheme (new default).** Two colors: focal-call green vs. off-focus washed out green. replacing the old Hybrid default. Use the toggle in the sidebar to access the old default.

## Fixes (pre-existing behavior)

- **Probe samples no longer stale until the next edit:** Placing a probe (or autoprobe) showed the ∅ indicator until the next edit, because the statics debounce left `probe_targets` stale and `IncrEval.reuse_check` reused a sampleless slice. Now a probe-id change forces a full statics refresh. (Also makes auto-probe work in exercise mode.)
- **Step-into for indirect calls.** Extends the existing step-into to higher-order calls, partial applications, and `let f x = …` sugar, by carrying a resolved call frame (`fn_def_id`) through evaluator state into each sample.
- **More stable Sample-ids to prevent collisions on deep recursion** — fixes double-indication, twin resize handles, and broken scroll anchors via collision-resistant ids.
- **Accurate Tab projector/refractor decoration offset** — Code/decoration row desync from out-of-order deferred-linebreak counting is fixed.
- **Projector action index crash** — a stale render-time index now drops the action instead of raising.
- Smaller: duplicate manual-refractor entry (assoc-list vs map disagreement), stuck pending probe cursor, a sibling-cleanup toggle that re-added forever, and pointer/drag guards.

## Modifications / polish

- **Sample-count indicator moved** from an overlay circle on the projector to an inline badge at the start of the samples row (hidden for a single sample).
- **Sample dropdown now uses right-/alt-click.** The sample dropdown (which shows environment variables and pin/step options) opens on right-click or alt-click (was hover-only), with click-outside / scroll dismissal. Hover activation proved to hyperactive.
- **Function-sugar probing.** Putting a multi-probe on `let f(args) = body` now probes the arguments on the header line, not just the body.
- **Sample-focus navigation now scrolls horizontally:** When using ←/→ move the focused sample it should scroll-follow it into view; this previously only worked vertically.
- Indeterminant samples e.g. holes no longer colored differently than value samples; this proved confusing to multiple people.
- Removed the dashed connector line between probes and samples; added visual noise doesn't pay for itself.
- Sidebar quick-reference updated for new interactions (alt-click for env, right-click for pin/step, an expand-probe row).
- Focus bar: "Clear all" also turns auto-probe off; the editor caret stays visible after a focus-bar / sidebar jump.
- Scroll stability for drawer refractors: drawer-height changes above the caret are prevented from shifting it via scroll trigger.
- Tuple pretty-printing breaks symmetrically
- The test pass/fail badge no longer floats above probe sample menu.

## Performance

- Viewport culling now re-enabled, but only for auto-probe All mode (infra already existed on dev but was inert): off-screen probe views are culled in the single-editor modes (Scratch / Documentation / Tutorial); Exercises stays unculled.
- Cull-before-build for probe views, memoized multi-probe expansion + placeholder calcs, and phys-equality gating on rebuilds.

## Late additions: cards + rich-view UX (2026-08-22)

- Cherry-picks Alexander's card RichProbe renderer (authorship preserved) (from `card-rich-probe`), forward-ported to this branch's registry API (`empty`, `drawer_rows`), with card/hand shape-matching intact.
- Rich views render **inside** the sample chip (green backing, inert content) rather than replacing the row — the chip keeps the dropdown (Hide), sample capture, dbl-click, and resize. The anchored modal is retired: small rich views (≤4 rows) embed in the row; taller ones auto-open the drawer on activation. Many mode shows one card/fan per sample.
- **Rich Views** toggle in the probes sidebar (default on): probes auto-render the first applicable renderer when it fits; double-click flips an individual probe back to text. Tables remain opt-in.
- Empty hands render a card-footprint silhouette (dotted outline, ∅) instead of nothing.
- Offside **stagger**: an after-display pass floors each display at the end of every code line it spans and first-fits it among displays from rows above, so multi-row content (card fans) overlaps neither program text nor other probes.

title: Fix char-level copy regression: copying sub-token range copies whole token
body:
## Bug
Copying a sub-token selection copies the **whole token** instead of the selected characters. E.g. selecting `ll` inside the string literal `"hello"` and pressing Cmd/Ctrl+C puts `"hello"` on the clipboard.

## Root cause
This regressed in #2306 ("fix: Cmd+C/V/X in Firefox after editor focus"). That PR removed the page-level copy handler — which computed the clipboard text via `cursor.selected_text` → `Zipper.trim_selected_text` (correct char-level trim) — and replaced it with a new `CodeEditable.copy_selection` that prints `z.selection.content` **without** the trim:

```reason
let str = Printer.of_segment(~indent=" ", ~refractors=..., z.selection.content);
```

The trim logic (`Zipper.trim_selected_text` / `selection_trim_offsets`) and its tests already existed (added with char-level selections), but only the test path and `CodeWithStatics` called it — so the copy handler quietly skipped it and the existing tests stayed green.

## Fix
- Add `Printer.selected_text` as the single source of truth for "what gets copied" (print the selection content, then trim to the char-level boundaries).
- Route all three callers through it: `CodeEditable.copy_selection`, `CodeWithStatics`'s `selected_text` accessor, and the `test_copy` test helper — so the trim can't silently regress in just one path again.
- `copy_selection` caches the segment for paste reuse **only when nothing was trimmed** (a trimmed sub-token string must re-parse on paste, not round-trip back to the full segment).

## Tests
`test_copy` now exercises the same `Printer.selected_text` the UI uses (previously it duplicated the logic, which is why it couldn't catch this). Added cases for:
- sub-range inside a string literal (`"he§ll¦o"` → `ll`)
- sub-range inside an int literal (`123§45¦6` → `45`)
- cross-token range with both ends inside tokens (`le§t x = tr¦ue` → `t x = tr`)
- cross-token range ending inside a string

Verified red→green: without the trim, `Copy middle of token: ppl from apple` fails; with it, the full suite passes (`@test-quick`, 0 failures).

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

---

## Follow-up commit: Unicode over-trim (emoji in string literals)

A second bug in the same trim path: copying a sub-range inside a string containing a wide character (e.g. selecting the emoji in `"😀"`) copied `😀"` — one extra trailing quote.

`selection_trim_offsets` computed the trim using `Caret.inner_offset_for_token`, which returns **display columns** (a wide char like an emoji is 2 columns), but the clipboard slicing (`Unicode.length` / `Token.split_nth`) counts **graphemes** (emoji = 1). So the right trim under-counted by one grapheme. ASCII strings were unaffected (columns == graphemes there).

Fix: add `Caret.inner_grapheme_offset` (grapheme-based, `idx + 1`) and use it in `selection_trim_offsets`; `inner_offset_for_token` (columns) stays for caret/highlight positioning, which legitimately needs columns. Tests added: emoji inside a string literal, and an ascii char before an emoji.

title: Type slicing v2
body:
## Summary

This adds query-driven polymorphic type slicing to Hazel. It is an approximation of [this paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.12197).

When selecting a term, it has a synthesised type and (sometimes) an expected type. Slicing allows us to omit parts of either of these types to form a **query**, and retrieves a fragment of the term and respectively the surrounding context around the term which _explains the **queried** part of the type_ (omitting regions by ID).

Formally, if we place holes at omitted locations, a sliced program should synthesise / expect a type at least as strong as we queried at the term we were selecting.

Further, it also calculates subparts of the types each variable/type constructor needs. i.e. a slice of the typing context at the term.

| Type | Definition | What it holds |
|---|---|---|
| `gamma` | `VarMap.t_(Typ.t)` | the assumptions: one refined type per free name the slice still needs |
| `sty` (sliceable type) | `{shape, dispatch, finalize}` | a node's own type, plus a lazy `query => result` |
| `result` | `{omitted, gamma, psi, context, ana}` | a slice: omitted ids, `gamma`, the sliced type `psi`, and the minimal context/analysis type it still needs |
| `child_mode` | `Keep`, `Omit`, or `Source` | which let operator tagged a sub-term's recursion |

The implementation is *lazy*, and does not require full reconstructing a full info map, though slicing follow the same flow as type checking, so has similar asymptotics.

It intentionally piggybacks upon the existing statics system. Slicing mechanism follows the same dataflow as slicing in most cases (reversed for binders), and tries to integrate into it with minimal changes to the type checking infrastructure. 

This should mean that you can write new type checking rules mostly how you would before, then simply annotate how slicing works on top. I expect that you should generally be able to get most slicing behaviour correct using just a few *heuristics* (below). The only slight differences are reworking the interface to type matching functions (arrow_tolerant etc.) and CoCtx (which now tracks constructors and aliases too).

## Adding to `Statics.re`

1) Write a new typing rule normally first, using ordinary `let` bindings and `type formers`. 
2) Check your typing rules etc. etc.
3) Annotate recursive bindings (`let ... = go(...)`) with custom let operators which act as heuristics describing how each sub-term’s type contributes to the result.

### Type formers

Use a `MatchedTyp` former to describe how types can be matched and rebuilt, i.e. projections from a product, and building a1 product.

### List Cons Example

```
let* (hd, hd_elab, m) =
  go(~ana=MatchedTyp.list_tolerant(ctx, ana), hd, m);

let& (tl, tl_elab, m) =
  go(~ana=List(hd.ty) |> Typ.temp, tl, m);
```

The head supplies the list's element type (`let*`): the query is matched against the `List` former, routed in to `hd`, and the result is rebuilt from what comes back. The tail is only checked (`let&`), since a cons cell's type already comes from its head — slicing `tl` further couldn't add anything the head didn't already supply.

### Binding Example
```
let (p_syn, _, _) =
  go_pat(~co_ctx=CoCtx.empty, ~ana=syn, p, m);

let$ (def, def_elab, m) =
  go(~ana=p_syn.ty, def, m);

let* (body, body_elab, m) =
  go(~ctx=p_ana_ctx, ~ana, body, m);

let@ (p_ana, p_elab, m) =
  go_pat(~co_ctx=body.co_ctx, ~ana=def.ty, p, m);
```

Use `let$` for definitions behind bindings. Use `let*` for any expression whose type feeds the result directly, whether it's one component of something larger or, as with `body` here, the whole thing unchanged. Use `let@` for final slices on patterns.

### Alternative branches

Use `let&` for subterms which are type checked against (e.g. conditional in an if statement). Use `let+` for types which are met to compute an overall type (e.g. branches in if statements):
```
let& (cond, cond_elab, m) =
  go(~ana=Atom(Bool) |> Typ.temp, cond, m);

let+ (cons, cons_elab, m) = go(~ana, cons, m);
let+ (alt, alt_elab, m) = go(~ana, alt, m);
```

  Each branch receives the query remaining after the preceding branches. Their types are still combined using
  Hazel’s existing `Typ.meet` operations.

 ### Co-contexts

A co-context (`CoCtx.t`) is the dual of a context: a map from variable name to every use of it in scope, each entry carrying the id and expected type of that use site. Ordinary type checking already compares it against the context to find free and unused variables without a second pass over the term; slicing reuses it unchanged, except an entry can now come from a constructor or alias use as well as a variable, since a slice needs the same free/unused reasoning to decide which constructors and aliases it must keep.

  ### Operator reference

  | Operator | Use | Example |
  |---|---|---|
  | `let*` | An expression or pattern supplies the result type, or one component of it when the result is built from several. The whole-type case is just this with a single component. | A list element supplies the list’s element type; the body of `let p = d in body` supplies its type whole. |
  | `let&` | A sub-term is checked (so does not supply the result type). | An `if` condition. |
  | `let$` | Definitions behind bindings (defs, scrutinees) | The definition in a `let`. |
  | `let@` | On pattern bindings themselves (final call only if you call multiple times) | A function parameter. |
  | `let+` | A branch is an alternative source of the same result type. | An `if` branch. |

When the sub-term being recursed is actually a TYPE, you double the symbols: i.e. `let$$` is used for type aliases definitions.

There are also some more specific adhoc binders or combinations:
  | Operator | Use | Example |
  |---|---|---|
  | `let^?` | A sub-term supplies the complete type but may be pruned for a shape only query. Requires a former. | List concatenation. |
  | `let&>` | As `let&`, with its expected query supplied by an explicit source. | An ascribed expression checked by its annotation. |
  | `let@+` | A pattern binds names for one corresponding alternative. | A `match` pattern and branch. |
  | `let^*` | The result is a named component projected from a sub-term’s type. | The codomain of a function application. |
  | `let^>` | A pattern supplies the complete type and is checked from an explicit type source. | An ascribed  pattern. |

TODO: have fewer adhoc binders.

## Architecture

- Lazily computed
- Extensible, due to not using explicit matches on type functions (at least in the direct slicing code)
- Slicing direction is reversed automatically by the use of operators (i.e. binders using `let$` reverse the direction)


## Testing strategy

- `Statics.Slicing.Synthesis`: ordinary slicing of synthesis typing rules
- `Statics.Slicing.Analysis`: analysis slicing of subterms querying the expected type.
- `Statics.Slicing.Binding`: binding operators (reverse slicing flow). This also tests the `gamma` storing the typing context slices.
- `Statics.Slicing.ExtendedExamples` covers larger examples, including subterms in synthesis position, and larger branching code.
- `Statics.Slicing.InvalidQuery` checks missing focus, wrong focus sort, and incompatible query shape exceptions.
- Type formers (`MatchedTyp`) aren't tested in isolation; they're exercised as part of a full rule, through the Synthesis/Analysis/Binding suites above.
- `TypeSlicing.UI` slicing is linked up to a overlay to fold away omitted regions correctly in the UI
- Property Tests: Validity (slices actually produce the same types), and Monotonicity (smaller queries produce monotonically smaller and _consistent_ slices).

title: Native terminal UI (tui.exe) on notty
body:
## Summary

A native terminal UI for Hazel: a new `haz3ltui` library + `tui.exe`, built on
[notty](https://github.com/pqwy/notty), running as a plain OCaml executable that reuses
the de-webbed core editing pipeline (no node / JS runtime).

**Stacked on #2349** (de-web the core) — please review/merge that first; the diff here is
TUI-only.

## Native terminal UI (`src/tui/`)

Launched with `./hazel-tui [file]` (`make tui` to build). It opens and edits plaintext
`.hz` source files directly and saves them with **Ctrl+S** (`./hazel-tui` with no
argument is a scratch buffer). Because the on-disk format is plain Hazel source —
including `^^probe(...)` triggers — files round-trip between the TUI and the web editor.

**Reused from `core` / `language`, unchanged:**
- The full editing pipeline — `Action.t` / `Perform` / `Measured`, `Editor.Update`,
  `CachedStatics` / `CachedSyntax`.
- Parsing, statics, elaboration, evaluation, and probes.
- The shared `Keyboard.handle_key_event` keymap (now in `core`).
- Token classification (the same `Code.re` walk the web uses).

**Reimplemented for the terminal** (the web equivalents are Vdom/DOM-bound):
- *Rendering*: views target a backend-agnostic `Frame.t` (styled rows + cursor);
  `EditorView` ports the web `Code.re` walk to styled rows (`Theme.re`); `NottyIO`
  turns frames into notty images.
- *Input*: notty key/mouse/paste events translate to `AnsiInput.event`; `AnsiInput.re`
  is also a standalone escape-sequence parser that drives `--replay` and the golden tests.
- *Projector views*: a `TermProjector` registry renders Fold, Checkbox, Slider/SliderF,
  Type, TextArea, Table, Probe, and Card. Kinds without a bespoke terminal view (Livelit,
  CSV) render their syntax as a dim chip.
- *Panes*: result pane (live eval, 200 ms debounce, evaluated async in a forked worker),
  cursor inspector (Ctrl+T), floating backpack chip, status bar, and offside probe-sample
  display.
- *Mouse*: SGR tracking — click to place caret, double/triple-click token/term select,
  shift+click and drag select, wheel scroll.

**Keybinding differences from the web:** Ctrl+S saves the buffer to its `.hz` file
(web's Ctrl+S pretty-print moves to Alt+P); Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y for undo/redo (terminals
can't see Ctrl+Shift+Z).

**Intentionally not ported (yet):** full probe UI (sample focus, step-into, pinning;
only offside sample values render); in-place editing for TextArea/Table projectors;
TyDi assist / completion buffer; slides / exercises / settings (single scratch editor only).

## Tests

- New `Test_TuiGolden` (golden replay) and `Test_TuiInput` (escape-sequence parser)
  suites, run by the native `haz3ltest.exe` (169 tests). `haz3ltest_common` links
  `haz3ltui` (which re-provides `haz3lcore`).

title: InfiAgent-DABench in Hazel: 242/257 solved + supporting CLI/evaluator improvements
body:
## Scope / status

**Draft for discussion.** Base branch is **`edit-time-csv-cli`**, which carries the
de-web-core + hazel-tui foundation and the initial `^^csv("path")` edit-time CSV hook.
Scoped against that base, this PR is just the benchmark effort and its direct supporting
changes — **22 commits, ~9 source files plus the `da-bench/` experiment** (267 files /
~4.4k lines). The foundation and the base `^^csv` work are not part of this diff; they
land via their own branches.

---

## 1. Improvements & fixes to Hazel / the CLI

Reusable changes in this PR (on top of the base branch's `^^csv` edit-time hook),
independent of the benchmark:

- **Evaluator stack-overflow fix (tail-recursive list traversals).** Large lists used to
  overflow the small js_of_ocaml/node stack because three run-path traversals grew one
  frame per element (`StaticsBase.map_m`/`map_m2` — which also did an O(n²) `xs @ [x]` —
  the `Statics` `ListLit` case, and `ValueChecker.req_all_final`). These are now
  tail-recursive (plus tail-recursive `ListUtil` helpers and `ExpToSegment`), so
  sort/median/quantile/correlation run on tables of thousands of rows.
- **`np_permutation` builtin** (`src/language/builtins/BuiltinsBase.re`): numpy-exact
  legacy `RandomState` MT19937 + descending Fisher-Yates, in native OCaml. Matches
  `np.random.RandomState(seed).permutation(n)` bit-for-bit, enabling reproducible
  train/test splits.
- **`^^seed(N)` edit-time hook** (`src/CLI/Seed.re`, `Cli.re`): mirrors the base `^^csv`
  hook by splicing a default integer seed as a literal *before* parsing (the language
  stays pure). Interactively the caller may keep the source default, override it, or press
  `r` for an OS-random seed; `--yes` keeps the source default so runs stay reproducible.
- **CSV header whitespace trim** (`src/CLI/Csv.re`): trims header whitespace on ingestion
  (extending the base branch's UTF-8 BOM strip) so padded column names are reachable.

## 2. The InfiAgent-DABench harness (`da-bench/`)

A self-contained experiment measuring Hazel's expressiveness on real data-analysis tasks
(**InfiAgent-DABench**, Hu et al., ICML 2024 — 257 dev questions). It does **not** ship
the benchmark's gold answers — solutions are graded against the external
`da-dev-labels.jsonl` at run time.

- **Solutions** (`da-bench/da*.hz`): one hand-written Hazel program per task, run via
  `run.sh` (which concatenates `prelude.hz` + the solution and evaluates it).
- **`prelude.hz`**: a from-scratch, pure-Hazel numeric library — descriptive stats
  (mean/median/std/skew/kurtosis, IQR & Z-score outliers), Pearson correlation **with
  p-values** (built on `erf`/`lgamma`/`betainc`), t-tests, ANOVA, χ², Kolmogorov–Smirnov,
  Mann–Whitney, Shapiro–Wilk, OLS and logistic regression, and a numpy-compatible
  MT19937 + `train_test_split` — all verified against scipy/sklearn.
- **`check_label.py` + `test.sh`**: the regression harness. `test.sh` lists solution
  filenames only; `check_label.py` looks each answer up by task id in the external labels
  file and grades by comparing answer *values* order-independently (numeric to the label's
  precision, case-insensitive strings). No gold answers are stored in the repo.
- **`RESULTS.md`**: the ledger of what passes, what doesn't, and *why* (with the recurring
  classes of inexpressibility / unreproducible-label / defect documented per task).

## 3. Results overview

- **242 / 257 dev tasks solved and verified** against the InfiAgent-DABench labels.
- Demonstrates Hazel can express the full arc of a data-analysis workflow purely:
  descriptive statistics, **hypothesis testing with a hand-built special-function
  library** (the p-value half that needs distribution CDFs), correlation and regression,
  **reproducible RNG-based train/test splits**, and several fitted models (OLS, logistic
  regression, a linear-regression classifier).
- Along the way it surfaced and fixed the general evaluator stack-overflow above, and
  motivated the CLI data hooks and the `np_permutation` builtin.

## 4. Performance & runtime considerations

Hazel evaluates through a **tree-walking interpreter** compiled to JS (js_of_ocaml) and
run under Node — built for interactive editing, not big-data throughput. The benchmark
pushed it well past its usual scale, which drove several of the changes above:

- **CSV ingestion is AST-spliced, not re-parsed.** `^^csv` builds the table directly as
  AST so the data never goes through the (slow) tylr surface parser — text-expanding +
  re-parsing a ~700-row table took ~4 min vs. ~5 s for the splice.
- **Raised stack/heap.** The prelude is large and recursion-heavy, so `run.sh` runs Node
  with `--stack-size=8192` (up from the ~1 MB default) and `--max-old-space-size=8192`
  (8 GB heap) to avoid stack overflow / OOM on big tables.
- **Traversal cost is still linear-interpreted.** The tail-recursion fix removed the
  O(n²)/overflow behavior, but sort/median/quantile/correlation are still O(n) interpreted
  passes — seconds to minutes on thousands of rows.
- **A few large-table tasks dominate.** Most tasks grade in seconds; the cost is
  concentrated in the ~4k–17k-row tables (abalone, tree, veracruz, baro). The extreme is
  **da363 (`weather_train`, n=16,684)**: it builds thousands of functional gather-trees for
  a seeded split and, under memory pressure near the 8 GB cap, can thrash for a very long
  time (observed effectively hung at ~2 h in one full-suite run). A plain full
  `test.sh` run is therefore long (tens of minutes to hours) and best driven per-case or
  on a subset; routine use is `test.sh da0-mean-fare.hz`.
- **Native RNG for speed.** A pure-Hazel MT19937 was *correct* but far too slow (32-bit
  ops by bit-decomposition; abalone n=4,177 even crashed). The `np_permutation` native
  builtin replaced it — instant, and it's what makes the seeded-split tasks tractable.

## 5. Why the remaining 15 aren't solved

Every unsolved task is accounted for in `RESULTS.md`; none is a silent gap. Grouped by
cause:

**Require sklearn's *internal* RNG, not numpy's (2):** the model is implementable, but the
graded metric depends on sklearn's internal C tree-builder RNG, which is brittle/version-
specific to replicate.
- **674** (decision-tree regression): a from-scratch CART matches sklearn's root and ~96%
  of the tree, then diverges at a 5-sample node where two features tie on the split proxy
  *bit-for-bit*; sklearn breaks the tie with its `our_rand_r` feature-shuffle (≠ numpy
  MT19937). No deterministic tie-rule reproduces the labeled 0.6419.
- **424** (random-forest feature importance): strictly harder — needs the seeded ensemble
  (bootstrap + per-split feature subsampling × 100 trees) *and* each tree's internal RNG.

**Label not reproducible in the reference's own tools / underspecified (3):**
- **137** (logistic, `class_weight='balanced'`): sklearn itself gives 0.59 (unweighted) or
  0.64 (balanced) — never the labeled 0.61.
- **523** (KNN Age-imputation): the labeled child-count (72) isn't reproducible in sklearn
  (got 91/69 across configs); the KNN setup is underspecified.
- **432** (split MSE): the task states **no `random_state`**, so its split — and thus the
  labeled MSE 263.19 — isn't reproducible by any seed.

**Benchmark label defects — our computation matches pandas/the spec, the label doesn't
(6):** **252, 297, 298, 300, 361, 662**. (E.g. 300: our Pearson r = 0.53, which `df.corr`
agrees with, vs label 0.54; 252: a degenerate NaN-`idxmax` picks the wrong country.) Each
emits the honest value and is excluded from `test.sh`.

**Impractical input parsing / convention (1):** **431** — duration must be parsed from
en-dash + non-breaking-space month ranges ("July 30 – August 1"), beyond Hazel's ASCII
string ops; even a calendar-correct pandas duration gives 0.57 vs the labeled 0.56.

**Answer isn't a computable value (2):** **741** (graded answer is the literal column name
`"ratio"`) and **743** (graded answer is a written-out file path — Hazel is pure and writes
no files). Both compute the honest part and are documented.

**True language blocker (1):** **618** — the column name `#photo` contains `#`, which
collides with Hazel's comment delimiter, so the backtick label is unparseable and the
column can't be projected.

title: Edit-time projector resolution with CSV and random-seed loaders
body:
## What

Based on #2349. Adds **edit-time data projectors** to the CLI: a projector resolves to
real program syntax (an `Exp`) at parse time, which is substituted in place before the
program is evaluated.

- `^^csv("path-or-url")` — loads and parses a CSV into program data (a list of rows).
- `^^seed(N)` — resolves to a chosen integer seed.

~~The syntax is `^^csv("path")` where the path is the unix-style file path on your device.~~
The CSV argument may be a **local file** (unix-style path, resolved relative to the program
or `--data-dir`) **or** an **`http(s)` URL**. The CLI asks for consent before reading the
data (skippable with `--yes`), then inserts the parsed result directly into the program source.

## How

Projectors gain a small resolution lifecycle in `ProjectorBase`:
`init` (sync placeholder at parse time) → `resolve` (a **one-shot CPS thunk** that performs
the projector's own IO via injected `UrlFetch` / `SeedChoose` hooks) → `update` (fold the
result action) → `expand` (the projector's pure `Exp` contribution). `ProjectorInitPhase.run`
drives each projector once; `substitute` replaces each projector node with its expanded `Exp`
**in place** — no segment, no re-parse, no global side table. IO stays out of `haz3lcore`: it
lives in the projector modules behind `util` ref hooks, wired up by the CLI
(`install_url_fetch` / `install_seed_chooser`) and the web (`ProjectorView.run_init_phase`).

Also includes: `round : Float -> Float` builtin; CSV BOM/whitespace stripping; the `Seed`
projector kind + web view.

## Testing

`make dev` and `make test-quick` green. Verified via the CLI: `^^seed(42)` → 42,
`length(census_500)` → 500, aggregations over loaded CSV tables. The web editor path compiles
but has **not** been browser-tested.

title: Add D3 chart projector (^^chart) with optional auto-display
body:
## Summary

Adds a `^^chart` projector that renders a Hazel value as a chart, modeled on the existing
Table projector. The same labeled-tuple data that feeds tables is naturally chartable, so
this gives bar / grouped-bar / line / scatter / pie views of evaluated results.

Charts are described by a new built-in `Chart` ADT. Rendering is done **by d3 itself** (d3
owns the DOM): the selection/axis/shape code lives in JS, and OCaml recognizes the data and
hands d3 the container node.

## The `Chart` ADT (`BuiltinsADT.re`)

```
type Chart =
  + BarChart([(label=String, value=Float)])
  + GroupedBarChart([(name=String, data=[(label=String, value=Float)])])
  + LineChart([(x=Float, y=Float)])
  + ScatterChart([(x=Float, y=Float)])
  + PieChart([(label=String, value=Float)])
```

Bar/Pie share the categorical shape; Line/Scatter share the points shape; GroupedBarChart is
a list of named series. Constructor names are namespaced (`BarChart`, not `Bar`) to avoid the
flat global constructor namespace (JSON already claims `Float`/`Int`/`String`/`List`/`Bool`).
Registered via a single `type_aliases` row.

Data must be `Float` in the surface language — there is **no implicit `Int`→`Float` coercion**
(use `float_of_int`), matching the ADT's payload types.

## Architecture

- **`ChartCore.re`** — a pure, D3-free recognizer (`parse_chart : Exp.t => option(chart_spec)`),
  reusing `TableCore.parse_table` + `HazelJson`'s wrapper stripping. Unit-tested natively. Also
  exports `is_chart_ctr_ap`, the cheap type-level test that gates auto-display (below).
- **`ChartProj.re`** — marshals `chart_spec` to a JS object and drives d3 through **one generic
  `Attr.create_hook`** (like the existing `ScrollIntoViewHook`). The container `<div>` has no
  vdom children, so vdom leaves d3's subtree alone across re-renders. Mirrors `TableProj` for
  `init`/`get`/`placeholder`/`error`.
- **`prebundle.js`** — `window.HazelD3.render(el, spec)` dispatches on `spec.kind` using real d3
  (`d3.axisLeft`/`axisBottom`, `.data().enter()`, `d3.line`, `d3.pie`/`d3.arc`). Series colors come
  from CSS vars (`--chart-1..8`, an earthy palette in `variables.css`), with native `<title>`
  tooltips, hover highlight, bar value labels, per-series legends, and pie-legend truncation.
- Registered in `ProjectorKind` (`^^chart` via lexer + `of_name`), `ProjectorInit`, context menu.

Adding a chart kind is a `chart_spec` variant + a `js_of_spec` branch + a JS render function.

**Grouped series align by label** ([review](https://github.com/hazelgrove/hazel/pull/2350#discussion_r3460638264)):
the category axis is the union of every series' labels in first-seen order, and each series looks
its own values up by label. `series.values : list(option(float))` is positional against that axis,
with `None` crossing to JS as `null` so `renderBar` leaves a gap instead of shifting a series'
remaining bars into another category's slot. Series need not carry the same categories, or the
same number of them.

## Auto-display in eval output (`project_charts` setting)

Mirrors `project_tables`: a `Chart` value in an evaluated result auto-renders when the **"Charts"**
toggle is on (Nut menu → Value Display). No conflict with tables — tables fire on bare list
literals, charts on `Chart`-constructor applications. Off by default (opt-in), like Tables.

The gate is the constructor's **type**, not its name
([review](https://github.com/hazelgrove/hazel/pull/2350#discussion_r3431328434)):
`is_chart_ctr_ap` peels arrows off the type statics puts on the constructor and compares the
result against `BuiltinsADT.Chart.t`. Every variant is covered without enumerating names, and a
user ADT that shadows a Chart constructor name is not projected as a chart.

## Testing

- `test/Test_ChartCore.re` (17 cases): all kinds incl. grouped, empty/ragged/non-finite data,
  Int-value rejection, a positional-tuple case verifying the ADT registration drives
  auto-labeling, grouped series with differing and short label lists, and the auto-display gate
  (accepts all five constructors; rejects a shadowed constructor name and unelaborated syntax).
- `make dev` builds clean; `make test-quick` passes (3326 tests).
- Manually verified rendering for every kind in the browser (manual `^^chart` and auto-display).
  The label-union grouped rendering wants one more browser pass.

## Notes / trade-offs

- ~~Grouped/multi-series bars are supported by the recognizer but not reachable through the
  single-value-column ADT… open question whether to add a dedicated grouped-bar constructor.~~
  **Resolved:** added the `GroupedBarChart` constructor (typed, explicit), rendered with
  per-series colors + a legend.
- A multi-numeric-column inner `data` table is unreachable from a well-typed program (the ADT
  types the payload as a single `(label, value)` list), so `parse_grouped` reads the first
  numeric column and says so in a comment rather than guarding it. The multi-column path in
  `parse_categorical` is deliberate — that's how one wide-format `BarChart` becomes grouped.
- d3 owning the DOM means per-kind drawing lives in JS — outside OCaml's type checker and unit
  tests. In exchange it's less code overall and each kind is cheap to add; the recognizer
  (`ChartCore`) stays pure OCaml and is what the tests cover.
- Adds `d3-scale`/`d3-array`/`d3-selection`/`d3-axis`/`d3-shape` (`bundled.js` ~1.1 MB).

title: De-web the language and core libraries
body:
## Summary

The `language` and `core` (`haz3lcore`) libraries no longer depend on js_of_ocaml /
Vdom and now compile as ordinary native OCaml. All web-specific code (Vdom views, DOM
listeners, the LLM agent layer) moves out into the `web` library.

This is the base for a stacked PR — **#2354** adds a native terminal UI on top of it.
(Previously this branch also contained the TUI; that has been split out into #2354.)

## De-webbing

- **`util`**: web-only modules (`BonsaiUtil`, `*MenuListener`, `FloatingElement`,
  `JsUtil`, `SafeTriangle`, `SvgUtil`, `WebUtil`) move into the `web` library. Regex,
  grapheme segmentation, and URI coding get pure implementations (`Unicode`,
  `StringUtil`, `API`); `Key.re` is dropped.
- **`language`**: livelit *views* move to a web registry; `Livelit.re` keeps only the
  core definitions.
- **`core`**: each projector is split into pure core logic (stays in `core`) and a web
  Vdom view (`web/projectors/`). Time and DOM-focus become **injection points**
  (`CoreEffects` in `web`). The LLM agent layer moves to `web/agent/`. The `Keyboard`
  keymap moves into `core` so it no longer lives in the web library.
- **Projectors**: pure helpers lift to file level (`docs/projector-backend-split.md`);
  `TableProj` gains a sizing-backend hook (`WebApprox` vs `TextGrid`) so a non-web
  frontend can reserve exact space — the web keeps `WebApprox`.
- **`nativecheck`**: a native smoke-check executable parses and evaluates `1 + 2` with
  no js_of_ocaml dependency, guarding against native-buildability regressions.

## Tests

- Harness split so web-free suites run natively (`haz3ltest.exe`, ~2750 quick tests, no
  node) and the seven web-dependent suites run under node (`haz3ltest_web.bc.js`).
  Shared modules live in `haz3ltest_common`; see `haz3ltest.re` / `haz3ltest_web.re`,
  `run_node.sh`, `run_tests`, and `test/dune`.

title: Automerge read/write projectors
body: Introduces a pair of Automerge projectors that can read from and write to Automerge documents. The read projector pulls in an Automerge document specified by URL and converts the raw JSON into a Hazel JSON value that can then be manipulated programmatically within Hazel. It includes buttons for hot-reloading and, if not hot-reloading, manual refreshing. These are instantiated via `^^Automerge(Null)` (where `Null` is the initial JSON value getting projected over and will be replaced by whatever Automerge JSON doc is loaded in). The write projector takes an Automerge url and pushes whatever JSON value it is projecting over to that url. These are instantiated via `^^AutomergeWriteBack()` where `` is whatever Hazel JSON value you want to write back - in the screenshots below, this is just the empty `Null` value. Validating behavior here requires creating Automerge documents through tiny.patchwork.inkandswitch.com (or some other Automerge doc interface), copying and pasting Automerge URLs into the read/write projectors, and assessing the JSON values read into Hazel and written back to the Automerge doc.
