title: Perfmageddon
body:
Currently offers an up to an order-of-magnitude speedup on best-case edit action keystrokes

The biggest gains are due to eliminating extraneous Incr_dom cycles happening on ~ every keystroke:

- Due to the legacy doubletap detection, every KeyUp event was triggering a new cycle. Removing this gives a ~50%+ overall speedup
- Saving was happening every keystroke, in fact sometimes twice (on keyup as well). This was a double-whammy, as saving on edit actions was being done in Keyboard by scheduling an additional event. The ability of the key handlers to return a list of updates, each of which triggers a full incr_dom cycle, is a moral hazard and has been removed; each key event now returns an option(Action) instead. Saving also no longer happens after every edit action; rather it happens 1 second after the last edit action happened. Together this is a ~200-400% overall speedup.
- There was a check in the on_display hook which scrolled the caret into view which was gated on detecting a change in the model. This is expensive, not because of the model comparison, but simply because the old_model is in the Incr monad, and mapping into Incr triggers a cycle. Removing this check gives a ~50% speedup.

Other gains:

- 5x speedup to Paste by bypassing Editor Meta recalculation
- Huge speedup in very imbalanced states by memoizing Backpack.shard_info
- 10x speedup in Holes Deco by just scanning info_map instead of recursing
- 2x speedup for Termranges.mk; was called twice with no memoization. I now passing it through directly as it's clean to do so, but I also memoized it defensively
- 60% speedup for Code.view by recursively memoizing Text.of_tile
- 30% speedup for MakeTerm by memoizing Skel.mk

Remaining possible speedups:

- Logging: Gets slow with lots of entries. With localstore you can't just append, you need to set. Could switch to a system for which each entry gets its own a KV pair of something.
- Saving Editors to LocalStorage: I caused a bit of a regression when I moved to serializing the entire Editors. Probably not a priority with the new save delay system, but could use some TLC eventually.
- Backpack: If we are still experiencing too much slowdown in unbalanced states, shard_info could be greatly speeded up if we were to eliminate unrestricted pick-up functionality (i.e. the ability to have backpack selections containing multiple shards)
- Maketerm: The recursion structure in Maketerm makes recursive memoization difficult. We want to memoize something that's likely to have physical equality i.e. substructures which are likely literally preserved over edits, like segments or tiles. But the core Maketerm functions (go_s, unsorted) take both a segment and a skel as arguments; since the skel is derived, we're never going to have physical equality for substructures if the superstructure changes. I'm wondering if it's possible to internalize skel generation to these functions; instead of sending in a skel, send in a subsegment
- PtMaps/Maps/Hashtbls: Replace remaining ptmap use with plain maps and/or replace maps use with hashtbls everywhere. I'm unsure as to the overall impact but it could be significant; probably worth doing more bottom-up profiling. As a stopgap we're still unioning in some places which could be turned into traversals (e.g. TermRanges)
- Elaboration Views: Right now turning off dynamics can slow things down as it takes time to render large elaborations. This is partially addressed in `llmass` as it makes it possible to actually turn of statics, resulting in no elaboration being generated. There should probably be a separate toggle for elaboration though.
- Zipper pass fusion: In general we could probably consider some more structured architecture for passes over the zipper. Currently we have MakeTerm, Measured, TermRanges, and Code.view which all do zipper passes. Two or more of these could potentially be fused into a single 'SyntaxInfo' pass. SyntaxInfo could potentially collect some information which is either being reproduced ad-hoc in many places (expected sort) or currently lives in static info (term, cls, list of ancestor ids)

title: Loosened annotation requirements for recursive functions
body:
## Introduction
This pull request aims to loosen annotation requirements for recursive functions.

Currently, marking a function as recursive is achieved by adding an arrow type annotation to its corresponding variable. This makes all variables within the function body having the same name become bound, though shadowing within the body may change the expression they are bound to:
![image](https://github.com/hazelgrove/hazel/assets/108375845/1f68e942-3ab4-4d83-825f-9bd09036c067)

The new approach aims to make a function recursive as long as it's correctly annotated (specifically, normalized `Arrow`s, `Invalid`s, `MultiHole`s, `TypeHole`s, and free type variables). The new approach implements this by introducing a new function `Statics.is_recursive` that checks if the number of variables match the number of function literals in a let expression, and they are "correctly" annotated. It replaces `extend_let_def_ctx`.

The new approach also attempts to synthesize out more accurate types (at least arrow types) for unannotated recursive functions.

## Some special cases
The process of determining recursiveness doesn't consider whether the type of the definition (the function literal) matches the annotation. I believe this has already been addressed properly...?
![image](https://github.com/hazelgrove/hazel/assets/108375845/abc4c8c2-3366-4f1d-8ba5-3fa4010dd84b)

The tuple pattern for mutual recursive function variables can be annotated as a whole:
![image](https://github.com/hazelgrove/hazel/assets/108375845/082bdf0c-d4e0-4131-bf6a-cc9e12793e21)

There is also a case where the synthesize mode might be turned into the analyze mode: https://github.com/hazelgrove/hazel/pull/1069#discussion_r1320060919

## If this was merged, ...
* #965 would be affected because it modified `extend_let_def_ctx` (but in the good way, because they modified it to include the output of `is_recursive`.
* #1056 would be affected because it applied `extend_let_def_ctx`. But would let operators be related to recursions?

title: Partial application of non-curried functions
body:
Continuation of #957.
This feature introduces partial application of non-curried functions. As #514 mentioned:

> During elaboration, the partial application is replaced with a new function literal that takes in the unapplied arguments, then inserts them where they belong in the application of the original function.

The partial application of non-curried functions has been mostly implemented in #957, but it violates the principle that "deferral expressions should not synthesize to or analyze against any type." Additionally, there are some design issues to address. The purpose of this pull request is to resolve these issues.

### Examples

> ```
> val f: ('a, 'b, 'c) → 'd
> val x: 'a
> val y: 'b
> val z: 'c
> ```
> 
> |External Expression|Internal Expression|Synthesized Type|
> |:--|:--|:--|
> |`f (x, y, z)`|`f (x, y, z)`|`'d`|
> |`f (x, _, z)`|`λb.{f (x, b, z)}`|`'b → 'd`|
> |`f (_, y, _)`|`λ(a, c).{f (a, y, c)}`|`('a, 'c) → 'd`|
> |`f (_, _, _)`|`λ(a, b, c).{f (a, b, c)}`|`('a, 'b, 'c) → 'd`|

A function that has an input type inconsistent with a non-trivial product type cannot be partially applied. `(fun x : Int -> x)(_)` or `(fun x : () -> x)(_)` should result in some kind of error that prompts the user to work on the function rather than meaningless partial application.

If the input type of the function is a type hole, we cannot statically analyze whether the function can be partially applied. This means that the expression `(fun x -> x + 1)(_, 1)` is statically valid, and would be elaborated as `λy.{(λx.{x + 1}) (y, 1)}`. 

Providing a deferral singleton as an argument to such functions, like `(fun x -> x + 1)(_)`, is something programmers can do. There are different ways to handle such expressions statically:
* We can enforce that the argument for partial application must be a non-empty tuple, and then have this kind of expression result in an error to alert programmers about "meaningless partial application."
* Alternatively, we can refrain from imposing restrictions on the argument for partial application, allowing such expressions to be valid from a static perspective and be elaborated accordingly.
* ~~A more extreme approach would be to further restrict the input type of the function, disallowing type holes as valid input types.~~

### Implementation
* Add two new `UExp.term`s: `Deferral` and `DeferredAp(UExp.t, UExp.t)`.
* `_` introduces a `Deferral` expression. When a `Deferral` is either **a projection of the argument of a partial applicaton**, or **the argument of a partial application itself**, it's interpreted as bounded. Any other case would result in a `FreeDeferral` error. Adding extra parentheses around `_` would also result in a `FreeDeferral` error.
* Add a new `Info.error_exp` variant called `InconsistentWithDeferrableArrow` for functions that cannot be partially applied. ~~Assigning this error as Info to a function expression is challenging. Similar to the dilemma encountered in #957, although the current implementation of `Info.exp` includes `status_exp` to allow bypassing the function `status_exp` and directly assigning `status_exp` to an expression in `Statics.uexp_to_info_map`, the function `status_exp` is also used in other places like `elaborator.re`, resulting in inconsistent `status_exp` for the same expression in different locations. It would be best to restrict the use of the function `status_exp` to `Statics.re` only, but if that is not possible, to maintain data consistency, it would still require implementing the assignment of the new error in `status_exp`. Then,~~ a new variant of `Mode.t` called `SynDeferrableFun` would be needed, which, in addition to requiring the expression type to be consistent with the arrow type in `SynFun` mode, would also require its input type to be consistent with a non-trivial product type.
* If a function cannot be partially applied, it will match the arrow type `? -> ?`. If a function can be partially applied, the argument expression (arguments applied and deferrals) may not match the input type of the function. The verification process involves analyzing each element of the argument expression against the corresponding function input type, in which `Deferral`s are skipped.
* If there is a type inconsistency between the input and the argument types, a new variant of `Info.error_exp` called `InconsistentPartialApArg` will be assigned to the argument. In this error, `Deferral`s do not synthesize to or analyze against any type and appear only as placeholders (`_`) in the error message. ~~Similar to the challenges encountered with assigning `InconsistentWithDeferrableArrow`, if we want to implement error assignment within the function `status_exp`, the information about the *term* must be part of the input to `status_exp`. A better solution is to implement this within `Statics.uexp_to_info_map`, which currently leads to data inconsistency.~~
* The entire partial application is synthesized as an arrow type. If there is a type inconsistency between the input and the argument types, the input type of the arrow type is `Unknown`. In any case, the output type of the arrow type remains the same as the output type of the original function expression, providing as much as possible information to the programmer.
* In `elaborator.re`, when a partial application can be performed normally, the deferral expressions act as placeholders and are not elaborated. When there is a static error, partial application cannot be performed. To provide more reference information to programmers, a **full application** will be performed instead. This means that deferral expressions will be further elaborated into `EmptyHole`.
```
let plus = (fun (x, y) -> x + y) in
```
|External Expression|Internal Expression|Synthesized Type|
|:--|:--|:--|
|`_`|`InvalidText("_")`|`?`|
|`1 (_)`|`1 (?)`|`?`|
|`plus (_)`|`plus (?)`|`?`|
|`plus (_, 1)`|`(fun ~deferred0 -> plus(~deferred0, 1))`|`? -> Int`|
|`plus ((_), 1)`|`plus ((?), 1)`|`?`|
|`plus (_, _)`|`(fun (~deferred0, ~deferred1) -> plus(~deferred0, ~deferred1))`|`(?, ?) -> Int`|
|`plus (_, _, 1)`|`plus (?, ?, 1)`|`?`|

title: TyDi
body:
This adds type-directed autocompletion and a number of significant supporting features and related bugfixes.

Fixes:
- Closes #1013
- Closes #1076 
- Closes #1089

Abstract:
- TyDi offers per-token type-directed autocompletion for Hazel (closes #834, closes #837). This design is focused on labor-saving, with suggestion per se only a secondary goal. Currently, TyDi offers at most a single suggestion, and suggestion ranking is purely lexicographical. Implementation errors excepted, all suggestions are syntactically correct, and are type-correct in a sense that will be made precise.

Behavioral specification:
- The completion buffer appears after any `Insert` or `Destruct` action, when the caret is to the immediate right of a (non-empty) single-token term which has an error. The completion buffer displays suggested a (non-empty) affix which can be appended at the caret. For example if the token/term `sug` has an error, and the caret is to its right `sug|` then we may see `sug|gestion`, with affix `gestion`. 
- In some cases, the completion buffer may contain multiple tokens; e.g. `foo(` (2 tokens) or `foo( )::` (5 tokens), which suggest a function application, and an application and a cons operator respectively
- Note that the conditions above imply that suggestions will never be shown when the caret is on an empty hole or a type-correct token, and that single-character tokens will never be suggested.
- Pressing `tab` accepts a completion, which pops the buffer, parsing its contained tokens into the surrounding syntax. Note that this may result in tokens being added to the backpack, if for example a `)` if the buffer contains `foo(`.
- Any other edit or movement action removes the buffer; it will be regenerated only on `Insert` or `Destruct` actions.
- Completion can be disabled via a menu toggle
- In principle, TyDi has the following correctness and completeness goals: given the activation conditions above, any TyDi suggestion, if accepted, will decrease error count, and furthermore if there exist any error-decreasing completions of the existing token, then TyDi will make a suggestion
- However, the error criteria doesn't strictly hold. When the expected type is `Bool`, TyDi also suggests `Int`s, `Float`s, and `String`s, because these can become valid if followed up by a comparison operator. We don't want to fail to suggest something just because the combination of non-prefix syntax and linear typing order necessitates passing though a incorrect state. So more subtly, we wish to suggest all tokens which will result in less errors after enough subsequent tokens have been entered to definitively establish the parent of the original token, e.g. if the expected type is Bool, and we have `num: Int`, then we might suggest `n|um` since, even though this will still be an error after completion `num|`, it will become correct if we then insert a comparison `num<|`. The difficulty of this case is that there are multiple such operators which could follow, unlike the situation with cons (`::`) and function application

Supporting features:
- Type anything: Any printable ASCII character can be inserted in the editor. In particular, all characters except `"` are valid in strings; similarly for comments except with `#`. Variables can now contain `'` and begin with `_`. This change required a series of subtle adjustments to things like invalid token treatment, grout/whitespace interaction, and token split/merge logic. In particular , there is now a notion on 'default molds' which assign every token not otherwise molded by the language definition as and invalid token which is either convex or concave, depending (mostly) on its constituent characters (closes #852, closes #853, closes #1022)
- Improved Live Coding: Cursor inspector & cell evaluation feedback are no longer disabled when the backpack is nonempty. Instead, we attempt to complete the syntax by dropping everything from the backpack (using lightweight heuristics which don't always succeed) before parsing for semantics. (This will be unnecessary in the new syntax model)
- Smart Select Click: Double-clicking on a delimiter selects its tile e.g. `let x = 1 in` ; triple-clicking one selects its term e.g. `let x = 1 in body`, or if the tile and term coincide, selects parent term, e.g. triple-clicking on `foo` in `foo(bar)` selects the entire application. Similarly, double-clicking on an infix operator selects the operator, and triple-clicking selects its operands as well (closes #722)
- Nullary Ap: You can now write `f()` for `f: () -> ?`. If `f`'s argument type is not consistent with `()`, an error is placed on the whole ap. (closes  #1048)
- Toggle elaboration display: Off by default. Large elaborations present a perf issue, in some cases nullifying the advantage of turning off dynamics.
- Explicit hole '?': A temporary convenience; '?' has the same semantics as a convex hole, but is reified as a token and is persisted across the text representation. This is useful if you have long-lived holes and don't mess with reformatting due to whitespace issues, in particular when copy/pasting or otherwise parsing from text. Relatedly, the Printer now supports specifying a string (e.g. `?`) to use to print holes.

Internal changes:
- CoCtx in patterns: The CoCtx has been piped to patterns to enable unused variable suggestions.
- Core settings: A subrecord of settings for core systems (statics + dynamics); separate mostly for dependency reasons
- Interface.re Consolidation: All access to statics and dynamics in the view layer should go through Interface.re functions. These are now extended to take initial ctxs/envs as appropriate. Statics can now specify whether the buffer should be ignored or included, and whether to try to complete incomplete syntax before getting statics.
- Defunctionalization: Some info (Self.NoJoin) & actions (Move to piece goal) were taking function parameters. This is problematic as these types can end up in places where they get compared, e.g. for memoization, so these have been defunctionalized.
- Buffer selection: The selection has been co-opted as a buffer. The buffer is ephemeral in that it disappears on movement or edit. The buffer can either contain valid hazel syntax (Parsed variant) or an unparsed string (Unparsed variant). In the latter case, it will be parsed if the buffer is accepted.
- Model.meta:  A subrecord containing non-persistent content including UI state and eval results
- ModelSettings renamed to Settings

title: module system
body: Haz3l module system. Current progress: Type Module defined (with detailed information as name-type pair), keyword **module** and operator **.** implemented, Type annotation for modules implemented. Use a pair of curly parentheses around a tuple of patterns. Typically the tuple should contain only TypeAnn patterns, but Var/Tag will also be accepted and treated as hole-typed members. Type Inconsistency warnings includes both the pattern (which define the member) and the definition expression. For member name inconsistency, accessing members shown in module's typeann but not defined will be treated as a emptyhole (supposing users are to implement later), accessing members defined but not shown in module's typeann will be treated as free variables. ![P~M0}3R$CFZ%9@ORYXX$NUH](https://github.com/hazelgrove/hazel/assets/71319371/b6f6e578-f190-48fe-86f3-f941ff630dce) Basic Type member implemented. Type member in module type annotation implemented. For constructors defined by Sum types in module, either access directly by dot access, or access under analytic mode (dot access not necessary). ![8``TU` P}~5IH75ADL9NYMP](https://github.com/hazelgrove/hazel/assets/71319371/cc74ba19-a18b-468e-99f6-3337f6f50e49) Provided warnings for using type members that are not defined, and inconsistency for type members. Created documentations for module-related keywords. Some current rules of typing and casting: Module type consistency: module types are consistent only if they share the same member name list, and the types of every member are consistent. Therefore, the ground type of a module is one where all members have hole types. For module creation, the definition part will always be packaged as the exact same module type of the annotation as we mentioned amove. So nothing to worry about casting. Casts will be added on module aliases. Cast calculation will happen on dot operators.

title: Haz3l user defined operators
body:
Adding the ability for users to define their own operators.

This pull request makes changes to the external language's pattern and expression forms so that custom infix operators can be defined and applied. This then elaborates to an applied `DHExp.t` of the form `Ap(operator_variable, Tuple([arg1, a rg2]))`. The evaluator then continues unmodified to process the function application.

Features:

- `_op_` can be used in a normal let to define a new operator
- `arg1 op arg2` can then be used without the underscores to apply the operator's function

Potential Future Features:

- `_op_` can be used in expressions to allow for typical function application (of the form `_op_(arg1, arg2)`).
- `_op` and `op_` used to define postfix and prefix operators, respectively.

As reported by Adam Chen (I'm unable to find their github username, sorry), a fresh build yields the error message when building [incr_dom](https://github.com/janestreet/incr_dom):
```
[ERROR] The compilation of incr_dom.v0.15.0 failed at "dune build -p incr_dom -j 3".

#=== ERROR while compiling incr_dom.v0.15.0 ===================================#
# context     2.1.4 | linux/x86_64 | ocaml-system.4.14.0 | pinned(git+https://github.com/janestreet/incr_dom.git#7a89c037)
# path        ~/workspace/hazel/_opam/.opam-switch/build/incr_dom.v0.15.0
# command     ~/.local/share/opam/opam-init/hooks/sandbox.sh build dune build -p incr_dom -j 3
# exit-code   1
# env-file    ~/.local/share/opam/log/incr_dom-149222-7af57e.env
# output-file ~/.local/share/opam/log/incr_dom-149222-7af57e.out
### output ###
# (cd _build/default[...]
# File "vdom_file_download/vdom_file_download.ml", line 16, characters 5-35:
# 16 |   if Ppx_inline_test_lib.am_running
#           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
# Error: Unbound value Ppx_inline_test_lib.am_running
# (cd _build/default[...]
# File "vdom_file_download/vdom_file_download.ml", line 16, characters 5-35:
# 16 |   if Ppx_inline_test_lib.am_running
#           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
# Error: Unbound value Ppx_inline_test_lib.am_running
```
The cause is a change introduced by incr_dom commit [7a89c03](https://github.com/janestreet/incr_dom/commit/7a89c037f638059e2f7229cab073e8066075baf2).

Alternative approaches to solve the problem:
1. Pin incr_dom to eariler commit [d5d2da7](https://github.com/janestreet/incr_dom/commit/d5d2da716b35d566ac48b7140ea7e683525e8de8)
2. Only unpin and upgrade incr_dom to 0.15.1
3. Do a dependency audit and bumps versions. I think we can unpin all pinned packages, and upgrade some janestreet ocaml packages to 0.15.1. Not sure how it will turn out.

title: Fantasyland Hazel
body:
This is an 𝑒𝓍𝓅𝑒𝓇𝒾𝓂𝑒𝓃𝓉𝒶𝓁 hazel branch to try variations on the core type system. It is not intended for production, just to try things out for discussion. At the moment, it:

1. Eliminates the synthetic/analytic distinction. There are no modes, only an **expected type**, which may be unknown.
2. Every expression/pattern has three type-like things associated with it. Besides the aforementioned **expected type**, each expression has:
3. a **given/self type** which can be either none (represented as《》, covering errors like unbound variables), Just a type, or inconsistent types (represented as《ty1,ty2,...》)
4. and an **is/actual type** which can be either unknown (if the given type is《》or《tys...》, or if it's《ty》and ty doesn't join with the expected type. otherwise it's the join
5. for debugging/experimentation purposes, there is a precise and complete provenance tracking system for all possible origins and operations on unknown types:`  type type_provenance = | ErrorHole | EmptyExpHole | EmptyPatHole | EmptyList | PatVar | TrueSyn | TypeHole | EmptyJoin | Join(type_provenance, type_provenance) | MatchedArrow(type_provenance) | MatchedProd(type_provenance) | MatchedList(type_provenance);`
6. Inconsistent branches errors are styled as a warning. They are shown in all cases where branches are inconsistent (after fixing), except they are suppressed when the expected type is unknown-typehole.

title: Algebraic Datatypes II
body: Replaces #960. Closes #608, Closes #626, Closes #860, Closes #909, Closes #1002, Closes #1036, Closes #1041, Closes #1044, Closes #1045, Closes #1065, Closes #1072, Closes #1073, Closes #1074, Closes #1075. **Abstract** This extends Hazel's type system with type aliases, anonymous labelled sum types, and recursive types, although the latter are not surfaced in the syntax, and are created implicitly in named sum type definitions. Additionally, this PR makes a number of other significant functional and internal changes as detailed below, as well as the bug fixes indicated above. **Sum types** 1. Sum type constructors are either nullary (have no argument; their type is the sum type), or unary (having arrow type from their parameter type to the sum type). 2. Unary constructors are valid on their own as expressions; you can pass them as arguments and map over them. However we have restricted pattern-matching on bare unary constructors to avoid confusion. 3. If a sum type is defined in an alias, its constructors are added to the context (a new type of context entry, albeit one that behaves the same as regular variable entries). This allows its constructors to be used, even in synthetic position, anywhere in the scope of the relevant type alias. 4. OTOH, if an anonymous sum type is created as a type annotation, its constructors are NOT added to the context, and are only valid in positions which are analytic against that type. 5. Two sum types are considered equal if they have the same constructors with the same types; order doesn't matter. 6. Two sum types are considered consistent if they have the same constructors with consistent types. 7. Constructor name must be unique within a type, but can shadow the constructors of previous types. 8. There is currently no way refer to a shadowed constructor in synthetic position; you must make the position analytic against the appropriate type through a type annotation **Type aliases** 1. A type alias must have a capitalized name. 2. Type aliases can shadow other aliases, but do not shadow base types 3. Type aliases do not escape their scope; the returned type of a type alias expression has the type alias substituted away. **Deprecations** - Previous built-in ADTs removed (Color, ALFExpr, ALFTyp, Option_ALFTyp) **Other Functional Changes** - New editor mode: Examples. This is a collection of named editors, each consisting of examples intended either for exposition or testing. - New operators: New unary operator `!` for boolean negation. New binary operators: `@` for list concatenation, `++` for string concatenation, `!=` for integer inequality, `!=.` for float inequality, and `\/` for boolean disjunction. The latter is temporary syntax since in current syntax engine, leading delimiters must have unique prefixes, and `||` overlaps with `|` used in case rules. - Improved Builtins: There are now ~40 builtin functions for int, floats, and strings, all pass-throughs to their OCaml equivalents, extending those added in #1058 and #1062. The process of adding builtins has been refined to require fewer changes. Builtin functions are now added directly to the initial environment instead of spliced into the elaboration, so they no longer clutter the elaboration display (what you see when dynamics are turned off). - Elaboration/Evaluation exception reporting: Internal exceptions (implementation errors) during elaboration and evaluation are now caught and will now be reported in the results area under the cell. Previously these either crashed the editor or were inconsistently reported to the console. Pic-related is about-to-be-fixed issue #1044. - Improved Cursor Inspector messages: Messages now take into account the specific syntactic form as well as the typing information to provide more user feedback. Adding more specific feedback should now be more straightforward for implementors. Error and ok status messages are more consistent, and some technical details regarding unknown type provenance have been relegated to tooltips. - Improved Context Inspector: Visual overhaul to support heterogenous context entries, which now include type aliases; long types are now truncated by default, but are visible on-hover. - Hole-based navigation: You can use TAB to move to the next hole, and SHIFT-TAB to move to the previous. If the top backpack item it currently droppable, the drop action will preempt the move action. - Token merging change: Previously, if you deleted an infix operator/grout, all whitespace between the enclosing operands would be removed. This feels overly aggressive, and confusing in some situations, so I've removed this behavior. The one downside is that, in situations like `1 +|2`, pressing backspace will result in `1 |><2` and again will result in `1|><2`, so to remove the infix grout, we'd need to move right and backspace. This was the primary reason for instituting the aggressive merge behavior, but I now believe that, seeing as there are downsides to both options, we should default to the more predictable one. - New menu action: Export persistent data: This saves a file called Init.ml which serializes settings and the states of the example and scratch pad editors. This file can be used to replace the identically-named file in the Haz3lweb directory in order to specify initial app state. Note that due to technical issues Exercises mode editors and Langdocs settings are not currently serialized. **Internal Changes** - Statics Refactoring: Statics is now divided into Statics.Info, which defines the basic info data structured, and Statics.Map, which concerns the buildup of the Id map. Although this is not a perfectly realized division, the intention is that Statics.Info focusses on concentrates the logic for calculating statics attributes, and Statics.Map focusses on the tree traversal dataflow to collate the information necessary for calculation. Furthermore, Self and Mode have been split off into separate modules; all non-trivial logic related to calculating the self type of a term, or the mode of its children, should be located in those modules. See the tops of all of these modules for more documentation. This refactor includes converting the buildup of the map to a traversal from its previous bottom-up union-based approach, resulting in a 30x-speedup to statics generation. - Code views can now specify a custom root sort (besides just Exp); useful for e.g. Langdocs - School Mode is internally renamed to Exercises Mode - New sort, TPat, to support type alias definitions - The 'free' entry in CursorInfo has been renamed 'co_ctx'; see CoCtx.re for documentation - DHExp now uses same binary operator types as UExp, reducing redundancy - All implementations in Typ and Ctx modules relocated to TypBase for dependency reasons

title: Fix linebreak in comments bug
body:
Currently having linebreaks in comments is not supported for multiple reasons; needs special support in metrics and elsewhere. However it is not explicitly disallowed, resulting in broken behavior. This specifically disallows linebreak insertion in comments until linebreak support is implemented more generally.

Incidentally, this also makes the structural change of inverting the dependency between Secondary and Form. Secondary should be considered a semantic module, not syntactic. As far as possible, all lexer/token concerns should be handled in Form to facilitate future abstraction of the syntax model.

title: Fix term/tile decoration lengths on chrome
body: This fixes a longstanding bug with long term/tile decorations and error holes being too short or long on chrome. Introduces a new svg wrapper, code_svg_sized, which actually sets the exact viewbox size needed for its content. Previously the viewbox for all elements was a fixed size. When the elements were much bigger than the viewbox, this resulted in them becoming increasingly mis-sized in chrome. I'm not sure whether this constitutes a bug per se, or just a case of firefox being more robustly designed in the face of viewbox sizes being set smaller than the content. This had been partially addressed in the past by setting the fixed viewbox size to be very large, but this causes runoff issues, including making it awkward to inspect decoration elements, as the viewbox is what determines the bounding box of the element shown in devtools.

title: Add support for replays from student logs, along with a step-through/scrubbing control panel
body:
**Summary**

It would be nice to be able to step through a student log by hand for data analysis purposes, both in real-time and incrementally. This PR provides support for this functionality.

**Implementation**

The new module `Replay` is essentially a log with a position pointer. It supports three main operations: forward, backward, and step. Step is distinguished from forward because it also returns a delay, which is used for real-time playback from a student log.

The new module `ReplayControls` allows a `Replay` to be visualized on the front-end, and provides buttons for interactive replay.

A couple minor issues:

- Backward does not work properly in the presence of user actions. As a concrete example, if the log contains actions 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and you play through 1, 2, 3, then move the cursor (action A), then press backward, we will undo the cursor movement and also scroll one position backwards through the log (so now the replay incorrectly believes we have only finished actions 1 and 2). The cleanest approach to fix this might just be preventing user actions during a replay.
- I am not super happy with the UI/UX of the control panel, but I am also not an expert in CSS.

**Video**


https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/87710069/217106548-c6a2199f-1497-40ed-9758-466d7fdf64e8.mov

title: Fix cyclical dependency issues
body:
**Summary**

This PR makes no changes to functionality; it's pure refactors. Practically, this PR helps break dependency cycle issues, and stylistically, I believe that one type per module is also generally preferred.

**Implementation**

- `Log.Entry` is now `LogEntry` (breaks cycle `Model -> Replay -> Log(.Entry) -> Model(.timestamp)`)
- `Model.settings` is now `ModelSettings` (breaks cycle `Model -> Replay -> LogEntry -> UpdateAction -> DebugAction -> LocalStorage -> Model`)

Extra context: https://hazelgrove.slack.com/archives/C038TL4C2KG/p1675628741667559

**Testing**

Code still compiles, and my `Replay` module no longer causes dependency cycles 🎉

title: Add button to reconstruct state from a session export via log replay
body:
**Summary**

Meta issue: https://github.com/hazelgrove/hazel/issues/969

It's currently possible to save a snapshot export of a user session as a file, then import it later. However, this import functionality simply loads the exact snapshot rather than building the state procedurally using the action log. For data analysis purposes, it would be nice to be able to build the state incrementally, which this PR introduces.

**Implementation**

First, load the export file. Next, parse the log and turn the list of timestamps into a list of time diffs. Then, kick off the first action in the log. Each action is responsible for executing, delaying, then kicking off the subsequent action.

**Caveats**

- Button has same icon as import button.
- Since the log does not include information about whether the original action succeeded, on replay, we don't know if the action failed because of a state mismatch or because the original action failed.
- `Update.apply` is now recursive.
- `Update.t` and `Log.t` are vaguely mutually recursive now, since logs contain actions, but certain actions (like `StartReplay`) reference logs. I get around this in a slightly hacky way, but I don't think it's a big deal.

**Testing**

Manually tested with some replays I generated. 

Eventually, we might want to set up an automated check to see if the log-replay state matches the imported final state at some point, but unless there's an easily accessible "session state ~matches" function that already exists, I'm not sure it's worth it right now.

**Example**

Other than triggering the replay, I do not take any action (eg: typing or clicking) during this clip.

https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/87710069/215351495-8944491e-0436-4488-b37d-6ab33831c80c.mov

title: Explicit Polymorphism with typfun and typap
body:
What’s working:
1. Type checking for typfun and typap
2. Recursive typfuns
What’s not working:
1. Type alias in typfun
2. ADT (Built-in ADTs and sum...end)

Working examples:
1. Polymorphic map
```
let map : forall X -> forall Y -> (X -> Y) -> [X] -> [Y]
 = typfun X -> typfun Y -> fun f -> fun xs ->
  case xs
    | nil => nil
    | x::xs => f(x)::map@<X>@<Y>(f)(xs)
  end
in
let even = fun x -> x / 2 * 2 == x in
let id = fun x -> x in
map@<Int>@<Bool>(even)([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
```

2. Polymorphic fold left
```
let fold_left : forall X -> forall Y -> (Y -> X -> Y) -> Y -> [X] -> Y =
  typfun X -> typfun Y -> fun f -> fun acc -> fun xs ->
    case xs
      | nil => acc
      | x::xs => fold_left@<X>@<Y>(f)(f(acc)(x))(xs)
    end
in
let add_bools = fold_left@<Bool>@<Int>(fun acc -> fun x -> acc + if x then 1 else 0)(0) in
add_bools([true, false, true])
```

3. Polymorphic fold right
```
let fold_right : forall X -> forall Y -> (X -> Y -> Y) -> [X] -> Y -> Y
= typfun X -> typfun Y -> fun f -> fun xs -> fun acc ->
  case xs
    | nil => acc
    | x::xs => f(x)(fold_right@<X>@<Y>(f)(xs)(acc))
  end
in
let add_bools = fun xs:[Bool] ->
  fold_right@<Bool>@<Int>(fun x -> fun acc -> acc + if x then 1 else 0)(xs)(0)
in
add_bools([true, false, true])
```

title: Partial application of non-curried functions for Haz3l
body:
Continuation of #514 (partial application for Hazel 2)

This feature introduces partial application of functions that accept tuple arguments. This is implemented with a UExp `_`, which does not elaborate a DHExp or synthesize a type. Deferral expressions may only be elaborated in the context of a function application. If the number of arguments on a partial application does not match the signature of the function, then a runtime exception is raised. Upon elaboration, a new function is created which accepts any non-deferred arguments. For example:

```
let div = fun (a, b) : (Int, Int) -> a / b in
let halve = div(_, 2) in
halve(4)
```

The expression yields 2. In the elaboration semantics, `div` has type `(Int, Int) -> Int` and `halve` has type `Int -> Int`.

Implementation:

* Added two new UExps: Deferral and DeferredAp.
* `_` introduces a Deferral expression. A Deferral on its own does not type-check nor elaborate.
* Function applications on tuple arguments including Deferrals are interpreted as DeferredAp instead of Ap.
* DeferredAp is elaborated into a Lambda containing an Ap. For example, the DHExp for `halve` (from above) is `fun ~defer0 -> div(~defer0, 2)`.
* The DHExps for DeferredAps take the unapplied arguments as a tuple, unless there is only one unapplied argument, in which case they take a single argument of that type.

Static error:
- `Free(Deferral)` is assigned to a deferral expression when:
* The deferral expression is neither e_arg itself nor a projection of an e_arg tuple.
* The deferral expression is enclosed in brackets that are not part of the syntax of an application.
- `TypeInconsistent` is assigned to e_arg when:
* `? -> _`/not-a-function case: no errors
* For the case when the input type of e_fun is neither a product type nor the type hole: e_arg is not a single deferral expression
* `() -> _` case: e_arg is not a single deferral expression
* For the case when the input type of e_fun is non-trivial product: when e_arg is a single deferral expression, an incorrect number of arguments is supplied, resulting in `InHole(TypeInconsistent(Unknown(Internal), ty_ana))` (not the most precise error, maybe adding a new error variant is better?); otherwise, the error checking has the same behavior as the error checking of a full application, in which deferrals synthesizes the type hole.

Dynamic error:
Unbounded deferrals are elaborated into `InvalidText`.

title: Better expansion/barfing (expansion bug fix)
body:
This overhauls the entire expansion and backpack barfing system, fixing the expansion bug and attempting to make both the behavior and implementation clearer and more consistent.

As a reminder the expansion bug (as i've been calling it, but barfing bug is more accurate) affects situations like this:
"let a = b|in", where pressing space fails to drop "in" from the backpack.

First, recall some vocabulary:

- expansion: the process of a monotile expanding into a multitile. a given form can be configured to expand from either its first delimiter, its second delimiter, or both. furthermore, the expansion for each of those delmiters can be configured to be either instant or delayed 
- instant expansion: when expansion occurs immediately after a delimiter is created, e.g. for "(" or ")"
- delayed expansion: when expansion occurs only after a token boundary event, e.g. when " " (or "," or whatever) is pressed on "let|"
- barfing: when the token adjacent to the caret matches the token at the top of the backpack and is replaced by the dropped backpack token
- insertion: the action of inserting a new character. this can result in either a modification insertion, where an existing token is modified (either at the ends or internally) or a creation insertion, aka a token boundary event. modification insertions can result in instant expansions, but only token boundary events result in delayed expansions.
- token boundary event: when insertion would not result in a valid token, so a new token must be created. this occurs in two different cases: (a) the caret is at an outer position and the new character cannot be appended to either neighbour, or (b) the caret is at an inner position, resulting in the token being split.

Previously, token boundary events only triggered delayed expansion on the token to the left. Now, they can trigger up to three expansions/barfings: one for the left neighbor of the caret, one for the newly inserted thing, and one for the right neighbor. for example, pressing "(" on "if|if" will trigger three expansions. It's debatable whether the expansion of the last "if" is desired behavior, but I think there's a consistency case to be made, since we definitely do want to trigger a barf if we press " " on let a = b|in", and I feel the behavior is easier to predict if expansion and barfing happen in exactly the same circumstances I think... please debate if you disagree.

Another similar (but technically independent) consistency change  is that now barfings use the same delayed/instant behavior as expansions. Since parentheses are still instant, typing ")" on "(|" results in an instant drop. however, on "if 1 the", typing "n" no longer results in a drop; you need to press the space first. I think that this feels better... the instant drop feels to me a little jarring. It also seems to be necessary to permit entry of variables which have a keyword as a prefix.

One current sub-optimal but farily niche behavior: consider "(if|if" with ")" in the backpack. if ")" is pressed, i would guess that the first "if" would be expanded, and then the ")" would be barfed, and then the second "if" would be expanded. however, because the expansion of the first if, the ")" is no longer top of the backpack, so the ")" is treated as fresh and a "(" is added to the backpack. This is addressable in principle but I'm not sure whether it's worth it at this point.

Implementation note, mostly for @dmoon1221: backpack selection foci direction is no longer used at all, I felt they were complicating things. construct now takes two directional parameters, one reflecting the direction you want to insert it wrt to the caret, and the other reflecting what order you want to add shard to the backpack in. This means that after you insert a fresh ")" you end up on the 'wrong' side, but i think this is probably principle-of-least-surprisey.

title: Empty list literals and tuples

This adds support for 'dual' syntactic forms which have both mono- and duo-token versions, such as (empty) list literals and (empty) tuples. New such forms can be added by adding cases to Form.duosplits and Form.duomerges functions, as well as adding the forms themselves to Form.forms and Form.atomic_forms as usual. Updating Form in this way should be sufficient to support proper insertion and deletion behavior, including splitting and merging where appropriate.

Replaces:
- nil with [] in expressions, patterns, and docs.
- triv with () in expressions, patterns, and docs.
- Unit with () in types and docs

Behavior:
- Typing "[]" will result in a (monotile) empty list
- More generally, typing "]" when on "[|" will result in an empty list
- Typing "[ ]" will result in a singleton list with hole
- Typing space (or anything else) on "[|]" will split the (mono) empty list into a (duo) list literal
- Typing backspace on "[|]" will convert the (mono) empty list to a (duo) list literal and put the "[" in the BP
- Typing backspace on "[]|" will convert the (mono) empty list to a (duo) list literal and put the "]" in the BP

title: Haz3l exponentiation
body:
This pull request implements the `**` (integer exponentiation) and `**.` (floating-point exponentiation) operators in Hazel 3.

- `**` uses the efficient exponentiation by squaring algorithm (O(log n) time complexity).  Its precedence is one level tighter than multiplication/division and one level looser than negation.  It has right associativity.
- `**.` reduces to Reason's `**`.  Its precedence and associativity is the same as the integer version of this operator.

Possible source of errors:  `**` overflows at 2 ** 31.

title: Add undefined keyword
body:
Adds an undefined keyword to the language. The goal is to provide users the ability to express intent not to fill an empty hole. This may be useful when there is no coherent value to return in certain branches. For example, consider the the following operation on lists:
```
let head = fun xs -> case xs
    | hd::tl => hd
    | nil => undefined
end in
(head([2, 3, 4]), head(nil))
```
This evaluates to `(2, undefined)` because the left has a coherent value, but the head of an empty list is undefined.

The one difference between an empty hole and `undefined` is that `undefined` should not be a valid pattern in a case expression. I'm still working on making that behavior work properly.

This could be extended by allowing users to specify an error message along with the undefined value to be more clear as to what error led to the undefined behavior. This would require a more major overhaul which adds the possibility for a message/value associated with any empty hole (which could be a desirable feature in itself)

title: Add pipeline operator
body:
This pull request is only three lines. It adds a pipeline operator. Some things to note:

* Since the current parsing engine doesn't support invalid partial states for operators, I've added an auxillary operator '|' which creates a binary op form (with no evaluation semantics). Perhaps this can be fixed if the parsing engine is reworked, or if bitwise-or is added. If any operators beginning with '|' are added with a different precedence, then this could definitely cause some weirdness (it just so happens that '||' and '|>' share the same precedence level).
* As a side effect, the auxillary '|' operator also makes the binary op for OR ('||') possible to synthesize in the editor.
* The mold for 'Rule' has some ambiguous states with the pipeline operator '|>'. Of particular concern is that if you add a whitespace after an expression like '1 | ', then it instantly becomes a Rule as per the deferred expansion rule (without a chance to change it back into a pipeline operator).
* The evaluation for the pipeline operator is the same as function application, since it is just syntax sugar.

title: Haz3l small step
body:
Implement/Port small step evaluator to Haz3l.

## Progress update

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/29998228/198864374-609f34e6-dc6e-461b-9dce-fd30ea8f7a22.png)

## Implementation

Instead of using indices to locate the mark, we store the whole context into annotation, and can be composed directly when the user clicks.

We use substitution to achieve evaluation of let-expression and plan to use it on function applications, since environment would let the user to click on each site of a bound variable for it to get substituted.

## Known Bugs

- [x] Z combinator doesn't work. Works in `dev`, might due to cast issue.
- [x] #949 

## Roadmap

- [x] Clickable subexpression
- [x] Basic arithmetics and let expressions.
- [x] Use a standalone `DHDoc_Step` module to annotate steps.
- [x] "Previous Step" button.
- [x] History (record in legacy code)
- [x] Add description for each step. (We have tooltips for now)
- [x] Populate `EvalCtx` so that more expression can be decomposed.
  - [x] Projection
  - [x] List Literal (`[1, 2, ...]`)
  - [x] BinStringOp
- [x] Automatic evaluation of Builtin variables and functions.

## Future work

- "Next Step" button. Sometimes the history is long and we accidentally step back too far. (Move to future work since this can be more "correctly" handled by incremental step evaluation)
- Bring back evaluator options and add more to it. Blocked by #985
- Show environment alongside the expression.

## Similar work

- [A stepper for untyped lambda calculus](https://lambdacalc.io/)
  - Shows transformation application on the right hand side.
- [Another stepper for untyped lambda calculus](https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/~rmk35/lambda_calculus/lambda_calculus.html#)

title: Haz3l mutual recursion
body:
Goal: 
```
let (even : Int -> Bool, odd : Int -> Bool).= (
  fun n -> 
    if n == 0 then true else odd(n - 1), 
  fun n -> 
    if n == 0 then false else even(n - 1)) in

title: Built-in ADTs
body:
This adds hardcoded algebraic data types. Types can be added in BuiltinADTs.re. Type names AND constructor names must be globally unique. This is enforced by startup assertions. Types may be (mutually) recursive.

This introduces basic type variables, intended to be supplanted by type aliases. These are of the form Var(string). These are globally scoped, and type equality is nominative, not structural, although this doesn't currently matter because of the enforced uniqueness constraints.

Constructors (Tags) are essentially a new kind of atomic literal. Constructors may be nullary, in which case their type is simply Var("name"), or unary, in which case their type is Arrow(something, Var("name")), where 'something' may be a tuple, to achieve n-ary constructors.

Given the above type assignment, constructors/tags are treated basically the same was as function literals by the static semantics. Both function and constructor application pass through the same Ap form. Constructors are first-class and may be used any way functions can. The dynamic semantics are essentially the same as for tuples.

This implementation is fully functional AFAICT. I've written a basic LC interpreter, which doesn't quite work due to casting issues, but these should (probably, hopefully) be resolved separately in the forthcoming casting branch

title: Haz3l string literals
body:
This adds string literals with basic statics + dynamics.

This is the intended syntax spec which string literals should conform to:

1. Pressing `"` inserts an empty  string literal `""`, with the caret being positioned between the quotes
2. Trying to delete either bounding " results in the deletion of the whole literal
3. Trying to insert a " anywhere inside or adjacent to a string literal results in no insertion and the caret being moved to the end of the literal
4. String literals can contain any character which is otherwise valid in the syntax, except for " due to the above logic
5. linebreaks are currently not supported

title: Introduce n-ary skels and use for tuples, lists, and case expressions
body:
`Skel.t` has changed from
```
type index = int;
type t =
  | Op(index)
  | Pre(index, t)
  | Post(t, index)
  | Bin(t, index, t)
```
to
```
type t =
  | Op(root)
  | Pre(root, t)
  | Post(t, root)
  | Bin(t, root, t)
and root = Aba.t(index, t)
```
The formerly bijective correspondence between tiles and terms is now many-to-one. The term forms with potentially more than one corresponding tile are tuples, list literals, and case expressions; their corresponding tiles are, respectively, the tuple commas, the list brackets coupled with the inner element-separating commas, and the `case`-`end` brackets coupled with the inner expression-separating rule patterns of the form `| <pat> =>`. If we decide n-tuples require parentheses (which I agree with @disconcision is the right way to go), then an n-tuple's tiles would also include the surrounding parentheses.

In the process of rewriting `MakeTerm.re` to take advantage of the generic n-ary structure (previously hardcoded into form-specific functions), I also fleshed out the existing logic so that term formation recurses beyond unrecognized forms into their children and the result is a multi-hole of the children terms. This involved extending the `MultiHole` constructors for each sort to take terms of any sort, meaning the term types need to be mutually recursive, and I did this via mutually recursive modules (sequestered in `TermBase.re`) in order to preserve the current constructor name overlap -- not opposed to avoiding this by just having unique constructor names. More terms, more static feedback.

I also laid some groundwork in `MakeTerm.re` for generating completions of segments with incomplete tiles so that our existing statics logic can be used for feedback in children terms of incomplete tiles. The process of completion may insert holes with negative ids, which will not appear in the user's code but may appear in the evaluated result. I think this is fine; we can visually distinguish them and explain that they're auto-inserted. This is still a work-in-progress; in the next PR, this completion process coupled with better sort-and-heuristic-guided regrouting should make it so that you can always get static feedback when writing things left to right.

title: Basic concave grout => n-ary holes
body:
This parses sequences of concave grout to a new kind of term, n-ary holes.

The basic idea here is that a run of subterms saperated by concave grout is treated as if it was a non-empty hole which contains all of those subterms. This is intended to be accomplished in a way such that an empty hole is semantically isomorphic to a 0-ary hole, and a hazel2 non-empty hole is semantically isomorphic to a 1-ary hole.

N-ary hole terms are always regarded as errors. They contain lists of terms of whatever the parent sort is. Otherwise, their semantics is basically: regard the contained subterms as if they were in the place of the n-ary hole; so e.g. expression n-ary holes pass the context to the subterm, etc.

note: this is the first case where the term and tile correspondence is non 1-1. as such, n-ary hole terms also hold a list of ids. this is mostly an implementation detail, to help collate them to make sure that when the caret is on a concave grout it is gets appropriate CI.

Not totally satisfied with the approach here so I'm putting it up for comment. I'm somewhat concerned with how to display these... we frequently get these intermediary states with concave grout... not sure this would feel great if it results in a hole being drawn around the entire segment? Also not totally sure on the treatment of sorts... right now I am just saying that we basically ignore the mold sort on constituents and use the sort expected by the syntactic context. to do otherwise would require some more explicit notion of sort holes, as we'd have to have data structure support for a kind of term that can contain a variably-sorted list....this sounds probably more complicated than its worth.

title: Better remolding
body:
Relaxes assumption made for remolding optimization in https://github.com/hazelgrove/tylr/pull/9 that tiles should have same nib sorts as output sort, in exchange for other assumptions that match our grammars so far:
- right nib shapes are never ambiguous for a given label
- filtering molds by shape before sort does not create unnecessary sort inconsistencies (imprecise but enough for handling unary/binary minus and paren/ap)

This change may also have uncovered a bug where remolding should in general take place beyond the focal segment, eg any segment directly contained by or directly containing put down shards, but this was an existing bug introduced by https://github.com/hazelgrove/tylr/pull/9 so not fixing here. Concretely this is observed when picking up an `=` in a let and putting back down with caret ending up in the let definition, which leaves the pattern sort-inconsistent. I think previous optimization happened to get away with this because it happened to preserve the original pattern mold, but the proper fix is to reassign molds beyond focal segment.

title: Evaluation gas
body:
This PR adds gas to the evaluator to prevent freezes caused by bottomless recursion. A new `EvaluatorState.t` record is passed through evaluation:

- On each call to `evaluate`, the `step` count is incremented
- On each call to `evaluate`, the `gas` amount is decremented
  - If `gas == 0`, then `evaluate` stops with an indeterminate result indicating out of gas

**To-do**:

- [ ] Configurable initial gas

title: Enhance tuple completion
body:
# Expected Behaivors

https://github.com/hazelgrove/hazel/issues/583#issuecomment-1081008183

> I think we should place the cursor at the next position after the comma when tuple completion is triggered by a comma, regardless of where any holes may be inserted. Otherwise you'll have situations like 5| 6 when analyzed against a 3-tuple where the first hole skips past the 6.

> If tuple completion is triggered by open parentheses, then I think it makes sense to place the cursor at the first hole in the tuple, which will always either be in the first position if there was already a hole there or else in the second position.

## Cases Considered in This PR

### 1. Parenthesize a nonempty hole (✅ Fixed)

**Matching type:**
Before `let x : (Int, Int) = |1 in _`
After '(' `let x : (Int, Int) = (|1) in _`

Fixed to `let x : (Int, Int) = (1, |_) in _`

**Mismatched type:**
Before `let x : (Int, Int) = |true in _`
After '(' `let x : (Int, Int) = (|true) in _`

Fixed to `let x : (Int, Int) = (|true, _) in _`

### 2. Tuple completion on type annotation (Not fixed/waiting for updates to type annotation)

Before `let x| = (1, 2, 3) in _`
After ':' `let x : (Int), (Int), (Int) = (1, 2, 3) in _`

Before `let x : |_ = (1, 2, 3) in _`
After '(' `let x : (|_) = (1, 2, 3) in _`

### 3 . Tuple completion on mismatched tuple type annotation (Not fixed/waiting for updates to type annotation)

Before `let x : (Int|) = (1, 2, 3) in _`
After '(' `let x : (Int, |_) = (1, 2, 3) in _`

### 4. Parenthesizing mismatched tuple (✅ Fixed)

Before `let x : (Int, Int, Int) = |3, 4 in _`

After '(' `let x : (Int, Int, Int) = (3), 4 in _`

Fixed to `let x : (Int, Int, Int) = (3, 4, |_) in _`

### 5. Parenthesizing mismatched wrong typed tuple (✅ Fixed)

Before `let x : (Int, Bool, Int) = |true, 3 in _`

After `Async_kernel: Unhandled exception (Failure "extend_let_body_ctx: impossible ana")`

Fixed to `let x : (Int, Bool, Int) = (|true, 3, _) in _`

### 6. Inserting comma moves cursor NOT to the next hole (✅ Fixed)

Before `(1, 2|)`

After ',' `(1, 2,| _)`

Fixed to `(1, 2, |_)`

title: Evaluation using the environment model rather than substitution
body:
Evaluation with environments rather than environments. Evaluation with environments is useful because:
- Usually (?) better performance (i.e., don't substitute in unevaluated branches)
- Can memoize hole instances with the same environment/instantiation (to handle https://github.com/hazelgrove/hazel/issues/536)

Rough summary of changes:
- New data structure: `EvalEnv.t` (perhaps should be renamed? E.g., to `MemoEnvironment`?) which represents an environment tagged with an ID (`EvalEnvId.t`). Note that unique ID's are generated for an environment each time a new one is created by using `EvalEnvIdGen.t` (very similar to `MetaVarGen.t`). Note also that `EvalEnv.t` maps `Var.t` to `EvaluatorResult.t` rather than to `DHExp.t`, but the choice is somewhat arbitrary
- Change interface of evaluation functions (`Evaluator.evaluate`, `Builtin.evaluate`). `evaluate: DHExp.t => EvaluatorResult.t` becomes `evaluate: (EvalEnvIdGen.t, EvalEnv.t, DHExp.t): (EvalEnvIdGen.t, EvaluatorResult.t)`
- "Generalized closures" to represent any expression that can have a delayed evaluation (e.g., used to encapsulate let/case expr with failed match, lambda closure, hole closure), also neatens up some of the hole handling
- Implement a "postprocessing step" (`EvalPostprocess.postprocess`) that performs two actions:
    - Perform substitution inside closures (lambda bodies, bodies of let/case exprs with failed matches) so that the result matches that of substitution (i.e., context inspector should show same result as before)
    - Number hole instances. Notably, in order to solve https://github.com/hazelgrove/hazel/issues/536, holes that share the same environment are given the same number, i.e., each instantiation of a hole is a single "hole closure", potentially with multiple parents/paths, rather than being split into multiple "hole instances" each time it is encountered in the result. (This causes `HoleInstance.t`, `HoleInstancePath.t`, and `HoleClosureInfo.t` to become `HoleClosure.t`, `HoleClosureParents.t`, and `HoleClosureInfo.t`. Also requires slight changes to the context inspector to display all parents to a hole closure, rather than the (singular) path to the current hole instance.). The old hole instance numbering step, `Program.renumber`, is somewhat simplified and grouped into this postprocessing step.
- For performance reasons, change environments to use a BST implementation rather than a linked list. (`VarBstMap.t` -- currently replaces uses of `VarMap.t` only in `EvalEnv.t` but doesn't affect other usages of `VarMap.t`)
- Implement `DHExp.fast_equals` for fast equality checking memoized by environments, which doesn't recurse through environments, and `Result.fast_equals`, which performs `DHExp.fast_equals` on the result expression and on each expression in each environment
- No more need of `Evaluator.subst*` functions during evaluation. (Substitution is currently being used in one place only: during elaboration when introducing the `FixF` form for let expressions with an type-ascribed lambda binding)
- Evaluation of recursive functions still uses `FixF`, although it is possible to use recursive environments to achieve this (achieved in the [rec-closures](https://github.com/hazelgrove/hazel/tree/rec-closures) branch as a proof-of-concept).

This branch is a work in progress, probably needs more testing and maybe some changing of module interfaces.

Planning to branch off this branch to work on fill-and-resume. The implementation shouldn't be too different from evaluation with substitution, but we can benefit from the optimization in https://github.com/hazelgrove/hazel/issues/536.

I'm also working on a report to try to formalize and clarify some of the above changes, as well as future work with fill-and-resume, but it's not very complete yet.

Worked with Yuchen Jiang (@LighghtEeloo) on this.

Error boundaries are drawn around non-exhaustive case expressions and redundant rules.

title: Tests 1
body:
NOTE: when this gets merged, we might want to advise people to do a codebase-wide rename of u_gen to id_gen before they pull this in... might make it less painful.

Supersedes #402 and see also previous discussion on #287

Features:

1. Test Panel on sidebar: collects all instances of all tests, displayed and labelled in lexicographic order. indicates pass or fail status for each test (color, outline) and the joint status over test instances (check). the joint status check is also displayed on syntax. clicking on a row in the test panel moves the cursor to that test on the code. clicking in a hole in an incomplete test puts the caret in that hole on the code.

2. test display results are, if determinate, the boolean result of the predicate, EXCEPT in the case of an equality (==,==.), in which case, both sides are evaluated and the resulting equality with values on both sides is returned instead.

3. Test inspector on cursor: replaces cursor inspector when on a test. displays the result of the test (if any) at cursor.

4. Adds fuel, which is burned


Implementation:

0. Replaces u_gen with id_gen, for threading through multiple id generators. This is part of the big reason the diff is so huge.

1. New operand/data type Keyword, of which Test is the only current inhabitant. Some old 'Keyword' modules renamed to ExpandingKeyword. 

2. Evaluator now has a state map running through it. Useful for a lot of things. The evaluator could be formally monaded.

3. Loosely related cleanup of top-level UI in Page.re and elsewhere

Known issues:

1. Fuel isn't totally working. Trivial nonterminating programs fail successfully, but larger nonterminating programs seem to die on the way back down, ie after having run out of fuel

Addressed issues:

1. All of (Binary ops, unary aps, binary aps) now show the evaluated arguments in the test inspector/bench.
2. Switched to a lighter red/green to lessen xmas effect.
3. Added completion percentage.

Not in scope (separate projects):

1. Concurrent evaluation
2. Polymorphic equality (needs new error code - complicated refactor)
3. Value diff holes (needs polyeq plus DHDeco architecture to gets paths to draw)
4. Test labels/descriptions (needs strings, though I have a different idea to use comments as compositional labels)

title: Make string CommentLine reflect keyboard input
body:
Currently, CommentLine only allows `SChar` construction.

Goal of this PR is to make string CommentLine reflect exactly keyboard 
input, to achieve the following (as example):
- ``# Abl3 to +ype any symb0! 100.89*% ( [ ) ] \ = -_ '~"hello" ; let := >< ?? // $ ^& @hazel \` ``

Modify `JSUtil.is_single_key` to take in a variable `regex`, and then
within `CommentLine` match a wider `char_regex` (`^[^#]$` everything
except `#`) than `alpha_regex` (`^[a-zA-Z']$` all alphabets and `'`) on
regular lines.

![Screen Shot 2021-08-09 at 10 57 41 AM](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/47135468/128729078-e6ffe4cf-5bda-4ee1-9475-013455ca87d9.png)

Currently still doesn't support alt/opt-modified symbols.

title: Comment out code
body:
This feature aims to make it possible to comment out code lines. 

For example, the following are some examples of desired results:

```ruby
|let x : Float = 3. in
x +. 5.
#    =( # )=>
#| let x : Float = 3. in
x +. 5. 
```

> `=( <key> )=>` means resulting from pressing key `<key>`

Current:
- Deleting CommentLine delimiter # deletes entire line and replaces it with EmptyLine
- Inserting # at start of existing line of code constructs new CodeCommentLine with empty comment text 
  - unintended 'formatting' of code that was originally on the line

Proposed:
- [ ] Deleting CommentLine delimiter # parses line as UHExp.line (LetLine or ExpLine)
  - need text-to-HExp parser
- [ ] Inserting # at start of existing line of code constructs new CommentLine with existing line of code as the comment text 
  - handle holes in code originally on the line
  - handle parsing line above and line below as 'continuous', i.e. ignoring new CommentLine

Reference issue: https://github.com/hazelgrove/hazel/issues/147

title: Partial Application of Non-Curried Functions
body:
*Note: This is a just a preliminary plan for how this feature will be implemented. Things may change if anyone comes up with better ideas. See the discussion on this pull request (once there is some).*

If a function takes multiple arguments by currying, then it can be partially applied, but the arguments must be given in order. If a function takes multiple arguments by taking in a tuple, then it cannot be partially applied natively. The programmer *could* construct a new function literal that takes in the unapplied arguments, then inserts them where they belong in the application of the original function, but this rather cumbersome. It could be replaced with some sugar to simplify it.

The purpose of this pull request is to allow for non-curried functions to be partially applied. This will be (subjectively) more elegant than partial application of curried functions, since it will allow for arguments to be partially applied in any order.

It will work by introducing a deferral expression: `~`, which is an external expression. If a function that takes an n-tuple as input is applied to an n-tuple, some of the expressions in the tuple can be replaced with deferrals. This indicates that that argument is being skipped and will be applied later. The partial application will evaluate to a new function that takes in the skipped arguments and outputs the result of the original function applied to *all* arguments.

The deferral cannot synthesize to or analyze against any type. This is fine, as the only place it can exist (without being wrapped in an expression hole) is in an n-tuple literal that is being applied to a function that takes an n-tuple as input.

During elaboration, the partial application is replaced with a new function literal that takes in the unapplied arguments, then inserts them where they belong in the application of the original function. This process is the expansion of the sugar that was described in the first paragraph. Since this is all just sugar, the internal expression language doesn't have to be modified at all.

### Examples

```
val f: ('a, 'b, 'c) → 'd
val x: 'a
val y: 'b
val z: 'c
```
|External Expression|Internal Expression|Synthesized Type|
|:--|:--|:--|
|`f (x, y, z)`|`f (x, y, z)`|`'d`|
|`f (x, ~, z)`|`λb.{f (x, b, z)}`|`'b → 'd`|
|`f (~, y, ~)`|`λ(a, c).{f (a, y, c)}`|`('a, 'c) → 'd`|
|`f (~, ~, ~)`|`λ(a, b, c).{f (a, b, c)}`|`('a, 'b, 'c) → 'd`|

If anyone has a better idea of what to do in these cases, let me know.

title: Draw continuous err hole border in result box
body: Fixes https://github.com/hazelgrove/hazel/issues/485. Our old `DHCode` generated vdom from `DHLayout` in the straightforward naive way, where annotations in `DHLayout` were translated into vdom class annotations. This would cause discontinuous borders on layout nodes spanning multiple lines. This PR modifies `DHCode` so that it produces a separate layer of decorations along with the code text. Currently the only such decorations are err holes; other decorations are either just text decorations (e.g. bold a delimiter, gray out an elided case clause) or always decorate a single line layout node (e.g. a border around a free var) and thus can be left under the existing annotation->class procedure.

title: Smyth sketch-sensitive
body:
Currently, smyth is not entirely sketch-sensitive: the synthesizer keeps track of some state, which is not entirely recoverable from a sketch. This means that, even though a sketch is an intermediate step towards a solution, the synthesizer might not find that solution when starting from that sketch, because it lacks the relevant state.
A solution to this problem is to use the same state during type checking and store it in the holes so that its available to the synthesizer.

Ideally, the synthesizer should be monotone in the sense that adding more relevant information should not hamper the synthesis. It is not clear whether this is possible or general. More assertions could lead to timeouts and some intermediate states are nonsensical (e.g. `?? ??`).

title: User defined operators
body:
This adds expression level user-defined operators into Hazel. Some important tidbits of information for testing these changes:
- Precedence and associativity of operators are determined by the first operator in the user op (though the next thing-to-do is determining precedence by looking at each operator in the user op). 
- Operators are defined in let patterns by constructing on top of wildcards, and currently must be surrounded in underscores in order for them to be used as binary operators in expressions. (Future work could be to customize fixity like in Agda).
- User operators are constructed in expressions by constructing operators on top of hazel-defined operators (e.g. <+>+    -->    ++). 
- Type checking of user ops is the same as for 2-ary functions.

This PR also attempts to standardize the precedence of type level operators. Please verify the "type precedence test" in `SkelParserTests.re`.

title: Num op prediction
body:
Currently, the user has to manually input a `Float` type operator if they wish to perform some operation on two `Float` types.\
However, we suggest a type prediction system for operators where the user's input for an operator will be converted match the context.\
This idea can later be expanded to other types as well.
* Current behavior
    ```
    2.| -> 2. +|
    2.| 3. -> 2. +| 3.
    3| -> 3 +|
    2.| 1 -> 2. +| 1
    ```
* New behavior
    ```
    2.| -> 2. +.|
    2.| 3. -> 2. +.| 3.
    3| -> 3 +|
    2.| 1 -> 2. +.| 1
    ```

In predicting the operator type, we will use a four step rule.
"Type of interest" will denote the types of the arguments that is being considered to determine the appropriate operator to construct given an input.
1. If the edited expression is in an analytical position that is either `Int` or `Float`, the operator of the corresponding type will be used. 
2. When synthesizing, the type of the operand which the operator construction action was called from will be used to predict the operator type, if the operand type is a type of interest.
3. If the operand from which the operator construction was called is an empty hole, the type of the opposing operand will be used to predict the operator type, if this latter type is a type of interest.
4. In the case that neither arguments of the operator is of the type of interest, the "default" operator will be used, which will be the `Int` operator in the case of `Int` and `Float` operators.

Additional Examples
```
let i:Int = 2. | 3. in ... -> let i:Int = 2. +| 3. in ...
2.| 3 -> 2. +.| 3
3| 2. -> 3 +| 2.
3.|_ -> 3. +| _
true | true -> true +| true
```

**Current interface**

https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/47135468/124396382-c9009680-dd3b-11eb-96e1-1a96f98ed14b.mov

**Altered interface**

https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/47135468/124396391-d0c03b00-dd3b-11eb-9fe0-0052a90bfe8e.mov

title: Create proper unfocused state in Program, clean up settings
body:
Previously Hazel programs didn't have a proper unfocused state. You could set the focused/unfocused flag on a program, but it still retained a zexp. This meant that cursor dependent editor services would display information out of sync with the editor. This PR introduces a proper unfocused state in which programs may contain an unfocused uhexp instead of a zexp. In addition to resolve in the aforementioned out-of-sync issue, this also lays necessary foundations for upcoming livelits changes in which a livelit needs to be able to clear the cursor as it sets splice contents.

At the root of these changes is a new `Program.EditState.t` datatype:
```
type term =
  | Unfocused(UHExp.t)
  | Focused(ZExp.t)
type t = {
  term,
  ty: HTyp.t,
  u_gen: MetaVarGen.t,
}
```
This datatype takes over the role previously played by `Statics.edit_state`.

As part of this change, I also performed the following housekeeping tasks:
- organized all of our settings (e.g. measure performance, configure evaluation) into a `Settings` module; renamed `OptionsPanel` to `SettingsPanel` (closes https://github.com/hazelgrove/hazel/issues/351)
- moved all pretty printing related modules in hazelweb, which we have discussed doing already and was induced by the need for dhdocs to take settings

@PPER please review changes relevant to undo history. Currently undo history assumes that every edit state has a cursor. Now that this is not the case, some care has to be taken such that only cursor-carrying edit states are pushed onto the undo history. Currently this is accomplished by raising exceptions anytime this invariant is broken. I think undo history should be refactored in the future to contain explicit zexps or something along those lines. In the meantime, let me know if you see a better way to handle the new unfocused states.

@hannahpotter this will likely affect your cursor inspector changes

title: Type annotations for operands in patterns
body:
This adds a new annotation form, which can be used to annotate operands in patterns with an explicit type. This serves as a generic replacement for the optional type field attached to letlines, lambdas, and case patterns. As with those previous cases, an annotation can be added using by inserting a `:`.

One complication with entry is that commas are now overloaded in patterns when inserted at the end of a type annotation; does `,` signify a pattern-level tuple or a type-level one? We default to a pattern-level tuple; type-level tuples at the type/pattern syntactic interface must be surrounded by parentheses. More generally, any operator which has both pattern- and type-level instances will be interpreted on the pattern-level, though there are currently no other such cases.
